stories.title: The First Baseball Game
stories.blurb: On June 19, 1846, the New York Nine beat Alexander Cartwright's Knickerbockers 23 to 1 in four innings at the Elysian Fields in Hoboken, in the first recorded game under the Knickerbocker rules.
music: Tarantelle Op.43, Frederic Chopin, Musopen recording, CC0, via Internet Archive
https://archive.org/details/musopen-chopin

stories.title: Where the Name Hoboken Comes From
stories.blurb: A 1630 patent describes a tract called Hobocan Hacking. Sources disagree on the origin: a Lenape term often translated as land of the tobacco pipe, or a Dutch village near Antwerp.
music: Mazurka Op. 59 no. 2 in A flat major, Frederic Chopin, Musopen recording, CC0, via Internet Archive
https://archive.org/details/musopen-chopin

stories.title: The First Steam Ferry
stories.blurb: On October 11, 1811, John Stevens's steamboat Juliana began ferry service between Manhattan and Hoboken, the first steam-powered ferry and first commercial ferry service in the US.
music: Fugue in A minor B. 144, Frederic Chopin, Musopen recording, CC0, via Internet Archive
https://archive.org/details/musopen-chopin

stories.title: The Terminal and Its Clock
stories.blurb: Hoboken Terminal opened in 1907, a Beaux Arts building designed by Kenneth Murchison, with a 225-foot clock tower. The tower came down in the 1940s and was restored and relit in May 2008.
music: Nocturne Op. 32 no. 1 in B major, Frederic Chopin, Musopen recording, CC0, via Internet Archive
https://archive.org/details/musopen-chopin

stories.title: Heaven, Hell or Hoboken
stories.blurb: In World War I the government made Hoboken the main port for the American Expeditionary Forces, and more than three million soldiers passed through. Pershing's promise was victory by Christmas 1917 or "Heaven, Hell or Hoboken."
music: Polonaise B.13In BFlat Minor, Frederic Chopin, Musopen recording, CC0, via Internet Archive
https://archive.org/details/musopen-chopin

stories.title: Frank Sinatra's Block
stories.blurb: Sinatra was born in Hoboken in 1915 and grew up in a small building on Monroe Street that has been demolished. A bronze star was set into the sidewalk where he was born in 1996.
music: Mazurka Op. 59 no. 3 in F sharp minor, Frederic Chopin, Musopen recording, CC0, via Internet Archive
https://archive.org/details/musopen-chopin

stories.title: On the Waterfront
stories.blurb: The 1954 film On the Waterfront was shot on location, mostly in Hoboken, with Marlon Brando as Terry Malloy. Brando won his first Academy Award for it.
music: Nocturne Op. 32 no. 2 in A flat major, Frederic Chopin, Musopen recording, CC0, via Internet Archive
https://archive.org/details/musopen-chopin

stories.title: The Smell of Coffee
stories.blurb: The Maxwell House plant at Hudson and Eleventh Streets filled Hoboken with the smell of roasting coffee for about fifty years. The closure was announced in 1990, and the site was later redeveloped as condominiums.
music: Prelude Op. 28 no. 1, Frederic Chopin, Musopen recording, CC0, via Internet Archive
https://archive.org/details/musopen-chopin

stories.title: Carlo's Bake Shop
stories.blurb: Carlo's Bake Shop opened in 1910, started by an Italian immigrant baker named Carlo. Bartolo Valastro bought it in 1964, and his son Buddy later became the Cake Boss on TV.
music: Mazurka Op. 7 no. 3 in F minor, Frederic Chopin, Musopen recording, CC0, via Internet Archive
https://archive.org/details/musopen-chopin

stories.title: Leo's Grandevous
stories.blurb: Leo's Grandevous was founded in 1939 by Leo and Tessie and is run by their descendants as one of Hoboken's oldest family-owned restaurants. Sinatra grew up in the tenement next door.
music: Mazurka Op. 7 no. 4 in A flat major, Frederic Chopin, Musopen recording, CC0, via Internet Archive
https://archive.org/details/musopen-chopin

stories.title: Twenty-Three Days as Mayor
stories.blurb: In July 2009 Peter Cammarano became the mayor of Hoboken. Less than a month later the FBI arrested him on charges of taking $25,000 in cash bribes from an undercover witness. He pleaded guilty and was sentenced to 24 months in prison.

stories.title: The Cigar Girl
stories.blurb: In July 1841 a young New York woman named Mary Rogers told her fiance she was visiting relatives in New Jersey. Three days later her body was found floating in the Hudson near Sybil's Cave in Hoboken. The papers called her the Beautiful Cigar Girl and her death became a national sensation. It was never officially solved.
stories.flag: Poe's link to the case comes from the Smithsonian headline and Wikipedia.

stories.title: The Raid at Paulus Hook
stories.blurb: On August 19, 1779, 23-year-old Major Henry Lee, called Light Horse Harry, led about 300 Americans in a night raid on the British-held fort at Paulus Hook. They took 158 prisoners with few losses.
music: Polonaise B.1In GMinor, Frederic Chopin, Musopen recording, CC0, via Internet Archive

stories.title: Jackie Robinson's First Game
stories.blurb: On April 18, 1946, Jackie Robinson played his first game in Organized Baseball at Roosevelt Stadium for the Montreal Royals against the Jersey City Giants. He hit a three-run homer, scored four runs, drove in four and stole two bases.
music: Symphony No.3In EFlat Major Eroica Op.55-1.Allegro C, Ludwig van Beethoven, Musopen recording, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Internet Archive

stories.title: The Blast at Black Tom
stories.blurb: At 2:08 a.m. on July 30, 1916, a munitions depot on Black Tom Island was sabotaged. The blasts were felt as far away as Maryland and damaged the Statue of Liberty's skirt and torch.
music: Nocturne Op. 48 no. 1 in C minor, Frederic Chopin, Musopen recording, CC0, via Internet Archive

stories.title: The Colgate Clock
stories.blurb: The octagonal Colgate Clock is 50 feet across and was set going at noon on December 1, 1924. In 1985 it was moved about 1,300 feet south.
music: Nocturne Op. 48 no. 2 in F sharp minor, Frederic Chopin, Musopen recording, CC0, via Internet Archive
https://archive.org/details/musopen-chopin

stories.title: Loew's Jersey Theatre
stories.blurb: Marcus Loew built five Wonder Theatres in 1929. The fourth opened September 28 in Journal Square, designed by architects George and C. W. Rapp, and it has since been restored.
music: Nocturne Op. 55 no. 1 in F minor, Frederic Chopin, Musopen recording, CC0, via Internet Archive
https://archive.org/details/musopen-chopin

stories.title: The Terminal at Liberty State Park
stories.blurb: The Central Railroad of New Jersey built its harbor terminal in 1889, part of the largest railroad complex in the New York Harbor region. It was listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1975.
music: Nocturne Op. 55 no. 2 in E flat major, Frederic Chopin, Musopen recording, CC0, via Internet Archive
https://archive.org/details/musopen-chopin

stories.title: The Hudson Tubes
stories.blurb: An 1880 blow-out during tunnel construction killed 20 workers and stalled the project. William McAdoo restarted it in 1901, and on February 25, 1908 President Theodore Roosevelt sent a telegram to start the power. The line became PATH.
music: Nocturne Op. 62 no. 2 in E major, Frederic Chopin, Musopen recording, CC0, via Internet Archive
https://archive.org/details/musopen-chopin

stories.title: Ellis Island Is Mostly New Jersey
stories.blurb: On May 26, 1998 the Supreme Court ruled 6 to 3 that the filled-in part of Ellis Island belongs to New Jersey. New York keeps the original 3.3 acres and New Jersey has the other 24.
music: Nocturne Op. 9 no. 2 in E flat major, Frederic Chopin, Musopen recording, CC0, via Internet Archive
https://archive.org/details/musopen-chopin

stories.title: Laico's, Fifty Years of Red Sauce
stories.blurb: Laico's Italian Restaurant opened in 1972. In 2022 the city council passed a resolution celebrating its 50th anniversary, and a food critic called it one of the last red-sauce joints in town.
music: Valse, Frederic Chopin, Musopen recording, CC0, via Internet Archive
https://archive.org/details/musopen-chopin

stories.title: Liberty State Park
stories.blurb: Liberty State Park is less than 2,000 feet from the Statue of Liberty. It was railroad yards and factories before it was a park, and a Dutch ferry ran here in 1661.
music: Nocturne Op.72No.1In EMinor, Frederic Chopin, Musopen recording, CC0, via Internet Archive
https://archive.org/details/musopen-chopin

stories.title: Bobby J
stories.blurb: Robert Janiszewski, called Bobby J, was the Hudson County executive, based in Jersey City. In 2002 he pleaded guilty to taking more than $100,000 in bribes. He then worked undercover for the FBI, the highest-ranking elected official in state history to do so.
music: Goldberg Variations, BWV. 988 - Variation 6. Canon on the second, Johann Sebastian Bach, Musopen Kickstarter recording, Public Domain Mark, via Internet Archive
https://archive.org/details/musopen-dvd-in-lossless-flac-format

stories.title: The Mayor and the Marina
stories.blurb: In December 1991 a federal jury convicted Jersey City Mayor Gerald McCann. He had been charged with defrauding a Florida savings bank of at least $267,000 it put into a marina deal with him. The jury found him guilty on 15 counts.

stories.title: The Duel on the Ledge
stories.blurb: On July 11, 1804, Alexander Hamilton and Aaron Burr met on a ledge below the Weehawken cliffs in the most famous duel in American history. Hamilton was mortally wounded and died the following day.
music: Nocturne Op.9No.1In BFlat Minor, Frederic Chopin, Musopen recording, CC0, via Internet Archive
https://archive.org/details/musopen-chopin

stories.title: Eighteen Duels
stories.blurb: At least eighteen duels were fought below the Palisades at Weehawken between 1700 and 1884. The spot could only be reached from the river.

https://archive.org/details/musopen-chopin

stories.title: The Rock and the Moved Boulder
stories.blurb: A red sandstone boulder says Hamilton rested his head there. In 1870 railroad tracks went through the old dueling grounds, the boulder was moved to Hamilton Street, and the ledge was quarried away.
music: Nocturne Op27No2, Frederic Chopin, Musopen recording, CC0, via Internet Archive
https://archive.org/details/musopen-chopin

stories.title: The Bronze Bust
stories.blurb: In 1935 a bronze bust of Alexander Hamilton was set up on the rock in Weehawken, sculpted by the Italian-born artist John Rapetti.
music: Prelude Op. 28 no. 10, Frederic Chopin, Musopen recording, CC0, via Internet Archive
https://archive.org/details/musopen-chopin

stories.title: The First Lincoln Tunnel Tube
stories.blurb: The first tube of the Lincoln Tunnel opened on December 22, 1937 after three years and seven months of work. It was the world's first mechanically ventilated underwater tunnel and carried one lane each way.
music: Prelude Op. 28 no. 11, Frederic Chopin, Musopen recording, CC0, via Internet Archive
https://archive.org/details/musopen-chopin

stories.title: Three Tubes
stories.blurb: The north tube opened on February 1, 1945 and the south tube on May 25, 1957, giving the tunnel thirteen toll lanes in total.
music: Prelude Op. 28 no. 12, Frederic Chopin, Musopen recording, CC0, via Internet Archive
https://archive.org/details/musopen-chopin

stories.title: Miracle on the Hudson, From the Weehawken Side
stories.blurb: On January 15, 2009, Captain Carl Lucas was readying the ferry Athenia in Weehawken when US Airways Flight 1549 landed in the Hudson. The first ferry reached the plane within three minutes, and 14 boats pulled 135 people from the water.

stories.title: The Water Tower
stories.blurb: The Weehawken Water Tower was built in 1883 for the Hackensack Water Company. It stands 175 feet tall, and the complex is on the National Register of Historic Places.
music: Prelude Op. 28 no. 13, Frederic Chopin, Musopen recording, CC0, via Internet Archive
https://archive.org/details/musopen-chopin

stories.title: Weehawken Terminal
stories.blurb: The West Shore Railroad opened Weehawken Terminal in 1884 with five ferry slips and sixteen passenger tracks. The last ferry, named Weehawken, left at 1:10 a.m. on March 25, 1959. The site is now Port Imperial.

stories.title: Where the Name Comes From
stories.blurb: Weehawken is a Lenape name, often translated as "rocks that look like trees." Henry Hudson docked in Weehawken Cove in 1609.

stories.title: The Weehawken Mayor
stories.blurb: In December 1983 a federal jury found the former mayor of Weehawken, Wally Lindsley, guilty of conspiracy to extort.

stories.title: The Bayonne Bridge Opens
stories.blurb: The Bayonne Bridge opened on November 15, 1931, three weeks after the George Washington Bridge. Its 1,675-foot steel arch was the longest of its type in the world for 46 years, and it replaced a ferry.

stories.title: Raising the Roadway
stories.blurb: Big container ships could not fit under the bridge, so the Port Authority raised the roadway. The first cars used the new elevated roadway at 5 a.m. in February 2017, 215 feet above the water, and the old lower deck was removed that June.
music: Prelude Op. 28 no. 16, Frederic Chopin, Musopen recording, CC0, via Internet Archive

stories.title: The Bayonne Bleeder
stories.blurb: Chuck Wepner grew up in Bayonne and was nicknamed the Bayonne Bleeder. In March 1975 he fought Muhammad Ali for the heavyweight title and went 15 rounds. His story helped inspire the movie Rocky.

stories.title: George R. R. Martin, a Kid From Bayonne
stories.blurb: George R. R. Martin was born in Bayonne in 1948. He wrote A Song of Ice and Fire, the book series behind HBO's Game of Thrones.

stories.title: Standard Oil on the Peninsula
stories.blurb: In 1877 Standard Oil took over a small refinery on the Bayonne waterfront. By the 1920s it was the city's largest employer, with more than 6,000 workers.

stories.title: The Naval Drydock
stories.blurb: The Navy opened a repair base off Bayonne in 1942 with the largest dry dock on the East Coast. It repaired Essex-class carriers and Iowa-class battleships, ran under the Navy until 1967 and the Army until 1999, and cruise ships leave from there today.

stories.blurb: Bayonne began as Bergen Neck. It became its own township in 1861, named for Bayonne Avenue, today's 33rd Street, and joined five villages into one.

stories.blurb: The Bayonne Golf Club is a links-style course on a 150-acre site on the Hudson, designed by developer Eric Bergstol and unveiled in 2006. A Rutgers turfgrass expert called building it an audacious and improbable journey.

stories.title: Little Scotland
stories.blurb: In 1875, the Clark Thread Company of Paisley, Scotland, opened two mills in Kearny. Thousands of Scottish immigrants followed. Soon afterward, another Scottish company, Nairn Linoleum, built a factory, and the town became a little Scotland. By the 1920s, streetcar conductors would call out "Paisley Cross" at the center of town, because so many residents came from Paisley. Scottish butcher shops in Kearny still sell steak pies, black pudding, bridies and shortbread. In 1992, the New York Times reported that the Scottish community had dwindled to about ten percent of the town's 35,000 people.

stories.title: The Schuyler Copper Mine
stories.blurb: In 1710, Captain Arent Schuyler bought a tract of land in what is now Kearny, for 300 English pounds. Shortly afterward, a strange green stone was found there. It turned out to be eighty percent copper. Schuyler opened a copper mine. It brought the first steam engine in America from England. The engineer was Josiah Hornblower. The engine and the mines were destroyed by fire in 1772. In September of 1777, General Henry Clinton chose the Schuyler Mansion as his headquarters during a British raid. The mansion stood until 1924, when a land development company tore it down.

stories.title: The Beehive of Industry
stories.blurb: Harrison is known as the Beehive of Industry. In 1912, President William Howard Taft visited. He told the crowds, "You have reason to be proud of this Hive of Industry." That gave the town its motto. The factories included Edison Lamp Works, Worthington Pump, Otis Elevator, and the Peter Hauck Brewery. RCA bought its Harrison plant in 1930, and it became RCA's main maker of receiving tubes. During both world wars, the town's factories ran twenty-four hours a day in three shifts. At the peak in World War Two, the town had about 14,000 residents, and 90,000 workers commuting in each day.

stories.title: The Birth of New Jersey's Smallest Borough
stories.blurb: In the spring of 1895, a group of citizens in Kearny's First Ward felt their local government was ignoring them. Led by a lawyer named Edward Kenny, they petitioned the county court on June 4 to hold a special election on forming their own borough. The judge approved it on June 20. On July 2, 1895, residents voted at poles set up at John Keenan's store. The vote created the Borough of East Newark, the smallest borough in New Jersey. Kenny became its first mayor, and was known as "The Father of East Newark." Legend says he made a midnight run to Trenton in a horse-drawn coach to get the law passed. The borough's own history says fact mixes with legend in that account.

stories.title: Two Thread Giants Side by Side
stories.blurb: In 1884, a description of East Newark's mills said the Clark Thread Company works were the surprise and wonder of residents and visitors, because of the huge proportions of the buildings. Right next to them stood another thread giant, the Clark Mile-End Spool-Cotton Company, organized in 1883. It employed seven to eight hundred people. The parent of the Clark works was the Anchor Mills, in Paisley, Scotland. In 1899, a company called Spool Cotton Company took over the United States sales of three brands: Coats Cotton Spool, Clark's O.N.T., and Mile End. At its peak, Clark Thread employed 3,000 people.

stories.title: The Borough That Seceded From Kearny
stories.blurb: East Newark is the smallest borough in New Jersey. It covers just sixty-four acres. Until eighteen ninety-five, it was part of Kearny. In the late spring of eighteen ninety-five, citizens of Kearny's First Ward decided they had been neglected. A lawyer named Edward Kenny led them. On June fourth, they asked the county court to allow a vote on forming a new borough. The election was held on July second, eighteen ninety-five. The vote was two hundred seventy-six in favor and fifty-seven against. People took to the streets and cheered, hats were tossed in the air, and a brass band paraded through the borough. Edward Kenny became the first mayor. According to legend, his drive for the new borough included a midnight run to Trenton by horse-drawn coach. The borough site says it is not known whether that really happened. [Petition and vote details come from one source, the borough website.]

Mail sent from Harrison could take five days to arrive, because it went to Newark first. Federal letters said the borough was already included in Newark's application for aid. Mayor Wilbert Hotaling and the council formed a committee to poll residents. Some people suggested Libertyville or Truman. One resident said to just spell East Newark backwards. It was even called the nation's summer capital, because of how often and how long Ulysses Grant visited. The first Monmouth Park racetrack opened on July 30, 1870, on land between Eatontown and Oceanport. Its grandstand seated about 7,000 people. At least 2,000 seats were empty on opening day, and President Grant was absent. Then Grant bought a box. By 1872, a record crowd of 25,000 watched the Monmouth Cup. A bigger Monmouth Park opened on July 4, 1890, on about 600 acres. It was said to be the largest racetrack in the world. It closed for good after the 1893 season, because New Jersey outlawed most forms of gambling in 1894.

His love of the ocean decided where he would go. On September sixth, he was taken to the Francklyn Cottage at Elberon. Railroad ties were laid to build a rail spur from the Elberon depot to the cottage. He died there on September nineteenth, eighteen eighty-one.

stories.title: The Organ Built for the Great Auditorium
stories.blurb: The Great Auditorium in Ocean Grove holds a famous pipe organ. It was built by Robert Hope-Jones, an Englishman who came to America in nineteen oh three. Ocean Grove's association says he is credited with ninety percent of the industry's organ innovations in the first decade of the twentieth century. It was the first and most famous instrument he built in America. The association dates it to nineteen oh seven. The Garden State Theatre Organ Society says it was installed in nineteen oh eight for twenty-six thousand dollars, half of it donated by the Hope-Jones company. The organ has since been rebuilt and expanded. Dr. Gordon Turk has been its organist for over fifty years.

stories.title: The Horn at Holmdel
stories.blurb: On a hill in Holmdel stands a big metal horn. In 1965 two radio astronomers, Arno Penzias and Robert Wilson, kept hearing a faint hiss in it that would not go away. It turned out to be the leftover glow of the universe from the Big Bang. They won the Nobel Prize in Physics for it in 1978.

stories.title: The Hiss That Would Not Go Away
stories.blurb: The horn antenna in Holmdel was built in 1959, on Crawford Hill, for a space project called Echo. Echo used giant shiny balloons in orbit to bounce radio signals from one place on Earth to another. The horn was made of aluminum, about fifty feet long, with an opening twenty feet square, and it weighed around eighteen tons. By 1962, Bell Labs no longer needed it for Echo. So it was handed to a radio astronomer named Arno Penzias, and Robert Wilson was hired to help. They wanted to measure faint radio signals from the Milky Way. To do that, they first had to clear out every bit of noise in the system. But there was a steady hiss they could not get rid of. They checked everything. At one point they even suspected pigeon droppings inside the horn, so they shooed the birds away and cleaned it out. The hiss stayed. Then they heard that a team at Princeton, led by Robert Dicke, had been working out a theory. If the universe began in a hot Big Bang, there should be a faint leftover glow everywhere. Dicke sent them a draft of his group's paper. The hiss was not coming from the horn. It was coming from the universe. Both teams published back to back in the Astrophysical Journal in 1965. The discovery was the final blow to the rival steady-state idea of the universe. Penzias and Wilson had not been looking for the Big Bang. They shared the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1978.

stories.title: Saving the Horn
stories.blurb: In 2021, the old Bell Labs hilltop in Holmdel was sold to a developer. The property had passed from Bell Labs to Lucent, then Alcatel, then Nokia. The new owner planned housing. On that hill sat the horn antenna, a National Historic Landmark since 1989. Scientists and neighbors pushed back. A petition to turn the site into a park gathered more than 6,900 signatures by March 2023. The township stepped in. It agreed to buy the hill, about 35 acres, for $5.5 million. The seller gave $750,000 back, so the net price was $4.75 million. On January 23, 2024, Mayor Rocco Impreveduto announced that the township had filed to take the property in state court. The hill and the horn now belong to Holmdel. The park is named for Dr. Robert Wilson, a longtime Holmdel resident who helped find the Big Bang's afterglow there.

stories.title: Bell Labs Holmdel
stories.blurb: On Crawfords Corner Road in Holmdel stands a building designed by the architect Eero Saarinen. It opened as the Bell Labs complex in 1962. Saarinen died the year before it was completed. The National Park Service says the building was constructed between 1959 and 1966, with grounds designed by Hideo Sasaki. From 1959 to 2007, it was a research and development center for Bell Laboratories and, later, Alcatel-Lucent. Work there related to radio astronomy, the transistor, lasers and physics. It was listed on the National Register of Historic Places on June 26, 2017. Today the building is called Bell Works, it sits beside a man-made lake, and it holds the town's public library.

stories.title: The Engineer Who Heard the Milky Way
stories.blurb: In the early nineteen thirties, an engineer named Karl Jansky built a large rotating antenna at Bell Telephone Laboratories in Holmdel. He was studying radio noise. He found that some of it came from the Milky Way. It was the beginning of radio astronomy. He published his detection in nineteen thirty-three. The New York Times covered it, and assured readers that the signals did not seem to come from extraterrestrial beings. The importance of his discovery was not recognized until many years later. Jansky was reassigned to other work. He died in nineteen fifty, at forty-four.

stories.title: The Horn Antenna and the Hiss From the Beginning of Time
stories.blurb: At Bell Labs in Holmdel, a twenty-foot horn-shaped antenna was built to work with the Echo satellite system. In nineteen sixty-four and sixty-five, radio astronomers Arno Penzias and Robert Wilson used it to map signals from the Milky Way. They kept hearing a steady noise from every direction. They ruled out the Milky Way and other space sources. They ruled out interference from New York City, and dismissed military testing. The noise was the cosmic microwave background, strong evidence for the Big Bang. The antenna became a National Historic Landmark on December twentieth, nineteen eighty-nine.

stories.title: The Twin Lights
stories.blurb: High above the water in Highlands stand the Twin Lights. The two towers were built in 1862. In 1899, Guglielmo Marconi showed off his wireless telegraph there.

stories.title: Marconi at the Twin Lights
stories.blurb: In 1899, a twenty-five-year-old Italian inventor named Guglielmo Marconi came to America. James Gordon Bennett Jr., who owned the New York Herald, had invited him to cover a boat race. Marconi put a transmitter aboard the passenger ship Ponce and an antenna mast on the grounds of the Twin Lights, in Highlands. On September 30, 1899, he used it to report the victorious return of Commodore George Dewey from Manila Bay. On October 3, the same apparatus reported the America's Cup races between Shamrock and Columbia, off Sandy Hook. In 1909, Marconi received the Nobel Prize in physics.

stories.title: A Town of Its Own, Highlands 1900 to 1920
stories.blurb: Highlands became its own town in March of 1900. Nine months later, it had its first fire company. It got its first police force in 1903, and its post office in 1904. Bay Avenue was first paved in 1913. By 1915, the borough hall was served by the railroad. And in 1917, Bahrs Landing opened at the water's edge.

stories.title: The Twin Lights and the Brightest Beam in America
stories.blurb: The Twin Lights stand on a promontory in Highlands, overlooking Sandy Hook. They were established in eighteen twenty-eight. The two towers kept sailors from confusing the station with the Sandy Hook light about five miles north. In eighteen forty-one, the first Fresnel lens used in this country was installed there. In eighteen sixty-two, new brownstone towers were lit. In eighteen ninety-eight, an electric arc lamp and a lens weighing over seven tons made it the first major lighthouse in the United States to use electric light. Its beam could be seen for twenty-two miles. Under certain conditions, it could be seen reflecting in the night sky seventy miles away.

stories.title: The Highlands Gold Rush
stories.blurb: In April of nineteen forty-eight, a lobsterman found a gold coin in the sand at the foot of Cedar Street in Highlands. It was about the size of a half-dollar. There were more nearby. For days, business in town stopped, as locals and outsiders sifted the sand, hunting for Captain Kidd's lost treasure. A considerable number of valuable collectors' coins were recovered. But Kidd was hanged in seventeen oh one, and most of the coins carried dates of seventeen thirty or later. The local history says they most likely came from the treasure chest of H.M.S. Looe, a British frigate that dragged her anchor and went ashore in the lower bay in seventeen forty-four.

stories.title: The Puritans Who Built Newark
stories.blurb: Newark began in May of 1666, when a band of Puritan families from Connecticut landed on the shore of the Passaic River and began building. Their leader was Captain Robert Treat. Treat had been born in England, settled in Milford, and became a local magistrate. The group came from the New Haven Colony, and they left for a reason. New Haven had been merged with a more liberal neighbor, Connecticut. The Puritans of New Haven wanted to keep political power in the hands of members of their own church. Under the merger, they were about to lose that power to people outside their church. So they moved to New Jersey and built a town where they could run things their way. In Newark, Treat became the town's magistrate and town clerk. He is said to have helped lay out Broad Street, still the widest street in the city. The church at the center of the settlement is today's Old First Church, on Broad Street near Branford, the mother church of New Jersey Presbyterians.

stories.title: The First Great Airport
stories.blurb: In October of 1928, Newark opened the first major airport in the New York area. The city built it on sixty-eight acres of marshland. It grew fast. The Port Authority says it quickly became the world's busiest commercial airport. The National Park Service says that in the early years, one-third of the world's air traffic passed down its runways. During World War Two the Army Air Corps ran it. In 1948, the Port Authority took over, and it added an instrument runway, a terminal building, a control tower and an air cargo center. Today it is Newark Liberty International, owned by the cities of Newark and Elizabeth.

stories.title: Everything in Newark Was for Sale
stories.blurb: Hugh Addonizio was the mayor of Newark from 1962 to 1970. Before that, he served in Congress. In 1970, a federal jury found him and four other defendants guilty on sixty-four counts, sixty-three of extortion and one of conspiracy. He was convicted of sharing in $1.5 million in extorted kickbacks from contractors on city water and sewer lines. On September 22, 1970, the judge, George Barlow, sentenced Addonizio to ten years in prison and a $25,000 fine. He said the crimes had torn at the very heart of our civilized society and our form of representative government. Addonizio served sixty-two months and died in 1981. One of the prosecutors, Garrett Brown Jr., later said there was a sense that everything in Newark was for sale at the time, and it was.

stories.title: Six Days in July, 1967
stories.blurb: On July 12, 1967, Newark police arrested a Black cab driver named John Smith, after he drove around a police car and double-parked. Civil rights leaders saw that he was hurt and demanded he go to a hospital. Rumors spread that he had died. That night, crowds gathered outside the Fourth Precinct. After midnight, Molotov cocktails were thrown at the building. At two-twenty in the morning, Mayor Hugh Addonizio asked Governor Richard Hughes to send in the National Guard. More than three thousand Guardsmen and five hundred state troopers came into the city. The violence lasted until July 17. Twenty-six people were killed, and hundreds were hurt. It was the worst civil disorder in New Jersey history. Historians point to causes that had built for years. Residents of the Central Ward feared losing their homes to a planned medical school on a hundred and fifty acres. And there were repeated complaints of police misconduct.

stories.title: The Cherry Trees of Branch Brook Park
stories.blurb: Branch Brook Park in Newark was the first county park in the United States. It is nearly four miles long, and it is named for a small brook that ran through the valley to the Passaic River. The famous Olmsted landscape firm began designing it in 1898. The cherry trees came later. Caroline Bamberger Fuld, whose brother ran Bamberger's Department Store, had seen the cherry blossoms in Washington, D.C. She set out to create a display in Essex County that would rival the capital's. The plan was drawn up in 1928, with about twenty-two hundred trees of more than twenty kinds. The planting was finished in 1932. Today the park has more than four thousand cherry trees, more in number and variety than Washington's display, according to Essex County Parks. At its height, the blossom festival draws more than ten thousand people a day.

stories.title: The Man Who Made Patent Leather
stories.blurb: Seth Boyden was born on a farm in Massachusetts in 1788 and moved to Newark in the 1810s. He became one of America's great early inventors. In 1819 he copied a secret European method of putting a glossy lacquer on leather. He set up the first factory in the United States to make patent leather, the shiny stuff of dress shoes. Then, in 1826, after six years of trying, he produced his first casting of malleable iron, a tough iron that bends instead of breaking. The Franklin Institute honored him for it two years later. He also built locomotives and steam engines, and he is credited with making the first daguerreotype in the United States. But he cared little about getting rich. He moved on to new experiments instead.

stories.title: The Ironbound and Ferry Street
stories.blurb: Ferry Street in Newark's Ironbound is a mile long, and it started as a road for ferries. In 1765 the colonial legislature chartered it as Old Ferry Road, to connect the ferries bringing goods from Manhattan and Jersey City to Newark's market. Ever since, it has been a landing place for newcomers, first Portuguese and Spanish, and more recently people from across Latin America. Since the 1970s, its Portuguese and Spanish restaurants have drawn visitors from all over. Within one block you can find Spanish paella, Brazilian rodizio, Portuguese custard tarts and Ecuadorian ceviche. One of the best-known places, Fornos of Spain, opened nearly a hundred years ago as a small pizzeria called Cortese, according to nj.com. In the 1970s a Portuguese family bought it and renamed it Fornos, Portuguese for ovens. In 1980, two new owners added "of Spain." People still go for the patatas bravas and the grilled octopus.

stories.title: Whitney Houston's Newark
stories.blurb: Whitney Houston was born in Newark on August 9, 1963. Her mother was the gospel and soul singer Cissy Houston, and her cousin was Dionne Warwick. She grew up singing at New Hope Baptist Church in Newark. Her family moved to East Orange when she was seven, but the church stayed her musical home. At fourteen, at the Town Hall, she got her first standing ovation for a solo. In 1983, Arista Records signed her. The New Jersey Hall of Fame says she went on to sell more than two hundred million recordings and win eight Grammy Awards. It was a long way from the choir loft in Newark.

stories.title: Longie Zwillman, King of Newark's Underworld
stories.blurb: Abner Zwillman, called Longie, became one of the most powerful underworld figures in the country. During Prohibition he smuggled whiskey into New Jersey. In 1956 he was tried for income tax evasion, but the jury deadlocked. Afterward, several of his associates were charged with trying to bribe jurors. On February 26, 1959, he was found dead at his home in West Orange. He was fifty-four. There is another side to his story. From 1933 to 1941, he founded a group called the New Jersey Minutemen, an anti-fascist group that fought the pro-Nazi German American Bund in Newark.

stories.title: Philip Roth and Weequahic High
stories.blurb: Philip Roth was born in Newark on March 19, 1933. He grew up in the Weequahic section of the city, and he graduated from Weequahic High School. Many of his stories came back to Newark and to middle-class life there. His first book, "Goodbye, Columbus," a collection of short stories, won the National Book Award. His first full-length novel, "Letting Go," came out in 1962. Seven years later came "Portnoy's Complaint." In it, he named real Newark places, including Weequahic High School, the Weequahic Diner and the Newark Museum. In 1995, he won a second National Book Award, for "Sabbath's Theater." In 1997, "American Pastoral" won the Pulitzer Prize for Fiction.

stories.title: Ballantine Ale and the Three Rings
stories.blurb: Ballantine was one of Newark's great beer names. Peter Ballantine, a Scottish immigrant, started brewing in Newark in the 1840s. In 1879 the company adopted its famous three rings, a trademark meant to stand for purity, strength and flavor. By the early 1900s, the brewery was putting out more than half a million barrels a year, in plants covering twelve acres. During Prohibition it stayed open by making malt syrup. In 1933, the brothers Carl and Otto Badenhausen bought it. Ballantine became the first television sponsor of the New York Yankees. Yankees announcer Mel Allen called home runs "Ballantine blasts." At its peak, it ranked second or third in the nation. In 1972, the New York Times ran the headline "Ballantine Closing Ends Newark Era."

stories.title: The Cathedral Basilica of the Sacred Heart
stories.blurb: The Cathedral Basilica of the Sacred Heart faces Branch Brook Park in Newark. The idea began in 1859, with Newark's first bishop, James Roosevelt Bayley. Construction began in January of 1898, and the cornerstone was laid on June 11, 1899. The first design was English-Irish Gothic. In 1913, church leaders decided on French Gothic instead, in the style of Notre-Dame and Chartres. The cathedral was dedicated on October 19, 1954. According to Wikipedia, it is the fifth-largest cathedral in North America. Its thirty-six-foot rose window is the largest of its kind in the Catholic Church in the Western Hemisphere.

stories.title: How Alexander Hamilton Founded Paterson
stories.blurb: In 1791, Alexander Hamilton helped start the Society for Establishing Useful Manufactures, called S.U.M. It was a company backed by wealthy New Jersey investors, and its goal was to make goods in America. Hamilton had sent his Report on Manufactures to Congress on December 5, 1791, and that report was the spark for the society. The charter was drawn up and revised by Hamilton himself. The place they chose was the Great Falls of the Passaic River. In May of 1792, the society bought seven hundred acres above and below the falls. That purchase created the city of Paterson. The first raceway, a channel to carry water from the falls to the mills, was built in early 1794. The city was named for William Paterson, the second governor of New Jersey. It later became known as Silk City.

stories.title: Twenty-Five Thousand Silk Workers on Strike
stories.blurb: The Great Falls powered Paterson's mills, which produced nearly half of the silk in the United States. In February of 1913, the broad-silk weavers walked out. The owners wanted each worker to run four looms instead of two. Soon about twenty-five thousand workers had shut down roughly three hundred silk mills and dye houses. The strike lasted almost five months. The workers brought in organizers from the Industrial Workers of the World, including Elizabeth Gurley Flynn, Carlo Tresca and Bill Haywood. The strike headquarters was the home of Pietro Botto, and speakers addressed crowds from the second-floor porch. On June 7, more than a thousand strikers performed a pageant about the strike at Madison Square Garden in New York. But the strike was defeated, and the workers' demands were not met. Even so, the owners held back the four-loom system for another ten years.

stories.title: Hinchliffe Stadium and Larry Doby
stories.blurb: Hinchliffe Stadium in Paterson was named for Mayor John Hinchliffe. It opened on July 8, 1932. It became a home for Negro Leagues baseball, and the New York Black Yankees made it their home ground. In 1933, a game billed as the Colored Championship of the Nation was played there, and the Philadelphia Stars beat the Black Yankees. Stars who played there included Josh Gibson, Monte Irvin and Satchel Paige. And one of the players was a local. Larry Doby, from Paterson, became the first African American player in the American League in July of 1947. The Baseball Hall of Fame inducted him in 1998.

stories.title: The Submarine in the Passaic River
stories.blurb: John Philip Holland was born in Ireland in 1841. He moved to the United States in 1873 and soon came to Paterson to teach math at St. John's. He had a dream: a boat that could travel under the water. In the spring of 1878, his first boat, Holland One, was moved to Paterson. It was fourteen feet long and weighed about two and a quarter tons. He tested it in the Passaic River, launching from a boathouse above the Great Falls. On June 6, 1878, it made two runs completely underwater, at a depth of twelve feet. Afterward, the boat was sunk in the river. It lay on the bottom until 1927, when it was found and raised. Today it sits in the Paterson Museum, along with his second prototype. Navies around the world later adopted the modern submarine his work led to.

stories.title: The Colt Revolver Was Born in Paterson
stories.blurb: In 1836, Samuel Colt got a patent for a revolving pistol. To build it, he organized the Patent Arms Manufacturing Company, and he put its factory in Paterson, right below the Great Falls of the Passaic River. The Paterson works made revolving rifles first, and then the Colt Paterson revolver. It had a trigger that folded out of sight until the hammer was cocked. It was the first commercially made repeating handgun tied to Colt's name. But the business did not last. The company had failed by 1842, and the Paterson factory stopped making guns. Colt's comeback came later, when Captain Samuel Walker suggested improvements and ordered one thousand revolvers, and Colt moved production to a factory belonging to Eli Whitney Junior.

stories.title: Rubin "Hurricane" Carter, Convicted and Freed
stories.blurb: Rubin Carter was born in Clifton, New Jersey, in 1937, and grew up in Paterson. At about two-thirty in the morning on June 17, 1966, three people were shot at the Lafayette Bar and Grill in Paterson. Shortly afterward, police stopped a car carrying Carter and a young man named John Artis. In 1967, a jury convicted both men of murder, and they were given life sentences. In 1976, Bob Dylan wrote a song about the case, called "Hurricane." In 1985, a federal judge, H. Lee Sarokin, overturned the convictions, citing prosecutors' misconduct and dubious eyewitness testimony. Prosecutors declined to try the case again, and Carter walked free that November at the age of forty-eight.

stories.title: The Paterson Silk Weaver Who Shot a King
stories.blurb: In July of 1900, King Umberto the First of Italy was shot dead at Monza. The man who fired the shots, Gaetano Bresci, had been living in Paterson. Bresci was born poor in Tuscany and came to America in the 1890s. He settled in Paterson and worked in a silk weaving mill. The city was a center of radical politics among Italian immigrants, and he helped start an anarchist newspaper, La Questione Sociale. In 1898, Italian troops had fired on hungry protesters in Milan, and the king then decorated the general in charge. Bresci resolved that the king should die. He traveled to Italy, and on July 29, 1900, he shot the king three times. He was found guilty and sent to prison. He died in his cell within the year. The New York Times headline read: "Assassin's Lot Fell Upon Anarchist Here."

stories.title: Paterson's Vice President
stories.blurb: Garret Hobart was born in Long Branch on June 3, 1844. He graduated from Rutgers with honors in 1863. Then he went to Paterson to study law under a lawyer named Socrates Tuttle, and in 1869 he married Tuttle's daughter Jennie. When Tuttle was elected mayor of Paterson in 1871, he made Hobart the city attorney. Hobart went on to the state legislature and became Speaker of the Assembly in 1874. In 1896, the Republicans nominated him for vice president, though he was little known outside New Jersey. He became the twenty-fourth vice president on March 4, 1897. People called him the Assistant President. He died on November 21, 1899.

stories.title: The Great Paterson Fire of 1902
stories.blurb: On the night of February 8, 1902, a fire broke out in the trolley car sheds on Broadway in Paterson. The first alarm sounded at ten minutes past midnight on Sunday morning. It was one of the coldest nights of the winter, and winds gusting to fifty miles an hour pushed the flames through the wooden buildings. Fire companies from Jersey City and Hackensack came to help. In the end, four hundred fifty-nine buildings had been destroyed across twenty-six blocks. The losses included banks, City Hall, five churches and the Free Public Library, with its thirty-seven thousand books.

stories.title: William Carlos Williams and His Poem "Paterson"
stories.blurb: William Carlos Williams was born in Rutherford, New Jersey, on September 17, 1883. He became a doctor, a pediatrician and family doctor in Rutherford, and he was head pediatrician at Passaic General Hospital. He practiced medicine by day and wrote poems at night. His epic work "Paterson" began as an eighty-five-line poem in 1926. It grew into five volumes, published from 1946 to 1958. It was built from his trips to the city, where he wandered the streets and sat in parks catching snippets of conversation. After his death, "Paterson" won the Pulitzer Prize for poetry in 1963.

stories.title: New Jersey's First Capital
stories.blurb: Elizabeth is called New Jersey's first city. In 1664, English settlers bought a large piece of land between the Raritan and Passaic rivers from the local Indigenous people. They paid in trade goods such as wampum, cloth and tools. By 1665, there was a growing village there called Elizabethtown, named in honor of Lady Elizabeth Carteret. Under Philip Carteret, it became New Jersey's first capital, and the colony's first legislature met there in 1668. In 1855, it was officially incorporated as the City of Elizabeth.

stories.title: The Singer Sewing Machine Factory
stories.blurb: In the early 1870s, the Singer Manufacturing Company built a huge factory on the waterfront in Elizabethport, on Newark Bay. It had begun buying land there in October of 1870. On October 18, 1873, Singer moved all of its United States manufacturing there. One source calls it the largest factory in the world devoted to a single product. By 1876, Singer was making more sewing machines than all of its American competitors combined. By 1912, it had about ninety percent of the world market, according to the federal Historic American Engineering Record. During the First World War, the plant even made cannons and pistols. A court record says the workforce reached about ten thousand at its peak. In February of 1982, Singer announced it would close the plant.

stories.title: The Shot at Connecticut Farms
stories.blurb: In June of 1780, British and Hessian troops landed at Elizabethtown, planning to march toward Morristown, where George Washington's army was camped. Their target was the camp itself. They had to pass through Connecticut Farms, now part of Union. There, about fifteen hundred Continental soldiers and militia, led by General William Maxwell, fought them. During the fighting, Hannah Caldwell, the wife of the local minister, Reverend James Caldwell, stayed in her house with her younger children, a nurse and a friend. According to the accounts, a soldier fired through the window and killed her. Her death increased the resolve of the colonists to keep fighting. Sixteen days later, at the Battle of Springfield, the British tried again. When the American soldiers ran short of paper for their muskets, Reverend Caldwell gathered hymnals, and the soldiers used the pages. The British retreated, after burning Springfield.

stories.title: Boxwood Hall
stories.blurb: Boxwood Hall in Elizabeth was built around 1750 by Samuel Woodruff, who was then the mayor of Elizabethtown. From 1772 to 1795, it was the home of Elias Boudinot, who served as President of the Continental Congress in 1782 and 1783. It was during his term, on October 31, 1783, that word reached Congress that the Treaty of Paris had been signed, officially ending the Revolutionary War. A young Alexander Hamilton studied in Elizabeth in 1773 and visited the house, and he and the Boudinots stayed friends for life. George Washington was a guest there too. Jonathan Dayton, the youngest signer of the Constitution, also lived in the house. In 1938, the building was threatened with demolition. Local citizens raised money to buy it and gave it to the State of New Jersey. It has been a museum since 1947.

stories.title: Judy Blume of Elizabeth
stories.blurb: Judy Blume was born in Elizabeth, New Jersey, on February 12, 1938, as Judith Sussman. Her father was a dentist. She graduated from New York University in 1961. Her first book, "The One in the Middle Is the Green Kangaroo," came out in 1969. In 1970, she published "Are You There God? It's Me, Margaret," which was controversial for dealing with serious topics, including teenage worries and religious identity. In the 1970s, thirteen of her books reached bookstores. Her 1975 young-adult book "Forever" became a frequent target of censorship. She served on the board of the National Coalition Against Censorship. The New Jersey Hall of Fame inducted her in 2010.

stories.title: Liberty Hall and Governor Livingston
stories.blurb: In 1760, a lawyer named William Livingston bought one hundred twenty acres in what was then Elizabethtown, New Jersey. He built a fourteen-room Georgian house there and called it Liberty Hall. He and his family moved in full time in 1773. Soon the Revolution pulled him away. Livingston served in the First and Second Continental Congress, and as a brigadier general of the New Jersey militia. On August 31, 1776, he became the first elected governor of the new state of New Jersey. He also signed the United States Constitution. During the first year in the house, young Alexander Hamilton lived there with Livingston. Later, the Kean family lived there. Today it is the Liberty Hall Museum, on the campus of Kean University, in Union.

stories.title: Boxwood Hall
stories.blurb: Boxwood Hall in Elizabeth was built around 1750 by Samuel Woodruff, who was then the mayor of Elizabethtown. From 1772 to 1795, Elias Boudinot lived there. He was President of the Continental Congress in 1782 and 1783. It was during his time there, on October 31, 1783, that word reached Congress that the Treaty of Paris had been signed. In 1773, a young Alexander Hamilton studied in Elizabeth, and he visited Boxwood Hall. In April of 1789, George Washington was on his way to be inaugurated in New York City. He reached Elizabethtown on April 23, and had lunch at Boxwood Hall before being ferried to New York. In 1824, General Lafayette stayed overnight in the house.

stories.title: Singer in Elizabethport
stories.blurb: In October of 1870, the Singer Manufacturing Company began buying land on Newark Bay, in Elizabethport. On October 18, 1873, it moved all of its United States manufacturing there. It chose the spot for the waterfront, the rail lines and the shipping. During World War One, the plant made 75-millimeter cannons and .45-caliber automatic pistols. By the start of World War Two, it had 5,000 workers on a 113-acre site, with 48 buildings. From June of 1942 to July of 1945, it made no home sewing machines at all. In February of 1982, Singer announced it was shutting the plant down, with fewer than 1,000 employees left.

stories.title: The Purchase That Started Elizabeth
stories.blurb: On October twenty-eighth, sixteen sixty-four, three Englishmen bought a tract of land from Native Americans. The buyers were John Bailey, Daniel Denton and Luke Watson. The land lay between the Raritan and Passaic rivers. The tract included all of present-day Union County. The Native American witnesses were Warinanco and Mattano. Both names are now attached to parks in the area. The price was twenty fathoms of trading cloth, two coats, two guns, two kettles, ten bars of lead, twenty handfuls of powder, and four hundred fathoms of white wampum. It was payable a year after the land was settled. There was a problem. Neither Governor Richard Nicolls nor the buyers knew that, four months earlier, the Duke of York had already given New Jersey to Lord Berkeley and Sir George Carteret. The settlers called their town Elizabethtown, probably after Sir George Carteret's wife. [The price and the Staten Island sellers come from one source.]

stories.title: Alexander Hamilton's Elizabethtown Years
stories.blurb: In seventeen seventy-two, a young Alexander Hamilton arrived in Elizabethtown. He came to study at the Academy of Elizabethtown, in the spot where the Snyder Academy stands today. While he was here, Hamilton lived nearby at Liberty Hall, with the family of William Livingston. Livingston would become New Jersey's first governor. Hamilton also became close friends with Elias Boudinot, who lived at Boxwood Hall. He was a frequent visitor at both homes.

stories.title: The Point
stories.blurb: Elizabethtown Point was the ferry landing that connected Elizabeth to Staten Island and New York. In January of seventeen seventy-six, Patriot forces under Colonel Elias Dayton and Matthias Ogden seized a British supply ship there. It carried arms and ammunition that were bound for Boston. The captured ship sat at the end of First Street for over a month. On January twenty-fifth, seventeen eighty, British and Loyalist troops crossed at the Point. Their raid burned parts of Elizabeth and destroyed the First Presbyterian Church. Later that year, British forces crossed at the Point again, ahead of the battles of Connecticut Farms and Springfield.

stories.title: Girls' Show
stories.blurb: At Passaic Valley High School in Little Falls, the event is called Girls' Show. It began in 1941, when the school had no varsity sports for girls, as a fundraiser for the Girls Athletic Association. The group's motto was "A girl in every sport, a sport for every girl." The school serves Little Falls, Totowa and Woodland Park. Girls compete on a Green team or a White team. Little Falls tends to be green, and Totowa tends to be white, but families often pick a side by which color their mothers and grandmothers wore. Each team performs a ten-minute dance, a cheer routine and an exercise routine, all choreographed by students. Five judges score it. At the end, the Girls' Show president twirls a green flag and a white flag and then raises one to declare the winner. In the 1980s, the school stopped Girls' Show for five years after outbreaks of vandalism and arguments between the two sides. It returned in 1986 with new rules. Fans of each color still enter by different doors. A documentary about it came out in 2015.

stories.title: The Brownstone That Built Trinity Church
stories.blurb: Little Falls was once a quarry town. Its brownstone became one of its first industries. In 1840, the architect Richard Upjohn was hired to rebuild Trinity Church on lower Broadway in New York. After a long search, he decided he wanted the brownstone from Little Falls. The Trinity Church Corporation leased the quarry lands, along with the right to cut and remove the stone. The sculptor James Thom carved the brownstone figures that ornament the church's spire. Today, the township says its brownstone was used in notable buildings, and Trinity Church is the one it names first.

stories.title: Franklin Sigler, Medal of Honor at Iwo Jima
stories.blurb: Franklin Sigler was born in Glen Ridge, New Jersey, in 1924. He went to high school in Little Falls, and he enlisted in the Marine Corps in March of 1943. On March 14, 1945, on Iwo Jima, Private Sigler's rifle squad lost its leader. Sigler took command. An enemy gun position had held up the advance of his company for several days. He led a charge and wiped out its crew with hand grenades. He was badly wounded, but he refused to be evacuated. He carried three wounded members of his squad to safety. On October 5, 1945, President Harry Truman presented him with the Medal of Honor at the White House.

stories.title: How Cedar Grove Became Its Own Town
stories.blurb: Cedar Grove was once part of Caldwell Township. By the 1800s it was known as Vernon Valley. It was renamed Verona, because there was another Vernon Valley, in Sussex County. In 1892, Verona Township split off from Caldwell. In 1902, it split again, into Verona Township and Verona Borough. And in 1908, Cedar Grove separated from Verona and became its own municipality, named for the cedar trees. That same spring, on May 18, 1908, thirty men met at Sam Brower's barbershop, at Pompton and Bradford Avenues. A Civil War veteran named Andrew Jackson Taylor suggested organizing a fire brigade. The men approved, and the Cedar Grove fire company was formally organized that day.

stories.title: The Canfield-Morgan Farm
stories.blurb: In eighteen forty-five, Benjamin Canfield built a farmhouse in Cedar Grove. His family grew tomatoes, pumpkins, apples and corn, and sold them in the Newark and Paterson markets. The Canfields farmed the land until nineteen ten, when James and Edith Morgan bought it. James Morgan experimented with different crops. He died of tuberculosis in nineteen twenty. Edith and her son Courtenay struggled to keep the farm going. The farm was Cedar Grove's last operating farm, and it ran from eighteen forty-five until nineteen eighty-five. That year, Courtenay Morgan donated the fourteen-acre farm to the township. Today the farmhouse and barn are a museum.

stories.title: Kip's Castle
stories.blurb: On the ridge of First Mountain, on the line between Verona and Montclair, stands a castle. It is called Kip's Castle, and it was originally named Kypsburg. Frederic Kip, a wealthy textile inventor and industrialist, built it with his wife Charlotte between 1902 and 1905. The 9,000-square-foot mansion copies a medieval Norman castle. It is built of trap rock trimmed with sandstone. Inside are thirty rooms, with vaulted ceilings and six fireplaces. Charlotte is credited with designing the building and the grounds, including an octagonal rose garden. She died in 1926, and the estate was sold. Today it is part of the Essex County park system.

stories.title: The Verona Hillbilly
stories.blurb: The mascot of Verona High School is a hillbilly. Nobody has found out who first picked the name, but it goes back to before the United States entered World War Two. The Hillbilly was the mascot at least as far back as nineteen forty-one, when the school was called H.B. Whitehorne High School. He is the only hillbilly mascot in New Jersey, and he is the only sleeping mascot in the country. In nineteen forty-five, the student council briefly replaced him with a hornet. In the early nineteen-fifties, a goat challenged him for several years. In nineteen ninety, his rifle, jug and pipe were replaced with a fishing pole and a dog. In two thousand twelve, a tougher, modern version appeared. The mascot has landed Verona in the pages of the New York Times. [Dates come from one source, a local history of the mascot.]

stories.title: The Clay and the Bricks
stories.blurb: Little Ferry is named for a rope-drawn ferry that crossed the Hackensack River between 1659 and 1826. In 1847, a freed Black woman named Elizabeth Sutliff Dufler bought land along the river there. She saw the value of the clay, and sold it to potteries in Newark and Jersey City. By the middle 1860s, brickmaking was well established in Little Ferry. Several brickyards supplied the growing cities of New York and northern New Jersey. The Mehrhof family bought brickyards and grew into one of the nation's largest brick makers. Most of the bricks were made for export, so the old houses in town were mostly wooden. Mehrhof Pond is a visible remnant of the industry.

stories.title: America's First Steam Engine
stories.blurb: Around seventeen twelve, copper was found on land owned by Arent Schuyler, near the Passaic River. The mine opened in seventeen fifteen. It sat in what is now North Arlington, right next to Belleville. By seventeen forty-eight, the mine kept flooding. John Schuyler ordered a steam engine from England to pump the water out. The equipment arrived in seventeen fifty-three, installed by an engineer named Josiah Hornblower, who settled in Belleville. In seventeen fifty-five, the engine started work. It is credited as the first steam engine assembled in America. It pumped water from a shaft over one hundred feet deep.

stories.title: Birthplace of the Industrial Revolution
stories.blurb: After the Revolutionary War, the owners of the Schuyler mine wanted steam engines. Instead of buying them from England, they set up a foundry and machine shop in Belleville. Starting in seventeen ninety-four, the first steam engine manufactured in the United States was built there. Belleville Engine Works was founded that same year. In seventeen ninety-seven, Josiah Hornblower and two partners built the first steamboat in New Jersey at Belleville. It probably helped Robert Fulton before his famous run of the Clermont in eighteen oh nine. In nineteen ninety-four, Congress passed a resolution recognizing Belleville as the birthplace of the Industrial Revolution in the United States. [The steamboat detail comes from one source, the township website.]

stories.blurb: The Dutch Reformed Church on Main Street in Belleville was founded in sixteen ninety-seven. The church was rebuilt in seventeen twenty-five, and again in eighteen oh seven. During the American Revolution, its steeple was used as an observation post. On November twenty-second, seventeen seventy-six, George Washington and his troops came down Main Street and then River Road, with the British close behind. A bronze plaque at the church lists sixty-two Revolutionary War veterans who are buried in the cemetery behind it. The current church building dates to eighteen fifty-three.

stories.title: The First Chinatown on the East Coast
stories.blurb: In September of eighteen seventy, a group of Chinese immigrants arrived in Belleville. Many had come from the West Coast, where some had worked on the Central Pacific Railroad. They came to work at a big laundry on the Passaic River, the Passaic Steam Laundry. The laundry's owner, a merchant named Captain James Hervey, wanted a steadier workforce. The Chinese workers formed what is called the first Chinatown on the East Coast. One author says Newark's Chinatown grew out of the settlement in Belleville. Today, a memorial to those immigrants stands in the graveyard of the Dutch Reformed Church.

stories.title: Why Belleville Is a Township Again
stories.blurb: Belleville has changed its legal title many times. It was first made a township in eighteen thirty-nine, when it had only about five hundred people. In eighteen seventy-four it became a city. Two years later, it was a township again. In nineteen ten, it became a town. Then, in nineteen eighty-one, voters made it a township once more. The reason was money. Under federal revenue-sharing rules, townships got a bigger share of aid per person. Belleville was one of seven Essex County towns to switch that year, joining four that had already done it.

stories.title: Where Grover Cleveland Was Born
stories.blurb: Grover Cleveland, the twenty-second and twenty-fourth President of the United States, was born in Caldwell on March eighteenth, eighteen thirty-seven. He was the first president to serve two terms that were not back to back. He was born in the manse, the pastor's house of the First Presbyterian Church, built in eighteen thirty-two. His father, Reverend Richard Falley Cleveland, was the church's minister from eighteen thirty-four to eighteen forty-one. Cleveland lived in Caldwell for the first four years of his life. In nineteen oh seven, friends of Cleveland began negotiating to buy the house. It opened to the public on March eighteenth, nineteen thirteen. It is the only house museum in the country dedicated to Cleveland's life.

stories.title: The Fighting Parson
stories.blurb: Caldwell, North Caldwell and West Caldwell are all named for one man, the Reverend James Caldwell. During the Revolution he earned the nickname the Fighting Parson, for helping Washington's men. In seventeen ninety-eight, the people of Horseneck renamed their home Caldwell in his memory. On June twenty-third, seventeen eighty, at the Battle of Springfield, American troops ran short of wadding for their muskets. Caldwell gathered hymn books written by Isaac Watts. He tore out the pages and handed them to the soldiers. The National Park Service says he shouted, "Put Watts into them, boys!"

stories.title: The Murder of the Fighting Parson
stories.blurb: The Reverend James Caldwell's wife Hannah was shot and killed by a British soldier through the window of their home during the Battle of Connecticut Farms, on June seventh, seventeen eighty. Caldwell himself was killed too. On November twenty-fourth, seventeen eighty-one, an American sentry shot him in Elizabethtown, during a dispute over inspecting a package. The sentry, James Morgan, was convicted of murder and hanged. At the trial, there were rumors that the British had bribed the sentry.

stories.title: The Case of the Missing Cannon
stories.blurb: A bronze cannon with dolphin handles once sat on the town green in Caldwell. It was said to be a gift linked to a visit in eighteen twenty-four. Sources disagree on the giver. One says the Marquis de Lafayette, another says a Colonel Decatur. In nineteen sixty-eight, the cannon was stolen from the green. Public works crews searched for it, without luck. An iron replica was put in its place. In twenty thirteen, the Caldwell Public Library was still asking anyone who knew what had happened to it to come forward.

stories.title: The Night the Park Theatre Burned
stories.blurb: On July fourteenth, nineteen seventy-four, many Caldwell residents gathered on the town green and watched firefighters battle a blaze. The fire destroyed the Park Theatre. The Park Theatre, at two sixty-five Bloomfield Avenue, opened around nineteen twenty-five with a Moller organ. It had eleven hundred seats, a balcony and a luncheonette in the lobby. In later years, a night out could mean a triple feature for four dollars. A bank now stands on the site.

stories.title: The Beatles' Drummer Lived in Caldwell
stories.blurb: On September eleventh, nineteen sixty-two, the Beatles were in a London studio, finishing their first single, Love Me Do. Their producer, George Martin, brought in a session drummer named Andy White. Ringo played tambourine. White's three hours of work earned him five pounds, and no royalties. Later, he moved to New Jersey, and settled in Caldwell. He died at home there in November twenty fifteen, at eighty-five.

stories.title: The Fire That Made Caldwell Build in Brick
stories.blurb: On October ninth, eighteen ninety-seven, a fire tore through Bloomfield Avenue in Caldwell. It burned down a pharmacy, a barber shop and four other shops. Caldwell had no organized fire company and no proper equipment. The pharmacy's owner wanted a building that could resist the frequent fires of that era. The new one, at two ninety-five Bloomfield Avenue, was the Hasler Building. It became the first brick building in Caldwell.

stories.title: The Amazing Kreskin of Caldwell
stories.blurb: The mentalist known as The Amazing Kreskin grew up in Caldwell as George Kresge Junior. He appeared eighty-eight times on The Tonight Show with Johnny Carson. He never called himself a psychic. He said he was a master of the power of suggestion. On his seventy-fifth birthday, in January of twenty ten, his hometown gave him a golden key to the borough. It also declared January "The Amazing Kreskin Recognition Month." He died in December of twenty twenty-four, at eighty-nine.

stories.title: Caldwell's Carnegie Library Makes the Endangered List
stories.blurb: The Caldwell Public Library is a one-story brick Carnegie library, designed by a Caldwell architect named Lynn Grover Lockward. It is one of four Carnegie libraries in Essex County still in their original buildings. In May of twenty twenty-two, Preservation New Jersey named it one of the ten most endangered historic places in the state. The building had suffered two major floods in four years. The most recent was caused by Hurricane Ida.

stories.title: Caldwell University Starts With Nuns
stories.blurb: Caldwell University began in nineteen thirty-nine as Caldwell College for Women. It was founded by the Dominican Sisters of Caldwell, led by Mother Joseph Dunn. It was incorporated on August tenth, nineteen thirty-nine. In nineteen seventy-four, it became the first school in New Jersey to award a Bachelor of Fine Arts degree. It voted to admit men in nineteen eighty-five, and welcomed its first full-time male students in the fall of nineteen eighty-six. It was renamed Caldwell University in twenty fourteen.

stories.title: The Soprano House
stories.blurb: In North Caldwell, at fourteen Aspen Drive, stands the house that played Tony Soprano's home on the HBO series The Sopranos. The show debuted in January nineteen ninety-nine. Every opening sequence ended with Tony pulling into that driveway. Only the outside was filmed here, the front, the patio and the pool. The indoor scenes were shot on a set, built to match the real house. It is a private home, and Frommer's asks visitors to be respectful. The show's creator, David Chase, grew up partly in North Caldwell.

stories.title: The Denver of the East
stories.blurb: North Caldwell has two nicknames. The borough calls itself the green jewel of Essex County. The older nickname is the Denver of the East. According to the borough's own history, North Caldwell had a reputation for a healthy climate. That drew many people in the summer. It was incorporated as a borough in eighteen ninety-eight.

stories.title: The Borough That Boroughitis Built
stories.blurb: In seventeen oh two, settlers bought the fourteen-thousand-acre Horseneck Tract from the Lenape for goods worth three hundred twenty-five dollars. North Caldwell was part of it. Settlers came for the hickory and oak forests. When the lumber ran out, the land turned to farms. In eighteen ninety-eight, the borough broke away from Caldwell Township, part of a statewide wave of new boroughs that historians call boroughitis.

stories.title: The Boroughs That Voted to Become Townships
stories.blurb: In the early nineteen eighties, a federal rule gave townships a bigger share of revenue-sharing money per person than boroughs. So more than a dozen Essex County towns voted to change their legal status to township. Caldwell voted in nineteen eighty-one. It briefly became the Township of the Borough of Caldwell. North Caldwell voted in nineteen eighty-two. Caldwell became a borough again in nineteen ninety-five, and North Caldwell in nineteen ninety-two.

stories.title: The Old Essex County Penitentiary
stories.blurb: On a hill on the North Caldwell and Verona border stood the Essex County Penitentiary. It was built in the early eighteen seventies of brownstone quarried nearby, in a style called Italianate Victorian. It was one of the oldest active penitentiaries in the state. Prisoners last served time there in two thousand four, when a new jail opened in Newark. The site was sold to the builder K. Hovnanian. When the old jail was torn down in twenty eleven, workers found prisoners' writing on the walls and beams, along with tin cups and a whiskey bottle more than one hundred years old.

stories.title: Jermaine Jackson Breaks Out of Jail in North Caldwell
stories.blurb: On the Fourth of July, nineteen eighty-four, singer Jermaine Jackson spent the day in an Essex County jail. He and a film crew of fifty-five, including sixteen dancers, were at the old jail annex shooting a music video for his song "Dynamite." The video included a foiled prison escape scene. It was directed by Robert Giraldi. United Press International reported that the shoot took place in an unused wing and did not interfere with the jail's operations.

stories.title: The Opera Star on Schumann-Heink Hill
stories.blurb: The opera singer Ernestine Schumann-Heink lived in North Caldwell. Her home stood on the Grandview Place hillside, from nineteen oh five to nineteen seventeen. The area is still remembered as Schumann-Heink Hill. The house was later used as a summer residence by New Jersey Governor Edward Edwards, from nineteen twenty-five to nineteen twenty-seven. It also became a banquet hall called The Clouds. The house was torn down in nineteen fifty.

stories.title: The TV Town Modeled on North Caldwell
stories.blurb: The NBC series Ed was set in a small town called Stuckeyville. The show's producer, Rob Burnett, grew up in North Caldwell and went to West Essex High School. The town of Stuckeyville was modeled after North Caldwell. In the show, Ed is a New York lawyer. He gets fired for leaving a comma out of a legal brief, and goes home to his small town.

stories.title: Walker's Pond Gets a Historic Marker
stories.blurb: On May second, twenty twenty-six, North Caldwell unveiled its first new historic marker since nineteen seventy-six. It honors Walker's Pond. A man named J.D. Armitage built the pond and a four-hundred-foot dam in nineteen twenty-eight and twenty-nine. Carlee and Elwood Walker bought the property in nineteen forty-nine. Neighbors formed a skating pond association, and a skating shack was built in nineteen fifty-six. The borough bought the property in twenty sixteen, to make it a park.

stories.title: North Caldwell's Five Bicentennial Markers
stories.blurb: In nineteen seventy-six, during the Bicentennial, North Caldwell put up historic markers at five locations. They included the Bach House, the Henry Francisco Homestead and the Sandford-Stager House. The Sandford-Stager House was first built around seventeen seventy-five. The Stager family lived there until nineteen oh six. The artist Lawrence Wilbur lived there from nineteen twenty-three to nineteen seventy-one. Another marker covers the old mill area along Green Brook. A grist and saw mill ran there from the late seventeen hundreds through nineteen hundred.

stories.title: The Mill on Pine Brook
stories.blurb: In Westville, now West Caldwell, Crane's Mill stood along Pine Brook. It was built by Caleb Hetfield. In the seventeen eighties, Samuel Crane bought it, and his family ran it. After a fire in eighteen fifty-one, four of his grandsons rebuilt it. The mill cut lumber and ground feed and flour. Even the sawdust was used to insulate local ice houses. It stopped working in nineteen sixty-seven, when Herbert Crane died. The mill complex was moved to Allaire State Park, but a historian says it was never rebuilt. A retirement community named Crane's Mill opened on the site in nineteen ninety-eight.

stories.title: How West Caldwell Became Its Own Town
stories.blurb: In the eighteen hundreds, doctors sent patients to Caldwell Township as a pure air retreat. By eighteen hundred, only about four hundred eighty-five people lived there. By nineteen oh four, the township had grown so spread out that the two sides of town could not agree on public improvements. So West Caldwell was incorporated that year as its own borough, with about four hundred ten people. It included the settlements of Franklin and Westville. Later, it became a township, one of the Essex County towns that switched to get a larger share of federal aid.

stories.title: The Watergate Burglar From West Caldwell
stories.blurb: G. Gordon Liddy was raised partly in West Caldwell. He went to Saint Benedict's Prep in Newark, and later became an FBI agent. As a Nixon White House aide, he helped organize the Watergate burglary of nineteen seventy-two. He was convicted of conspiracy, burglary and illegal wiretapping. He was sentenced to twenty years, and began serving it on January thirtieth, nineteen seventy-three. In nineteen seventy-seven, President Jimmy Carter commuted the sentence to eight years. Liddy died in March of twenty twenty-one, at ninety.

stories.title: Justice Alito's West Caldwell
stories.blurb: On October thirty-first, two thousand five, President George W. Bush nominated Judge Samuel Alito to the Supreme Court. Alito was fifty-five, born in Trenton. He and his wife lived in West Caldwell. His father, Samuel Alito Senior, had been director of the New Jersey Office of Legislative Services from nineteen fifty-two to nineteen eighty-four. The nomination brought national attention to West Caldwell.

stories.title: The Crane Homestead
stories.blurb: At two eighty-nine Westville Avenue in West Caldwell stands the Zenas C. Crane Homestead. An earlier house on the site, built in the early seventeen nineties by Caleb Crane, burned down in eighteen forty-eight. Zenas Crane rebuilt it in the eighteen fifties. The Cranes lived there until the nineteen sixties. Today it is home to the Historical Society of West Caldwell, which was founded in February of nineteen seventy-seven, out of a Bicentennial committee. It displays paintings by William Hasler, the Caldwell pharmacist.

stories.title: Crane's Mill Moves to Monmouth County
stories.blurb: A grist mill stood in the village of Westville, now West Caldwell. It was founded in the first half of the seventeen hundreds by the Hatfield family, and later run by the Crane family. It kept operating until Herbert Crane died in nineteen sixty-seven. His widow donated the mill to Allaire State Park, in Monmouth County. The mill was moved there, but it was never rebuilt. It was left to the elements and later dismantled. Today a retirement community on the old site is called Crane's Mill.

stories.title: The Swamp Named for a Loyalist Miller
stories.blurb: Hatfield Swamp is a wetland near West Caldwell. It is bordered by the Passaic, Rockaway and Whippany rivers. It was once part of a glacial lake formed during the last ice age. The swamp is named for Cornelius Hetfield, who owned a mill there before the American Revolution. Hetfield was a known Loyalist. His property was confiscated and sold to Cyrus Crane. Today you can explore the swamp by canoe or kayak.

stories.title: The Hardy Boys Author Lived in West Caldwell
stories.blurb: Andrew Svenson wrote or cowrote more than seventy children's books. They included the Hardy Boys, the Bobbsey Twins and Tom Swift. His first Hardy Boys book, "The Sign of the Crooked Arrow," came out in nineteen forty-nine. The New York Times called him a bestselling writer whose name was largely unknown to the public. He lived in West Caldwell and worked in his split-level home there. He died in August of nineteen seventy-five, at sixty-five.

stories.title: West Caldwell Gets a College Campus in an Old School
stories.blurb: In nineteen seventy-eight, Essex County College opened a campus in West Caldwell. It took over part of a former school, Roosevelt Elementary. The goal was to serve residents of western Essex County. In nineteen eighty-one, the college bought an eight-acre site in West Caldwell. The campus there is now called the West Essex Campus.

stories.title: West Caldwell Breaks Away From Caldwell Township
stories.blurb: In nineteen oh four, West Caldwell broke away from Caldwell Township. The township had grown so spread out that public improvements could not be approved by residents on both sides of town. The New Jersey Legislature made West Caldwell its own borough. Its first mayor was Caleb Crane, a deacon of the Caldwell Presbyterian Church. He died in nineteen thirty-seven, at ninety-two. West Caldwell has been a township since nineteen eighty-two.
