stories.title: Annie Oakley and the Nutley Circus
stories.blurb: Annie Oakley, the famous sharpshooter, called Nutley her home town. She and Frank Butler toured with the Buffalo Bill Wild West Show. She was presented to the Prince of Wales, and performed for Queen Victoria. In eighteen ninety-four, Nutley put on an amateur circus. It was produced by Henry Bunner, the editor of Puck magazine. It raised money for the Red Cross. Annie Oakley was the star, giving a rifle exhibition.

stories.title: The Enclosure, Nutley's Artists Colony
stories.blurb: In the eighteen eighties, the editor of Puck magazine, Henry Bunner, moved to Nutley. Writers and artists followed. One of them, the painter Frank Fowler, founded an artists' colony on a dead-end street called The Enclosure, near the Third River. Later artists there included Frederick Dana Marsh and his son Reginald Marsh. In nineteen seventy-three, a town commissioner proposed widening The Enclosure and adding sidewalks. Residents objected, got a restraining order, and applied to make the lane a permanent historic site.

stories.title: The Night Mark Twain Came to Nutley
stories.blurb: On the night of December tenth, eighteen ninety-three, Mark Twain came to Nutley. The New York Times reported that he drove in a cab to the house of his friend Henry Bunner, the editor of Puck. Rumors spread about why he had come. The Times said some thought he came to see the Papashon pig, an animal the paper had described. Nutley's artists and writers colony entertained Mark Twain along with other well-known visitors.

stories.title: The Nutley Velodrome
stories.blurb: In nineteen thirty-three, a wooden bicycle racing track opened in Nutley. It was called the Nutley Velodrome. It was built on a former quarry by a man named Joseph Miele. It had steep forty-five degree turns. Riders came from around the world to race there. On opening day, June fourth, the season opener drew twelve thousand people. In nineteen thirty-eight, the track reopened for midget car racing. The final checkered flag fell on August twenty-sixth, nineteen thirty-nine.

stories.title: Martha Stewart's Nutley
stories.blurb: Martha Stewart was born in Jersey City in nineteen forty-one, as Martha Kostyra. When she was three, her family moved to a house on Elm Place in Nutley. She was one of six children. She went to Nutley High School. She learned cooking and the domestic arts from her mother, and gardening from her father. The township later honored her by naming part of Elm Place after her.

stories.title: When Nutley's Martha Stewart Was Convicted
stories.blurb: Then, in March of two thousand four, a federal jury found Martha Stewart guilty on all four counts in her trial. She was convicted of conspiracy, obstruction of justice and lying to federal investigators. The case was about her sale of ImClone stock in December of two thousand one. She was never charged with insider trading. On July sixteenth, two thousand four, a federal judge sentenced her to five months in prison and two years of probation, including five months of house arrest.

stories.title: The Valium Lab on Kingsland Street
stories.blurb: Along Kingsland Street in Nutley sits the headquarters of the drug company Hoffmann-La Roche. A nineteen eighty-three New York Times article said Valium and Librium were invented there. The chemist was Leo Sternbach. He was looking for a replacement for the highly addictive barbiturates. His discovery of Librium was partly an accident. Valium followed in nineteen sixty-three. By the nineteen seventies, it was the most prescribed drug in the world. stories.title: The Statue House on Franklin Avenue
stories.blurb: In the nineteen sixties, a house on Franklin Avenue in Nutley was a coffeehouse called Villa Capri. It catered to local beatniks. Later, a storm dropped a big weeping willow in the front yard. The owner, Angelo Nardone, covered the tree with his own sculptures. Weird N.J. magazine reported he had been fighting the town for over fifteen years to keep it. The town saw it as an eyesore. The town council tried to close Villa Capri for decades. stories.title: Where the Name Nutley Came From
stories.blurb: Nutley was not always called Nutley. It was incorporated in eighteen seventy-four as Franklin Township. On March fifth, nineteen oh two, it was reincorporated under the name Nutley. The Nutley Historical Society says no one knows exactly where the name came from. Historians generally agree it is English, and means a field of nuts. The township's own history says the name came from a large estate of the Satterthwaite family, set up along the Passaic River in eighteen forty-four. The Historical Society says no other community in the country has the name.

stories.title: The Tough Guy Who Lived in Nutley
stories.blurb: The actor Frank Vincent lived in Nutley. He played mobsters on screen. He appeared with Joe Pesci and Robert De Niro in three Martin Scorsese films: "Raging Bull," "Goodfellas" and "Casino." On "The Sopranos," he played Phil Leotardo. Comedian Stephen Colbert once joked that Vincent was so manly, he lived in a town called Nutley. Vincent died on September thirteenth, twenty seventeen. Nutley's mayor, Joseph Scarpelli, said the town was proud to have him live there. He called him a local guy who made it big.

stories.title: The Parking Lot Where Ultimate Frisbee Was Born
stories.blurb: In nineteen sixty-eight, students at Columbia High School in Maplewood wrote down the rules for a new game. It was a lot like football, but played with a frisbee. The students were Joel Silver, Buzzy Hellring and Jonny Hines. They played in the student parking lot, and the game became Ultimate Frisbee. Since nineteen seventy, alumni have returned every Thanksgiving evening for a game. It is known as the longest-running tradition in the sport. In twenty twenty, it was interrupted for the first time. A plaque marks the spot.

stories.title: Why They Call It Brooklyn West
stories.blurb: Maplewood has a nickname. According to NJ.com, the town and its neighbor South Orange have been unofficially dubbed "Brooklyn West." In twenty fifteen, a Maplewood realtor told NJ.com that about eighty percent of the people at her open houses were from Brooklyn. She and others ran a bus tour from the Barclays Center, billed as a "luxury tour of Brooklyn West." It led to three sales. She said the draw was the diversity. In two thousand seven, The Real Deal reported a tip going around Park Slope. If you want more space, head for Maplewood. It is a thirty-minute train ride from Penn Station.

stories.title: The Maplewood Theater, Broadway West
stories.blurb: The Maplewood Theater opened on March fifteenth, nineteen twenty-seven. The first film was "The Four Horsemen of the Apocalypse," starring Rudolph Valentino. It had more than fourteen hundred seats. The theater was also a stage for vaudeville and live shows. The Durand-Hedden Historical Society says stars such as Tallulah Bankhead, Ingrid Bergman and Paul Robeson performed there. The theater closed in twenty twenty, after ninety-two years.

stories.title: Maplewood's Rainbow Crosswalks
stories.blurb: On June seventh, twenty eighteen, Maplewood unveiled permanent rainbow crosswalks. They are at the corner of Valley Street and Oakview Road. Town officials said it was the first town in New Jersey to put permanent rainbow crosswalks on a county road. Township Committee member Dean Dafis, the first openly LGBTQ member, said the town wanted a permanent symbol of its commitment to inclusion.

stories.title: Maplewood Memorial Park
stories.blurb: Maplewood Memorial Park covers about twenty-five acres. In nineteen twenty-two, the township hired the Olmsted Brothers to create it. The park was dedicated in nineteen thirty-one to the men and women of Maplewood who served in World War One. It is listed on the National Register of Historic Places. In twenty sixteen, it was named one of New Jersey's Great Public Places.

stories.title: The Father of Maplewood
stories.blurb: Edward Balch was a builder who lived in Maplewood from eighteen ninety until he died in nineteen thirty-four. He built about one hundred seventy-five houses in town, mostly on the western side. The New York Times called him the "Father of Maplewood" in its headline on his death. In twenty ten, volunteers identified the houses he built.

stories.title: The Town That Used to Be South Orange
stories.blurb: Maplewood was once called South Orange Township. It was created in eighteen sixty-one. In nineteen oh four, the village of South Orange separated from the township. That left two places with nearly the same name. To prevent confusion, the township was renamed Maplewood on November seventh, nineteen twenty-two. The name came from a railroad station. A land speculator named John Shedden built the station in eighteen thirty-eight, and called it Maplewood.

stories.title: Columbia High School's Clock Tower
stories.blurb: Columbia High School's roots go back to eighteen fourteen, when a group of local residents funded the first formal school in South Orange. The current building opened in September of nineteen twenty-seven, on Parker Avenue. It has a six-story clock tower with an observatory on top. The clock was originally mechanical. Its counterweights were wound up the tower every week, and the tunnels for those weights can still be seen on the front of the building.

stories.title: Roy Scheider Before Jaws
stories.blurb: Roy Scheider, the actor who played the police chief in the nineteen seventy-five movie "Jaws," was born in Orange, New Jersey, in nineteen thirty-two. His family moved to Maplewood, and he graduated from Columbia High School in nineteen fifty. He acted in school shows, including the senior night play, "The Bat." In nineteen eighty-five, as part of the school's centennial, Columbia created a Hall of Fame. Scheider was one of its first two inductees. He died in February of two thousand eight.

stories.title: The Landscape Painter Born in Jefferson Village
stories.blurb: Asher Durand was born on August twenty-first, seventeen ninety-six, in Jefferson Village. That is now Maplewood. His father was a watchmaker and silversmith, and taught him engraving. Durand became one of the foremost members of the Hudson River School of landscape painters. He was a friend and contemporary of Thomas Cole. One of his paintings, from eighteen forty-nine, is called "Kindred Spirits." He died in Maplewood in eighteen eighty-six, at ninety.

stories.title: Edison's Black Maria Studio
stories.blurb: At Thomas Edison's laboratory in West Orange, his team built the world's first motion picture studio. It was a stage of wood planks and tar paper. The roof opened to let in sunlight, because Edison's light bulbs were not bright enough for filming. The Library of Congress says the whole building sat on a pivot, so it could be turned to follow the sun. It looked like a police patrol wagon, so it was nicknamed the Black Maria. Strongman Eugene Sandow, the dancer Carmencita and sharpshooter Annie Oakley were filmed there. The earliest surviving copyrighted film, from January seventh, eighteen ninety-four, is a record of a sneeze. In April of twenty twenty-four, the National Park Service reopened a replica of the Black Maria.

stories.title: America's First Planned Neighborhood
stories.blurb: Llewellyn Park, in West Orange, is considered the country's first planned residential community. It was created by Llewellyn Haskell, a New York businessman, with help from the architect Alexander Jackson Davis. It was platted in eighteen fifty-seven. Instead of straight streets, it has curving roads and native and exotic trees. About one hundred seventy homes surround a fifty-acre common of ravines called the Ramble. Thomas Edison bought Glenmont, his home there, in eighteen eighty-six.

stories.title: The Night Edison's Plant Burned
stories.blurb: On Wednesday, December ninth, nineteen fourteen, a fire broke out at Thomas Edison's West Orange plant, at about five twenty-five in the evening. The National Park Service says it started in the film inspection building. By the next day, fifteen of the twenty-two Edison Phonograph Works buildings were badly damaged or destroyed. The fire burned all night and smoldered for weeks. Fire departments from nearby towns joined the plant's own crews. The fire never crossed Lakeside Avenue, and Edison's brick laboratory was spared.

stories.title: The Mountain Where Eagles Nested
stories.blurb: Eagle Rock Reservation sits on the crest of the First Watchung Mountain, above West Orange. Essex County Parks says the mountain got its name in the early nineteenth century, when bald eagles were said to nest in the cliffs. A trolley line to the foot of Eagle Rock Avenue opened in eighteen ninety-four. The park became a mecca for Sunday picnickers. Automobile enthusiasts raced up its cobblestone road. The county bought the first land in eighteen ninety-five and finished assembling the park by nineteen oh seven. The Olmsted firm designed it. The casino from nineteen eleven is now the Highlawn Pavilion restaurant.

stories.title: The Town That Began as Fairmount
stories.blurb: West Orange began as a town called Fairmount. The township says it was formed on March eleventh, eighteen sixty-two, by an act of the New Jersey Legislature. People living on top of the first mountain had a dispute over education, so the state created a new town with its own school district. The boundary with Orange was Perry Lane, which is now Prospect Avenue. The name West Orange was not used until eighteen sixty-three. Before seventeen eighty-two, the settlements on the mountain were known as the Mountain Society.

stories.title: The Oldest Golf Club in New Jersey
stories.blurb: Essex County Country Club in West Orange was founded in May of eighteen eighty-seven. It says it is the oldest club in New Jersey, and the sixth oldest in the United States. In nineteen hundred, ten New Jersey clubs met there over dinner. That meeting created the New Jersey State Golf Association. Baltusrol was one of the ten clubs at that first meeting. The club also says it is one of the twenty-five founding clubs of the U.S. Golf Association.

stories.title: The Course on First Mountain
stories.blurb: In nineteen sixteen, the architect A. W. Tillinghast designed a new eighteen-hole course for Essex County Country Club. It sat on one hundred eighty acres on top of First Mountain. A second eighteen-hole course, designed by Seth Raynor, was built in the late nineteen twenties. That course was sold in the nineteen seventies and became the Francis A. Byrne Golf Course. A New York Times headline in nineteen seventy-six read, "Sale of Golf Course Splits West Orange."

stories.title: The Thirteenth Oldest Golf Club in America
stories.blurb: Montclair Golf Club in West Orange was founded in eighteen ninety-three and calls itself the thirteenth oldest golf club in the nation. By eighteen ninety-nine, it had an eighteen-hole course designed by Tom Bendelow. In nineteen twenty, it hired Donald Ross. The USGA says the club hosted the nineteen seventy-three U.S. Women's Amateur and the nineteen eighty-five U.S. Amateur. The club says Carol Semple Thompson won the first and Sam Randolph the second. The USGA chose it to host the U.S. Women's Mid-Amateur in twenty twenty-six.

stories.title: Seton Hall Starts in South Orange
stories.blurb: Seton Hall University opened in eighteen fifty-six, in South Orange. It was founded by the first Bishop of Newark, James Roosevelt Bayley. He named it after his aunt, Elizabeth Ann Seton, the first American-born saint. Seton Hall says it is the oldest Roman Catholic diocesan university in the United States. In its first twelve years, it enrolled more than five hundred freshmen, from seventeen states and six foreign countries. The South Orange campus became coeducational in nineteen sixty-eight.

stories.title: The Grass Courts of South Orange
stories.blurb: The Orange Lawn Tennis Club in South Orange was founded on October fourth, eighteen eighty. Its first president was Richard J. Cross. The first site was ten acres, at Berkeley and Montrose Avenues. By April of eighteen eighty-two, it had eight courts and about one hundred members. It held a fall tournament starting in eighteen eighty-one. In nineteen sixteen, it moved to a forty-two-acre estate on Ridgewood Avenue. The club says it is one of the last remaining grass court clubs in the nation.

stories.title: The Lawyer Who Built Montrose
stories.blurb: The Montrose neighborhood of South Orange was built by a New York lawyer named John Gorham Vose. He bought a home on Scotland Road in eighteen fifty-eight. In eighteen sixty-two, he began buying large plots of land. In a few years, one hundred seventy-five acres between Scotland Road and Center Street were complete. Vose named the area Montrose. Wikipedia says its large houses attracted wealthy families from Newark and New York City between eighteen seventy and nineteen hundred. South Orange's Village Hall followed in eighteen ninety-four.

stories.title: The Water Cure on Ridgewood Road
stories.blurb: South Orange was once a destination for water cures. The Mountain House Hotel and Spa, also called the Orange Springs Mansion, stood on what is now Ridgewood Road, and was founded some time before eighteen thirty. It offered a "water cure" for a wide range of ailments. Visitors drank and bathed in water they believed was especially pure and rich in minerals. Guests came by stage coach from Newark, and later by train. Mountain Station was built to serve them, and Mountain House Road gave a direct route to the hotel. According to one report, Daniel Webster wrote from New York in eighteen fifty asking how to reach South Orange. Later, the hotel burned down. Water cures faded in popularity, the land was subdivided, and houses were built nearby. Today, Mountain Station and Mountain House Road are all that remain of the hotel.

stories.title: Hat City
stories.blurb: Orange was once a hat-making capital. New Jersey Future says that between eighteen seventy and World War One, the Valley neighborhood, in Orange and West Orange, was the hat-making capital of the world. By nineteen hundred, it had thirty-five hat factories. One was the Stetson Hat Company, which later moved to Philadelphia. The history site Clio says the factories could make thirty to forty thousand hats a day. In eighteen ninety-two alone, nearly four point eight million hats were made. Between nineteen fifty and nineteen seventy, most of the industry left.

stories.title: The Town That Kept Splitting
stories.blurb: The city of Orange was once the parent of several towns. It was set apart from Newark as a township on November twenty-seventh, eighteen oh six. After it became a city, it began breaking into smaller towns. The city says the main reason was local disputes about the cost of paid police, fire and street departments. South Orange, Fairmount, East Orange and West Orange were all carved out of it. East Orange was organized on March fourth, eighteen sixty-three. The city also says the first electric trolley in New Jersey ran on part of the Orange Crosstown Line, which was started in June of eighteen eighty-eight.

stories.title: The Church at Newark Mountains
stories.blurb: In seventeen nineteen, a congregation formed in what was then part of Newark. It was called The Church at Newark Mountains. It became the First Presbyterian Church of Orange. Over two hundred ninety-one years it worshiped in four buildings, under nineteen pastors. In the nineteen twenties and thirties, it had a peak of twenty-two hundred members. By twenty ten, about one hundred were left. That June, the congregation voted fourteen to thirteen to dissolve. The last service was held on July eighteenth, twenty ten.

stories.title: The Radium Plant on Alden Street
stories.blurb: This is a heavier story. At the corner of High and Alden Streets in Orange, the United States Radium Corporation ran a radium processing plant. It extracted and purified radium from carnotite ore, and it made a glowing paint that went on instruments and watch dials. At one time, more than one hundred workers painted those dials. Women who did that work ingested the paint by licking their brushes. Many developed an illness called radium jaw, and many died. The litigation that followed led to stronger worker protection laws. The company stopped radium processing in nineteen twenty-six. In September nineteen eighty-three, the site was placed on the federal Superfund list. Cleanup of the soil and building material was completed in September two thousand five, with one home that could not be reached.

stories.title: The Governor Behind the Town's Name
stories.blurb: Bloomfield's name comes from a Revolutionary War officer, Joseph Bloomfield, who later became the fourth governor of New Jersey. In seventeen ninety-six, a new church congregation named itself for him. When he visited in July of seventeen ninety-seven, he made a donation that helped pay for the lime to finish the outside of its building. That church still stands at the northern end of the Bloomfield Green. The township says the Green was bought for two hundred dollars, though it had already been used as a military training field and parade ground.

stories.title: The Lamp Factory That Fed the First Chain Reaction
stories.blurb: A lamp factory in Bloomfield helped make the first nuclear chain reaction possible. The Westinghouse Lamp Plant on Arlington Avenue was built in nineteen twenty. It made electric lamps. In nineteen forty-two, the University of Chicago hired Westinghouse to produce uranium. At the Bloomfield plant, John Marden and Harvey Rentschler developed a process for pure uranium metal. The Atomic Heritage Foundation says the company supplied more than three tons of uranium for Chicago Pile One, and about sixty-nine tons for the Manhattan Project. The U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission says the plant was later decontaminated for unrestricted use.

https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/

stories.title: The College That Started for German Ministers
stories.blurb: Bloomfield College began in eighteen sixty-eight, as a training school for German-speaking ministers. It was first called the German Theological School of Newark. Montclair State says it opened after nearly two million German immigrants arrived following the European revolutions of eighteen forty-eight. The township says its forerunner took over the old Bloomfield Academy building, which dated from eighteen ten. In July of twenty twenty-three, Bloomfield College merged into Montclair State University.

stories.title: The Green and the Stone Church
stories.blurb: Bloomfield was originally called Watesson. A settlement stood there by seventeen sixty-nine. By seventeen seventy-five, the Green was informally used as a military training ground and a meeting place. In seventeen ninety-six, the Presbyterian church went up beside it. Its walls are red sandstone, and Samuel Ward designed it. The Commons was officially created in seventeen ninety-seven. The Morris Canal later passed through town, and then the railroads. Bloomfield was incorporated as a town in nineteen hundred.

stories.title: From Strubbe's to Holsten's
stories.blurb: Holsten's, at one thousand sixty-three Broad Street in Bloomfield, opened in nineteen thirty-nine as Strubbe's Ice Cream Parlor. It became Martin and Holsten's, and then Holsten's. In nineteen sixty-four it was incorporated as Brookdale Confectionery. Ronald Stark and Christopher Carley have owned it since nineteen ninety-nine. The shop says it still has the wooden and glass candy cases that were first put in back in nineteen thirty-nine.

stories.title: The Last Scene of The Sopranos
stories.blurb: Holsten's is best known as the setting of the final scene of the HBO series The Sopranos. The scene was filmed there in March of two thousand seven. The episode first aired on June tenth, two thousand seven. The show's location manager told nj dot com they were looking for a typical period luncheonette in New Jersey. The song at the end is "Don't Stop Believin'" by Journey. Journey's one request was that the scene not contain any violence or deaths.

stories.title: The Fuze Factory on Bloomfield Avenue
stories.blurb: From mid nineteen fifteen to the end of nineteen eighteen, a factory at Bloomfield Avenue and Grove Street housed the International Arms and Fuze Company. The Historical Society of Bloomfield says it was one of the largest arms makers in the country. At its peak it employed ten thousand workers, including over four thousand women. They made millions of artillery shells and fuses for the Allies in World War One. The plant had its own railroad siding, medical facilities, and a cafeteria. The workers had their own band, baseball team, and bowling league. At first, its presence aroused fears of explosions in town.

stories.title: Glen Ridge Breaks Away From Bloomfield
stories.blurb: Glen Ridge was once part of Bloomfield. The borough says residents on the hill were unhappy with their representation on the Bloomfield Council. Roads stayed unpaved, there were no water or sewer systems, and the schools were miles away. In eighteen ninety-five, several men met on the third floor of Robert Rudd's house on Ridgewood Avenue. They marked out a one point four five square mile area to break away. On February twelfth, the vote to secede passed by only twenty-three votes. Robert Rudd became the first mayor, with about eleven hundred fifty residents.

stories.title: One of the Oldest Golf Clubs in America
stories.blurb: The Golf Club of Glen Ridge was founded on October tenth, eighteen ninety-four. Fourteen charter members started it at the home of John W. Stewart on Ridgewood Avenue. The Glen Ridge Historical Society calls it one of the oldest golf clubs in the United States. The first clubhouse was built on Oxford Street in nineteen hundred.

stories.title: The Basement
stories.blurb: In March of nineteen eighty-nine, in the affluent town of Glen Ridge, a seventeen-year-old girl with an intellectual disability was sexually assaulted in a basement. The boys had been her schoolmates since kindergarten. A crowd of the school's athletes was there, including its football co-captains. Within three days, she told her swim coach. Within a week, a social worker told her mother. On March twenty-second, the high school principal notified the police. Two months passed before charges were filed. The Washington Post reported in May of nineteen eighty-nine that the complaint shocked the affluent suburb.

stories.title: The Trial and the Town
stories.blurb: The trial began in Newark on October fifteenth, nineteen ninety-two. Four young men were tried. The jury deliberated for twelve days. On March sixteenth, nineteen ninety-three, all four were found guilty to varying degrees. The court allowed expert testimony on rape trauma syndrome, which Encyclopedia dot com says was a first for a New Jersey judge. CNN reported in nineteen ninety-seven that two of the defendants were ordered to serve fifteen years in a youth correctional center, and a third, seven. One defendant received probation. The case drew national attention. Wikipedia says it was mainly because of a perception that the boys had been given special treatment because they were local football stars. Journalist Bernard Lefkowitz wrote a book about it called Our Guys, asking what went wrong in a seemingly flawless American town.

stories.title: The Station at the Center of Glen Ridge
stories.blurb: For more than a century, Glen Ridge residents have passed through the train station on Ridgewood Avenue. The first wood building went up in eighteen seventy-two. It had a ticket office and a barbershop. In eighteen eighty-three, the station became the post office. The Glen Ridge Historical Society says that is when the name Glen Ridge was adopted by the new post office. The borough says the present Queen Anne-style station was built in eighteen eighty-seven, thanks to local developer A.G. Darwin. It is on the National and State Registers of Historic Places. In two thousand one, it reopened as the Senior and Community Center.

stories.title: Whitney Houston's East Orange
stories.blurb: Whitney Houston was born in Newark on August ninth, nineteen sixty-three. At age seven, she moved with her family to East Orange. Her mother was the singer Cissy Houston. She began singing in the choir at her mother's church, New Hope Baptist. Her elementary school in East Orange was later renamed the Whitney Houston Academy. She died on February eleventh, twenty twelve. The New Jersey Hall of Fame inducted her in its class of twenty thirteen.

stories.title: Upsala College Closes
stories.blurb: Upsala College was a Swedish-American school in East Orange. It was founded in eighteen ninety-three by the Augustana Synod, and it first held classes in church basements in Brooklyn. It became a four-year degree college in nineteen oh three. In nineteen twenty-three, it bought forty-five acres in East Orange, and it moved there in nineteen twenty-four. Through the nineteen eighties, enrollment kept falling. In nineteen ninety-four, a new president was hired to close the college. Upsala College closed on May thirty-first, nineteen ninety-five.

stories.title: The Copper Mine Under Dodd Street
stories.blurb: In seventeen twenty, a vein of rich copper ore was discovered in what is now East Orange. The mine, on the south side of Dodd Street near Brighton Avenue, was worked for a number of years. The ore was shipped to England. Young people of those generations tested their nerve by exploring the mine. A church was later built on the site. The shaft was filled in after part of Dodd Street caved in. Nothing of it remains to be seen.

stories.title: Whiskey Lane
stories.blurb: In the winter of seventeen seventy-six and seventy-seven, the British commander in New York sent out foraging parties. One had two thousand men, split into four groups. One night, a party of Hessians camped on a farm in what is now East Orange. Under a covering of hay were barrels of whiskey. A Newark merchant had hidden them there for safekeeping. For many years afterward, the lane was known as Whiskey Lane.

stories.title: Named for the First Governor
stories.blurb: Livingston, New Jersey, is named for William Livingston, the state's first governor. He was also a framer of the United States Constitution. The township says he served thirteen terms as governor before he died in seventeen ninety. Livingston became a township on February fifth, eighteen thirteen. It was carved from parts of Caldwell Township and Springfield Township. At its first town meeting, about one hundred people lived there, mostly farmers.

stories.title: Seven Hamlets and a Mall
stories.blurb: In eighteen eleven, a group of small hamlets asked to form a township. The township says they included Teedtown, now Livingston Center, and Cheapside, now the site of the Livingston Mall. Others were Northfield, Morehousetown, Washington Place and Squiertown. The first town meeting was held in a tavern at Livingston and Mount Pleasant Avenues. Shoemaking was a major industry during the Civil War. Dairy was the leading industry after it. The population jumped from about ten thousand in nineteen fifty to more than twenty-three thousand in nineteen sixty, and peaked at thirty-one thousand six hundred fifty-three in nineteen seventy.

stories.title: The Old Force Homestead
stories.blurb: On South Livingston Avenue stands the Old Force Homestead. It was built around seventeen forty-five, and it was expanded in the early eighteen hundreds. Samuel Force bought it in seventeen seventy-seven. In seventeen ninety-six, he gave the house and sixty acres to his son Thomas. Thomas had served in the Revolutionary War, and he had been captured and held prisoner on the British ship Jersey. Today the township owns the house. It is a museum, and both buildings are listed on the State and National Registers of Historic Places.

stories.title: The Horseneck Riots
stories.blurb: In sixteen ninety-nine, pioneers received a grant to settle the Horseneck Tract, which included what is now Livingston. In seventeen-oh-two, the land was purchased from native people for one hundred thirty pounds. But in the following decades, the East Jersey Proprietors, backed by the Crown, began claiming the land and dispossessing the pioneers. In seventeen forty-four, a fire at a home destroyed the deed to the tract. In September of seventeen forty-five, a man named Samuel Baldwin was arrested for cutting timber on land he did not have title to. He was jailed in Newark. On September nineteenth, more than a hundred men came to the jail, reportedly with clubs, axes and crowbars, and freed him. It was the first of four Horseneck riots over the next seven years.

stories.title: From Missile Base to Art Park
stories.blurb: From nineteen fifty-four to nineteen seventy-four, Cold War weapons were neighbors to suburban developments in Livingston. The United States Army's Nike Air Defense System was a chain of anti-aircraft missile sites encircling major American cities, designed to intercept Soviet nuclear bombers. On Riker Hill, the Army ran a Nike battery control area. It was decommissioned in nineteen seventy-four. Essex County took over the forty-three-acre site, at a price of one dollar, and the deed was recorded in nineteen seventy-seven. Most of the old buildings had no heat, water, or electricity. Artists took them over and transformed them. Today it is Riker Hill Art Park, and within a few years of the artists arriving, it had thirty-five studios.

stories.title: The Cider Apple Found in Livingston
stories.blurb: The Harrison cider apple was one of the most famous cider apples in eighteenth-century America. It was grown in New Jersey before and after the Revolution. It later fell out of favor, and many thought it was extinct. In September of nineteen seventy-six, a fruit collector from Vermont went looking for it. He found a large tree in Livingston. It was one of only two Harrisons left in New Jersey. He took cuttings and planted them in Vermont, which kept the Harrison from dying out.
stories.flag: The rediscovery is in Wikipedia and Newark Farms. Sources describe the Harrison as an eighteenth-century apple that later fell out of favor.

stories.title: Camptown Becomes Irvington
stories.blurb: Irvington used to be called Camptown. The township historian says it was first known as West Farms. It became Camp's Town because Joseph Camp and his relatives owned nearly one-third of the farmland. Wikipedia says that after Stephen Foster published the song "Camptown Races," residents worried their town would be linked to the activities in it. So the town was renamed in honor of the writer Washington Irving.

stories.title: Olympic Park
stories.blurb: From eighteen eighty-seven to nineteen sixty-five, Irvington was home to Olympic Park. It was a forty-acre amusement park on the border of Irvington and Maplewood. The main entrance was on Chancellor Avenue. When the park closed, its merry-go-round was sold and moved to Disney World in Florida. The township historian, Alan Siegel, wrote a picture history of the park called "Smile," published by Rutgers University Press in nineteen eighty-three.

stories.title: The Courthouse Election Voided as Corrupt
stories.blurb: In eighteen oh seven, Essex County voted on whether to move the county seat from Newark to a spot called Day's Hill. That spot lay inside what is now Irvington, near today's Springfield, Florence and Elmwood Avenues. It was called the Great Courthouse Election. Nearly fourteen thousand ballots were cast. Newark won, seventy-six hundred sixty-six to sixty-one hundred eighty-one. The number of ballots was about three times the number of eligible voters. A legislative inquiry found massive voter fraud. The State Legislature set the result aside as wicked and corrupt.

stories.title: Famous Names From Irvington
stories.blurb: Irvington, New Jersey, was incorporated as a village on March twenty-seventh, eighteen seventy-four. Well-known people are associated with it. Queen Latifah, the rapper, singer and actress, is on the list. So is Pras, one of the founding members of the Fugees. Actress and director Vera Farmiga, who was nominated for an Academy Award, is on the list. So is Glen Burtnik, a former member of the band Styx. Swimmer Cullen Jones won a gold medal in the four-by-one-hundred-meter freestyle relay at the two thousand eight Olympics in Beijing. And mathematician Erna Schneider Hoover is noted for inventing a computerized telephone switching method.

stories.title: The Software Patent from Irvington
stories.blurb: Erna Schneider Hoover was born in Irvington in nineteen twenty-six. In nineteen fifty-four she took a research job at Bell Laboratories in northern New Jersey. She created a computerized telephone switching system. In nineteen seventy-one she filed one of the first software patents. It is United States Patent three million, six hundred twenty-three thousand and seven. In two thousand eight she was inducted into the National Inventors Hall of Fame.

stories.title: Babe Ruth's Promise to Johnny Sylvester
stories.blurb: In nineteen twenty-six, an eleven-year-old Yankees fan named Johnny Sylvester lived in Essex Fells. He was kicked in the head by a horse after a fall while riding, and a bad infection set in. Doctors feared he would not survive, although Princeton's archives say accounts differ on how sick he really was. Babe Ruth sent him two autographed baseballs and a note. It said, "I'll knock a homer for you on Wednesday." On Wednesday, October sixth, in Game Four of the World Series, Ruth hit three home runs. Johnny recovered. He graduated from Princeton in nineteen thirty-seven. A year after the game, Ruth reportedly asked, "Who the hell is Johnny Sylvester?"

stories.title: Did the Mulligan Start in Essex Fells?
stories.blurb: Every golfer knows the mulligan, a free second shot after a bad one. The Essex Fells Country Club says it began there, on its first tee, sometime in the nineteen thirties. According to the club's story, a locker room attendant named Buddy Mulligan hit a poor opening shot and begged for another. Members began giving themselves mulligans. A sportswriter for the Newark Evening News then began using the word in print. The United States Golf Association says the true origin is debated. Several clubs and people claim it, and the most widely accepted story points to a golfer named David Mulligan, in Montreal in the nineteen twenties.

stories.title: Anthony Drexel's Rustic Suburb
stories.blurb: In the seventeen and eighteen hundreds, the hills and valleys of what is now Essex Fells had only seven or eight farms, along what is now Roseland Avenue. Then, in eighteen eighty-eight, Philadelphia developer Anthony Drexel sent his representative, Charles Leavitt, to survey land near the railroad extension in the Caldwells. In eighteen eighty-nine, Drexel formed the New York Suburban Land Company and bought one thousand acres south of Caldwell. His son-in-law, John Fell, was the majority shareholder. Drexel hired the landscape architect Ernest Bowditch, and the new homes had electricity, indoor plumbing, and telephones. The name honors Essex County, and the word "fell" suggests a rolling, hilly area, though Mr. Fell may have had some input. Essex Fells was incorporated in nineteen oh two.

stories.title: A Paper Mill Becomes a Playhouse
stories.blurb: The Paper Mill Playhouse, in Millburn, really was a paper mill. Samuel Campbell opened the Thistle Paper Mill on the site in seventeen ninety-five. After a fire in the eighteen sixties, it was rebuilt and ran as the Diamond Paper Mill until nineteen twenty-eight. In nineteen twenty-nine, Frank Carrington and Antoinette Scudder founded the Newark Arts Theater. They answered an ad for the old mill, and in nineteen thirty-four Scudder bought it and turned it into a theater. The Millburn-Short Hills Historical Society says it now draws nearly half a million visitors a year.

stories.title: The Night the Playhouse Burned
stories.blurb: On June twentieth, nineteen seventy-two, Governor William Cahill proclaimed the Paper Mill Playhouse the State Theatre of New Jersey. Then, on January fourteenth, nineteen eighty, a catastrophic fire destroyed the theater, which had been in continuous operation since nineteen thirty-eight. During the rebuilding, it got upgraded technology, a larger stage, more seating, and accessibility options. The new theater opened on October thirtieth, nineteen eighty-two, with a production of Robert and Elizabeth.

stories.title: The Arboretum a Daughter Left to Millburn
stories.blurb: Short Hills was developed by a man named Stewart Hartshorn. In nineteen twenty-three, he gave a piece of land to his daughter, Cora. Cora Hartshorn developed it as a place where wild things could grow without harm. Her Stone House was completed in nineteen thirty-three, built with trap rock from her father's quarry in Springfield. When Cora died in nineteen fifty-eight, she left the property to Millburn Township. Today it is the Cora Hartshorn Arboretum and Bird Sanctuary, about sixteen acres with three miles of trails.

stories.title: Voices at the Paper Mill Playhouse
stories.blurb: The Paper Mill Playhouse in Millburn, New Jersey, is said to be haunted. The theater stands on the site of a paper mill from seventeen ninety-five. In two thousand thirteen, nj dot com reported that the playhouse's press director said employees, actors, and guests have had strange experiences. One director, alone on the stage, said he heard a voice ask, "Same time tomorrow?" An employee, alone in the lobby, said he heard a woman's voice tell him not to go out there. Five minutes later, a storm started. These are reported accounts, not confirmed facts.

stories.title: How Centreville Became Roseland
stories.blurb: Roseland used to be a section of Livingston called Centreville. In eighteen seventy-three, a local judge led an effort to get a post office. There was already a Centreville post office in Hunterdon County, so residents met to choose a new name. The borough says Sarah Condit Harrison suggested Roselyn. Whether by misspelling or by design, it became Roseland. The post office opened on April fourteenth, eighteen seventy-four. In nineteen oh seven, a Roseland delegation lost a vote on a new school. That led to a petition, and Roseland became its own borough on April tenth, nineteen oh eight.

stories.title: Roseland Loses a Vote and Leaves Livingston
stories.blurb: In nineteen oh seven, Roseland was still the Centreville section of Livingston Township. At a school district meeting, a large delegation from Roseland asked for a new school, and was outvoted. After that meeting, a resident named Bill Teed led a drive to petition the Legislature for a new borough. In nineteen oh eight, the Borough of Roseland came into existence. According to the borough, the Becker Farm, which operated from eighteen eighty to nineteen sixty-four, once covered a thousand to twelve hundred acres. That was almost half the town.

stories.title: The Fresh Milk Line
stories.blurb: The Becker Farm in Roseland ran from eighteen eighty to nineteen sixty-four, and at its peak covered one thousand to twelve hundred acres, almost half the town. On that dairy farm was a miniature railroad, the Centerville and Southwestern, with a live steam locomotive, number fifteen oh one. Passengers rode two miles out and back. It was called "The Fresh Milk Line," and children got chocolate milk after a ride. The railroad's last season was nineteen seventy-two. Today, most of the old farm land is the center of large corporate office complexes.

stories.title: The Miniature Railroad on the Becker Farm
stories.blurb: On the Becker dairy farm in Roseland, Eugene Becker built a miniature railroad. It was called the Centerville and Southwestern. It dated back to nineteen thirty-eight, and the first paying rides came ten years later. It was modeled on the Delaware, Lackawanna and Western's Sussex Branch. It had a live steam locomotive and about seven thousand feet of track. A ride was a two-mile round trip. Tickets were twenty cents for children and forty cents for adults at first. The farm once made up nearly half of Roseland. It is now mostly a large business complex, and some vestiges of the railroad still exist.

stories.title: The Horseneck Tract
stories.blurb: In seventeen oh two, settlers bought the Horseneck Tract from the Lenape for goods worth three hundred twenty-five dollars. It was fourteen thousand acres. It was called the Horseneck Tract because its irregular shape suggested a horse's neck and head. It covered much of western Essex County, from the First Mountain to the Passaic River. Today, it includes Caldwell, West Caldwell, North Caldwell, Fairfield, Verona, Cedar Grove, Essex Fells, and Roseland, and parts of Livingston and West Orange.

stories.title: The Airport That Opened to Forty Thousand People
stories.blurb: In April of nineteen twenty-nine, a man named Walter Marvin and six others formed the Essex Airport Corporation. They wanted an airport to serve Montclair, seven miles away. The grand opening was on October twenty-sixth, nineteen thirty. There was parachute jumping, bomb dropping and stunt flights. Researcher Alex Davidson says about forty thousand people showed up. Fairfield was still called Caldwell Township then. The site was picked partly because the Orange Mountains kept haze and fog away from the field. Today it is Essex County Airport. The county's improvement authority has owned it since September fifth, nineteen seventy-five.

stories.title: Gansegat, the Duck's Pond
stories.blurb: Before it was Fairfield, this place was called Gansegat. That is Dutch for duck's pond. Dutch settlers came to the Passaic River here in the sixteen-sixties. The land was later part of the Horseneck Tract, and officially part of Newark Township. Then, on February sixteenth, seventeen ninety-eight, it was formed as Caldwell Township. It was named for the Reverend James Caldwell. NJ dot com says the town took the name Fairfield in nineteen sixty-four.

stories.title: The Township That Gave Its Land Away
stories.blurb: Caldwell Township was formed in seventeen ninety-eight, and it was big. Over the next century it gave pieces away. Livingston was taken from it on February eighth, eighteen thirteen. Fairmount Township, now part of West Orange, followed on March eleventh, eighteen sixty-two. In February of eighteen ninety-two, Caldwell Borough and Verona Township both broke off. North Caldwell left in March of eighteen ninety-eight. Essex Fells left in March of nineteen oh two. West Caldwell left in February of nineteen oh four. Fairfield is, in the police department's words, the only remaining part of the original seventeen ninety-eight township.

stories.title: The Constable Who Bought His Own Revolver
stories.blurb: In nineteen twenty-four, Fairfield was still Caldwell Township, and it still used part-time constables. Chief Constable Morris Collerd patrolled about four hours a day. He was paid seventy-five cents an hour. As the story goes, the revolver he was issued could not hit the side of a barn. So he bought his own, more accurate ones. The police department says they were probably used most often to put rabid animals out of their misery. He worked out of his own home.

stories.title: Scared Straight at Rahway State Prison
stories.blurb: In nineteen seventy-eight, a documentary was filmed inside Rahway State Prison. It was called Scared Straight. The idea came from a Reader's Digest article about a program at the prison. A group of inmates called the lifers, mostly convicted of murder or armed robbery, met with teenage offenders. They tried to terrify the teens out of a life of crime. The film was narrated by the actor Peter Falk. It first aired on Los Angeles television on November second, nineteen seventy-eight, and drew a thirty-nine percent share. At the Academy Awards on April ninth, nineteen seventy-nine, it won the Oscar for Best Documentary Feature. Director Arnold Shapiro says it saved lives. Later studies found mixed results, and some concluded that programs like it make later crime more likely.

stories.title: The Battle of Spanktown
stories.blurb: In the Revolutionary War, Rahway was known as Spanktown. In January of seventeen seventy-seven, a fight took place on St. Georges Avenue between the British and General Maxwell's men. It lasted twelve hours. The Americans got the best of it. The British lost close to one hundred men. The town says nobody is certain where the name Spanktown came from. A historic marker on St. Georges Avenue still marks the fight.

stories.title: The Carriage City of the World
stories.blurb: A railroad came through Rahway in eighteen thirty-five. By the middle of the century, Rahway was known as the Carriage City of the World. It had no less than thirty-five carriage factories. Rahway became a city on March twelfth, eighteen fifty-eight. But half of it was in Middlesex County and half in Union County. The legislature fixed that in eighteen sixty. The city also says the first coin with the words E Pluribus Unum was struck at New Jersey's first state mint, in Rahway.

stories.title: The Sheriff Who Wanted to Save a River
stories.blurb: In nineteen nineteen, Union County Sheriff James Warner wrote to the Cranford Citizen, asking to save the river as a memorial to the young men who died in the First World War. Cranford committeeman D.C.N. Collins took up the idea. On May fifth, nineteen nineteen, the Elizabeth Daily Journal called it a duty rather than an opportunity. The county later hired the Olmsted Brothers firm to design its park system. Rahway River Park was developed from nineteen twenty-one to nineteen twenty-nine.

stories.title: Rahway's Merchants and Drovers Tavern
stories.blurb: At the corner of Saint Georges Avenue and Westfield Avenue in Rahway stands a building that began, around seventeen ninety-five, as a two-story home with a general store. In seventeen ninety-eight, John Anderson bought it and applied for a license to run a tavern. His business was successful, and he extended the building by eleven feet. Over the years it served as a stagecoach stop, as worker housing, and during Prohibition, as a place to buy illegal liquor. Later it became headquarters for the Girl Scouts. Today it is the Merchants and Drovers Tavern Museum.

stories.title: The Car Plant That Built Fighter Planes
stories.blurb: The General Motors plant in Linden opened in nineteen thirty-seven. From then until nineteen forty-one, it built about three hundred forty-three thousand cars. Then the war came. In early nineteen forty-two, General Motors formed its Eastern Aircraft Division to build Navy Wildcat fighters. At Linden, the factory roof was raised twenty-six feet to fit overhead cranes. A new runway and hangar were built nearby. More than thirty-five hundred planes rolled off the line. It closed on April twentieth, two thousand five. The airfield is still there, now called Linden Airport.

Cranford was set off on March fourteenth, eighteen seventy-one. Linden Borough was formed on March thirtieth, eighteen eighty-two. Roselle followed on December twentieth, eighteen ninety-four.

stories.title: The Tavern That Named Linden
stories.blurb: Before it was Linden, this place was called Wheatsheaf. It was named for a tavern built in seventeen forty-five, at what is now Saint George's Avenue and Chestnut Street. It was a meeting place, a spot to swap news, a social hall and an inn. During the Revolution, it served as a stop on the road. In eighteen thirty-six, the railroad came through and put a stop near the old tavern. Then in eighteen sixty-five, a New York City restaurant owner named Ferdinand Blancke bought land around the Wheatsheaf station, and named the area Linden.

stories.title: July, 1967 in Plainfield
stories.blurb: In July of nineteen sixty-seven, Plainfield had one of the worst outbreaks of violence in New Jersey history. It began two days after the Newark riots started, and the New York Times calls it the second largest in the state's history. About a third of Plainfield's forty-eight thousand people were Black. Mack Trucks had closed its plant in nineteen sixty-one, moving more than twenty-five hundred jobs to Maryland. The trouble began on July fourteenth. Accounts differ on the end date, July sixteenth or July seventeenth. A police officer was killed. One local paper counts forty-six people injured, twenty-three of them by gunfire, and damage near seven hundred thousand dollars. Arrest counts range from about one hundred fifty to one hundred sixty-seven.

stories.title: Plainfield, Settled by Quakers
stories.blurb: Plainfield was settled in sixteen eighty-four by Quakers. It began as a township on April fifth, eighteen forty-seven, carved out of Westfield Township, back when the land was still part of Essex County. On March nineteenth, eighteen fifty-seven, it became part of the brand new Union County. On April twenty-first, eighteen sixty-nine, voters held a referendum, and Plainfield was incorporated as a city the same day. Some buildings from its early years still stand, including a Friends' meetinghouse from seventeen eighty-eight, and the Martine house, from seventeen seventeen.

It stayed in the Cory family until nineteen twenty-one, for one hundred thirty-seven years. People called it the old Cory Farm. Before that, many of them made the all-day trip to Elizabeth to attend church, and the men carried firearms along. In seventeen thirty-four, the congregation bought forty acres.

Today it is the Presbyterian Church of Westfield, on Mountain Avenue. Its historic cemetery holds veterans of the Revolutionary War.

stories.title: From Cranford Golf Club to Echo Lake
stories.blurb: Echo Lake Country Club in Westfield began in Cranford. In May of eighteen ninety-nine, a group from Cranford organized a nine-hole golf club. The course was designed by Willie Dunn, the designer of Shinnecock Hills. It was called the Cranford Golf Club. The Westfield Historical Society says that in nineteen twenty-one, the club took the name Echo Lake after merging with the Westfield Golf Club.

stories.title: Twenty-Six Women and 126 Books
stories.blurb: The town library's history page says its story began with a book club. <short pause> It says 26 local women started to collect and exchange books. <short pause> It says they had a collection of 126 volumes and a treasury of $16.21. <short pause> It says the town later voted overwhelmingly for a free public library, and Andrew Carnegie donated $10,000 for a building. <short pause> It says over 80 townspeople also donated, and the new building opened with a collection of 5,000 books.

stories.title: The Oldest House in Summit
stories.blurb: The Carter House is believed to be the oldest building in Summit. Land on the Passaic River was deeded to Benjamin Carter in seventeen forty. He built a cottage there in seventeen forty-one. When he died in seventeen sixty, he left nine children. In the nineteen eighties, the new owner planned to knock it down for a commercial building. In nineteen eighty-six, it was moved about a quarter mile to its current spot on Butler Parkway. The owner donated the house. It is now home to the Summit Historical Society.

stories.title: The Clearing, A Summit Estate That Became An Arboretum
stories.blurb: In Summit sits a thirteen-acre estate that was built in eighteen eighty-nine. It was called The Clearing, and it was created by John Hornor Wisner. Mrs. Wisner planted the first daffodils. The Wisner family hired Calvert Vaux, a partner in creating Central Park, to plan the grounds. Three families owned The Clearing, one after another. The Reeves family, who held it from nineteen sixteen, hired landscape architect Ellen Biddle Shipman in nineteen twenty-four. In nineteen seventy-four, local citizens raised most of the money to save the estate. It became the Reeves-Reed Arboretum, and there is a daffodil display every April.

stories.title: Six Families Start a School for Girls
stories.blurb: In the spring of eighteen ninety-four, independent schools for boys were opening across New Jersey. Six Summit families felt strongly that their daughters should have the same opportunities. They met to talk about starting a school for girls. A few months later, Kent Place School opened in the former summer home of New York State Chancellor James Kent. Sixty girls enrolled that first year. In nineteen seventy-three, the school's headmaster and trustees ended merger talks with the nearby Pingry School, keeping Kent Place devoted to girls. Today, more than six hundred eighty students are enrolled.

stories.title: The Velvet Underground's First Show
stories.blurb: On December eleventh, nineteen sixty-five, the Velvet Underground played their first show in the auditorium of Summit High School. It was the first time the original lineup of Lou Reed, John Cale, Sterling Morrison, and Maureen Tucker played together. Their manager, Al Aronowitz, organized the show, with the Myddle Class and the Forty Fingers. Admission was two dollars and fifty cents, and it sold out. They played three songs. In the Myddle Class newsletter, one writer said that half the audience loved their different sound, and the other half left the theater.

stories.title: How Canoe Brook Began
stories.blurb: Canoe Brook Country Club began in nineteen oh one. A group of residents of Summit, Chatham, and Madison, led by Carroll P. Bassett, set out to start a country club. The Summit Herald reported in June of nineteen oh one that the committee had chosen an estate on the Chatham Turnpike. It had over a hundred acres and a mansion from eighteen twenty. The golf expert Jack Vickery said it was well suited for a course. On November sixteenth, nineteen oh one, the committee set the club's bylaws. The first nine holes opened in nineteen oh two.

stories.title: Two Courses, Many Designers
stories.blurb: Canoe Brook has thirty-six holes on two courses. Walter Travis overhauled the original course in nineteen sixteen, and both courses were later renovated by Rees Jones. The club says Robert Trent Jones Senior rerouted the North Course in nineteen seventy-three. His son, Rees Jones, was a young apprentice on that project. The club hosted the New Jersey State Amateur in two thousand thirteen.

stories.title: The Summit Diner
stories.blurb: The Summit Diner was built by the Jerry O'Mahony Diner Company. It replaced an older diner, and nj dot com says the original Summit Diner was built in nineteen twenty-nine. In two thousand fifteen, nj dot com called it the state's oldest diner. A Summit history presentation in two thousand sixteen said Al Pacino shot scenes of the movie City Hall there. Legend has it that Ernest Hemingway was once a regular.

stories.title: The First Town Lit by Edison
stories.blurb: On January nineteenth, eighteen eighty-three, the streets of Roselle lit up. So did homes, businesses and the railway station. Thomas Edison had picked Roselle for an experiment. He wanted to prove that a whole neighborhood could be lit by electricity from one central generating station. It was the first electric lighting system to use overhead wires. The experiment worked. Roselle was incorporated as a borough on December twentieth, eighteen ninety-four.

stories.title: Who Was Roselle Named For?
stories.blurb: Roselle began as a railroad stop called Mulford, named for a prominent family in the Linden area. In eighteen sixty-six, the Roselle Land Improvement Company was created to lay out a town around the station on the Central Railroad. Where the name Roselle came from is said to be one of two things. It was either based on the company's founder, John Conklin Rose, or on John Pierre Roselle, a friend of the railroad's president. Voters held a referendum, and on December twentieth, eighteen ninety-four, Roselle was incorporated as a borough, from part of Linden.

stories.title: The Skating Rink the Olmsteds Planned
stories.blurb: Warinanco Park sits on the border of Roselle and Elizabeth, and covers two hundred five acres. Its website says it is named for a Lenape leader. The Union County Park Commission hired the Olmsted Brothers firm to plan its parks, and the plan for Warinanco included an artificial ice skating rink. But the rink was not built until nineteen sixty-one. It was billed as the first public artificial ice skating rink in Union County. By nineteen seventy-four, walls had been added so people could skate in bad weather. In nineteen eighty-five, lights at one field made Warinanco the first park in the county system to play night games. Renovations in twenty sixteen and twenty seventeen doubled the complex, and it was renamed the Warinanco Sports Center.

stories.title: Hannah Caldwell at Connecticut Farms
stories.blurb: On June seventh, seventeen eighty, British troops marched through Connecticut Farms, now part of Union. Hannah Caldwell, the wife of the Reverend James Caldwell, was in the parsonage. A shot came through a bedroom window, and she died. Her husband was known as the fighting parson, and the British had already burned his church that January. Some suspected it was a deliberate attack on him. The British burned the parsonage. It was rebuilt two years later. An artist's picture of her death is on the seal of Union County.

stories.title: Liberty Hall, the Governor's House
stories.blurb: In nineteen seventy-two, a mansion on Morris Avenue in Union was named a National Historic Landmark. It is called Liberty Hall. In seventeen sixty, a lawyer named William Livingston bought a hundred and twenty acres here, and had a fourteen-room Georgian house built. Livingston became New Jersey's first elected governor. British troops raided the house several times, trying to kidnap him. They never succeeded. He served as governor until he died in seventeen ninety. His descendants, the Kean family, lived in the house for six generations. Today it is the Liberty Hall Museum.

stories.title: When Union Almost Became Connecticut Farms Again
stories.blurb: Before it was Union, this place was called Connecticut Farms, for the farming families who came here from Connecticut, led by the Reverend Abraham Pierson. They built their own church in seventeen thirty. On November twenty-third, eighteen oh eight, the area was incorporated as Union Township, from part of Elizabeth Township. The church kept its old name anyway. Over the years, Union gave up land to form Linden, Roselle Park, Kenilworth and Hillside. And in nineteen forty-six, a campaign backed by the Union Exchange Club tried to change the township's name back to Connecticut Farms.

stories.title: How Kean University Landed in Union
stories.blurb: Kean University began in Newark, on April fourteenth, eighteen fifty-five, as the Newark Normal School. It started as a Saturday morning school for Newark's teachers, founded by the city's school superintendent, Stephen Conger. It was the first public college in New Jersey. It became New Jersey State Teachers College in nineteen thirty-seven. In nineteen fifty-eight, land from the Liberty Hall estate, the Kean family's ancestral home, was donated so the school could move to Union. It became Kean College in nineteen seventy-three, and Kean University in nineteen ninety-seven.

stories.title: The Church That Kept Its Name
stories.blurb: In sixteen sixty-five, about twenty-five farming families, led by Reverend Abraham Pierson, came from Connecticut to what is now Union. For more than sixty years, they traveled to Elizabethtown to worship. In seventeen thirty, they built their own wood-frame church. They called it the First Presbyterian Congregation of Connecticut Farms. On June seventh, seventeen eighty, General Knyphausen's force of five thousand marched toward Morristown. The New Jersey Brigade stood against them for nearly three hours. The settlement was pillaged and burned, and the church burned with it. The congregation built a new stone sanctuary, finished by seventeen eighty-eight. When the town was incorporated as Union in eighteen oh eight, the church kept its original name.

stories.title: Put Watts Into Them, Boys
stories.blurb: On June twenty-third, seventeen eighty, American troops fought a British force at the Battle of Springfield. The Americans began to run short of wadding, the paper that holds the powder and ball in a musket. The Reverend James Caldwell rushed to a nearby Presbyterian church and gathered up its hymnals. The hymns had been written by the minister Isaac Watts. Caldwell tore out the pages and handed them to the soldiers. He shouted, Put Watts into them, boys. The Americans won. The victory kept the British from reaching Morristown and George Washington.

stories.title: The Last Major Battle in the North
stories.blurb: On June twenty-third, seventeen eighty, about six thousand British soldiers pushed into Springfield. Facing them were General Nathanael Greene, with fifteen hundred Continentals, and five hundred New Jersey militia. The Americans won. As the British retreated, they burned the town, and the Presbyterian church along with it. It was the last major battle in the north. A new church was built in seventeen ninety-one. In its cemetery lie the graves of at least thirty-one Revolutionary War soldiers.

stories.title: Shunpike Road
stories.blurb: Until eighteen oh one, only a primitive road connected Morristown and Elizabethtown. Then a turnpike was built, and travelers had to pay a toll. To avoid the toll on the Morris and Sussex Turnpike, locals built a parallel road, and named it Shunpike Road. "Shun" means to avoid, and "pike" means turnpike. Shunpike and Milltown Roads were also alternate routes to avoid tolls on Morris Avenue, then called the Newark and Essex Pike. Springfield Avenue was first called Seven Bridges Road, because that many bridges were needed to cross small streams.

stories.title: Baltusrol and the Open
stories.blurb: Baltusrol Golf Club in Springfield dates to eighteen ninety-five. Its founder, Louis Keller, also owned the New York Social Register. The U.S. Open was played there in nineteen oh three, and Willie Anderson won it. Jack Nicklaus won the Open there in nineteen sixty-seven, and again in nineteen eighty. The club says it has hosted seven U.S. Opens. In two thousand fourteen it was named a National Historic Landmark, for its importance to the career of the architect A. W. Tillinghast.

stories.blurb: The Baltusrol Golf Club, the one in Springfield, is a private club. Visitors come as the guest of a member. It gave annual dues as around eighteen thousand five hundred dollars. Treat those as one magazine's report from that date, not a current price. Golf Monthly also noted that having the money is no guarantee of being accepted.

stories.title: The Venice of New Jersey
stories.blurb: Cranford calls itself the Venice of New Jersey. The nickname comes from the canoeists who paddle the Rahway River. In the summer of eighteen eighty-six, a water carnival on the river was described in the New York Times. Nearly a hundred boats were decorated with sky lanterns. The banks were lit with colored lights, and there were bands and fireworks. The canoe club grew out of a group called the Shanty Gang, which met at a canoe livery called the Lobster Shanty. The group became the Cranford Canoe Club in nineteen oh eight, though some documents give other dates. It is the last surviving canoe club on the Rahway River.

stories.title: The Venetians of New Jersey
stories.blurb: Cranford is known as the Venice of New Jersey, and the Rahway River is why. The Cranford Boating Club and Association held the first river regatta in eighteen seventy-nine. Later came river carnivals, with decorated boats judged by category. For the Labor Day carnival of nineteen oh eight, wire was strung along both banks to hang lanterns, and grandstand tickets went on sale at the Canoe Club grounds. That September, Harper's Weekly ran an article titled "The Venetians of New Jersey," by Frank C. Drake, about the town.

stories.title: The S in S&H Green Stamps
stories.blurb: If you grew up with S&H Green Stamps, you can thank a man from Cranford. In eighteen ninety-one, a traveling salesman named Thomas Sperry saw a Milwaukee department store giving out stamps with each purchase, which customers could redeem for merchandise. In eighteen ninety-six, Sperry, of Cranford, and Shelley Hutchinson, of Ypsilanti, Michigan, founded the Sperry and Hutchinson Company. They made their money by selling the stamps and redemption books to retailers. The S in S&H is Sperry. And in Cranford today, Sperry Park still carries his name.

stories.title: Taxation Without Representation Is Revolution
stories.blurb: Garwood began as a neighborhood of Cranford and Westfield. The borough's history says both towns treated it like a stepchild. They argued over who should provide services. About four hundred citizens pushed to break away and become one of the state's smallest municipalities. Cranford resisted, right up to the legislature. Frank Morse, who would become the first mayor, summed it up. Taxation without representation is revolution. Garwood became a borough on March nineteenth, nineteen oh three. It was named for Samuel Garwood.

stories.title: The Aeolian Factory
stories.blurb: In eighteen ninety-eight, the Aeolian Company bought the Votey Organ Company, and built a new factory for it in Garwood. The factory sat on North Avenue, with the Central Railroad tracks right behind it. Manufacturing moved there around August of nineteen hundred. Edwin Votey, whose company it had been, is credited as the inventor of the Pianola. Photos from the factory show a large Aeolian pipe organ under construction around nineteen twenty-five, and a Duo-Art grand piano being assembled around nineteen twenty-nine. Garwood became a borough on March nineteenth, nineteen oh three, and Aeolian was one of its big manufacturers.

stories.title: The Town Built Around a Railroad
stories.blurb: Garwood grew up with the Central Railroad of New Jersey. In eighteen ninety-one, Samuel Garwood and John Rogers Maxwell, a Jersey Central president, formed the Garwood Land and Improvement Company. Samuel Garwood was its first president, and the town took his name. Nearly seventy-five homes were built. Most housed workers at the Hall Signal Company, the first factory, and at the Hercules Tube works, famous for its bicycle tubing.

stories.title: Bicycle Tubing and the Signal Company
stories.blurb: Garwood grew up around its factories. According to the Garwood Historical Committee, the first modern settlers lived in seventy-five homes. Most worked for the Hall Signal Company, the first factory, or the Hercules Tube Works. Hercules was famous for bicycle tubing. It was built by John R. Maxwell, a onetime president of the Jersey Central Railroad.

stories.title: The First Public Building
stories.blurb: Garwood became a borough on March nineteenth, nineteen hundred three. Before that, the infant school was split between Cranford and Westfield. Fire protection was so uncertain that the Aeolian Company organized its own fire department. The first public building in Garwood was Jefferson School, built two years after the borough was formed. The first municipal facility was completed in nineteen fifteen.

stories.title: North Roselle Becomes Roselle Park
stories.blurb: Roselle Park was once part of Elizabethtown. In eighteen oh eight, it became part of Union Township, and it was known as North Roselle. It became an independent borough on March twenty-second, nineteen oh one. The new borough had seven hundred ninety acres, two hundred twenty-five homes, and about one thousand people. Its first mayor was John Cummins, with seven council members.

stories.title: The First Radio Station in New Jersey
stories.blurb: In Roselle Park, a building on Westfield Avenue was home to the Marconi Wireless Telegraph Company of America. During World War One, it made radio and wireless equipment for the United States Navy. Troops guarded the complex. David Sarnoff worked there as commercial manager. He later became chairman of RCA. In September of nineteen twenty-one, the station WDY received the first broadcast license issued in New Jersey. It first went on the air from Roselle Park on December fifteenth, nineteen twenty-one. The station operated for only about three months before moving to New York City.

stories.title: Stone's Store Gets the Light
stories.blurb: In the early eighteen eighties, Thomas Edison built his first generating station for isolated lighting in neighboring Roselle. An electrical line ran from the station to Charles Stone's general store on Westfield Avenue, in Roselle Park. In eighteen eighty-three, it was lit by Edison's incandescent lamp. Roselle Park's own history calls it one of the first commercial buildings to have the lamp. Other sources call it the first store in the world lit by Edison's lamp. Roselle and Roselle Park were called the Twin Boroughs.

stories.title: The Concrete School Built With Edison's Process
stories.blurb: In nineteen oh seven, Roselle Park built a high school. Many people thought it was foolish. The building is distinctive. It is the first poured concrete building, created by an experimental process invented by Thomas Edison. In nineteen sixteen, a new high school was built on Locust Street. The old one was renamed the Robert Gordon School, after one of the borough's first councilmen and a former Board of Education member.

stories.title: The Aldene Plan Changes the Commute
stories.blurb: In the middle of the nineteen sixties, the Central Railroad of New Jersey was losing money. It filed for bankruptcy early in nineteen sixty-seven. The Aldene Plan started on May first, nineteen sixty-seven. It used a connection in the Aldene neighborhood of Roselle Park between a Central Railroad line and a Lehigh Valley Railroad line. Passengers could now travel directly to Newark Penn Station instead of riding to Jersey City and taking ferries into Manhattan. Until twenty fourteen, passengers still changed trains at Newark for New York. That year, NJ Transit began a one-seat ride using dual-mode locomotives.

stories.title: The Town the Government Owned
stories.blurb: In nineteen forty-one, a housing project went up in Union County for defense workers at the Kearny shipyards. It had seven hundred units. The bill to make it a town first called it Lindark. On July twenty-first, Governor Charles Edison vetoed it. One week later, on July twenty-eighth, the Legislature overrode him. The new town was Winfield. The township says no other defense housing project was ever made its own municipality. As the Elizabeth Daily Journal put it, now Uncle Sam owns a town.

stories.title: The Rent Strike at Winfield Park
stories.blurb: In November nineteen forty-one, the first one hundred forty-five families moved into the unfinished Winfield Park housing project. They found shoddily built homes, very poor plumbing, muddy roads and sidewalks, and no electricity. The residents went on a rent strike. Federal investigators then found the contractor guilty of fraud and bid manipulation, and the Federal Works Agency had to hire a new company to finish the job. Afterward, clubs formed, along with a volunteer ambulance squad and a co-op grocery store.

stories.title: The Deserted Village of Feltville
stories.blurb: In the woods of Berkeley Heights sits a whole village that nobody lives in. It is called Feltville. In eighteen forty-five, a businessman named David Felt began building a mill town here. By eighteen fifty, about one hundred seventy-five people lived there. A post office opened by eighteen fifty-one. Felt sold the village in eighteen sixty. It was reborn in eighteen eighty-two as Glenside Park, a summer resort. The resort closed in nineteen sixteen. Today ten buildings survive, and the grounds are open to visitors.

stories.title: New Providence Township Becomes Berkeley Heights
stories.blurb: Berkeley Heights was first incorporated as New Providence Township on November eighth, eighteen oh nine. It was cut out of Springfield Township. Then it lost land. Summit was taken from it in eighteen sixty-nine, and the borough of New Providence in eighteen ninety-nine. On November sixth, nineteen fifty-one, voters chose a new name in a referendum. The township became Berkeley Heights. It was named for John Berkeley, Baron Berkeley of Stratton, one of the founders of the Province of New Jersey.

stories.title: Free Acres, Where Cagney Lived
stories.blurb: In nineteen ten, a New York reformer named Bolton Hall started a community on the old Murphy Farm, in what is now Berkeley Heights. He believed in economist Henry George's idea of a single tax, and called it Free Acres. Residents own their homes but lease the land from the Free Acres Association. The community runs its own water system and keeps up its seven streets. Early residents included Thorne Smith, and a struggling actor named James Cagney, who moved in around nineteen thirty. According to the story, he made his first call to Hollywood from one of the only two phones in town. And when he sold his home, he bought the community a lawnmower.

stories.title: The Feast of Mount Carmel
stories.blurb: Every July sixteenth, Berkeley Heights holds the Feast of Our Lady of Mount Carmel. The Mount Carmel Society has held it since nineteen oh nine. It honors a vow made by Italian immigrants, who prayed to the Blessed Mother for safe passage and promised gratitude. The day begins with a morning procession from Little Flower Parish. The Society hands out brown scapulars, and fires ceremonial cannons in tribute to veterans and past members. A Mass follows around eleven. That evening, there is food, music and games, and a fireworks show by the Santore family's Garden State Fireworks. The town calls it one of the largest fireworks shows in the state.

stories.title: The Nike Missile Radar Station at Berkeley Heights
stories.blurb: In nineteen fifty-eight, part of a Nike missile battery was installed in Berkeley Heights. The missiles were located in nearby Mountainside. The radar station was in Berkeley Heights. The battery was known as N-Y seventy-three. It stayed in operation until nineteen sixty-three. Remnants of the site are next to Governor Livingston High School.

stories.title: The Littell-Lord Farmstead
stories.blurb: The Littell-Lord Farmstead at thirty-one Horseshoe Road is an eighteen-acre museum around two houses. Inside are a Victorian master bedroom and a Victorian children's room furnished with period antiques. Outside are a summer kitchen and a nineteenth-century corn crib. There is also a spring house built around a spring and used for refrigeration. The farmstead was added to the National Register of Historic Places in nineteen seventy-nine.

stories.title: The Cannonball House
stories.blurb: In June of seventeen seventy-seven, the Battle of Short Hills was fought near Ash Swamp in Scotch Plains. A woman named Mary Osborn gave the soldiers everything eatable or wearable her house had. At about the same time, an American artilleryman fired his cannon at the British marching down Park Avenue. The shot was misdirected, and it thudded into the side of the Osborn house. From then on, the townspeople called it the Cannonball House. It was built in the early seventeen hundreds, and it still stands.
