stories.title: The Battle of the Short Hills, Fought in Scotch Plains
stories.blurb: The Battle of the Short Hills has a confusing name. It was fought on June twenty-sixth, seventeen seventy-seven, in Scotch Plains and Edison. No fighting took place in the town of Short Hills at all. British General William Howe marched out of Perth Amboy around one in the morning with two columns, led by Cornwallis and Vaughan. They went after a Continental force of about twenty-two hundred men under General William Alexander, known as Lord Stirling. Stirling was forced to retreat. But his stand gave George Washington time to pull his army back safely into the Watchung Mountains.

stories.title: The Baptist Church of 1747
stories.blurb: The Scotch Plains Baptist Church was organized on August fifth, seventeen forty-seven. It has kept an unbroken record of worship from that date. In the seventeen twenties, a Baptist named William Darby gave part of his land for a meetinghouse and a cemetery. It was christened the first meeting house in Scotch Plains in seventeen forty-two. The church sponsored five other churches between seventeen sixty-two and seventeen eighty-eight. The first was the First Baptist Church of New York.

stories.title: Scot's Plains, Settled for a Cent
stories.blurb: Captain John Baker bought the land around Scotch Plains from the Native people before sixteen eighty-four. He paid one cent for every ten acres. In sixteen eighty-four and eighty-five, Scotch immigrants, who had landed at Perth Amboy under a leader named George Scot, settled the hamlet. That is where the name Scot's Plains comes from. There were eight families in the original settlement, living in wigwams or log cabins. Their paths became Front Street, Park Avenue, Martine Avenue, Raritan Road and Westfield Road.

stories.title: The Farm With a Lake That Became Shackamaxon
stories.blurb: In nineteen oh eight, a businessman named Robert Nelson found a farm with meadows, woods, and a lake. It was the old Lambert farm on the Westfield border in Scotch Plains. The club's history says a friend looked at the land and said it would make a wonderful golf course. The course opened in nineteen sixteen, designed by A. W. Tillinghast. The club says it featured his first island green. Shackamaxon hosted qualifying for the nineteen nineteen PGA Championship, and in nineteen twenty-eight, Tommy Armour won the Metropolitan Open there.

stories.title: The Station That Named a Township
stories.blurb: In eighteen seventy-four, a new train station was built where Fanwood stands today. The president of the Central Railroad of New Jersey, John Taylor Johnson, named it Fanwood. A few years later, a new township took the station's name. In eighteen ninety-five, citizens living around the station separated and formed the Borough of Fanwood. It had three hundred thirty residents. The old township kept going until nineteen seventeen, when it was renamed Scotch Plains. The old station is the oldest original train station in Union County.

stories.title: A Book Club Starts a Library
stories.blurb: In eighteen seventy-four, a group of literary-minded women in Fanwood began meeting as the Saturday Book Club. In eighteen ninety-nine, they offered their collection of one hundred fifty-six books to the borough, on condition that the books be loaned for free. In nineteen oh two, Fanwood voters approved, and the Fanwood Free Public Library was born, with twenty-five dollars for its first year. The books sat in a small room at the rear of the post office. A library building was completed in nineteen fifty-one, and named the Fanwood Memorial Library in memory of the borough's war dead.

stories.title: The Curving Streets Near the Fanwood Station
stories.blurb: Near the Fanwood train station is a neighborhood of homes that was promoted by the railroad. The Fanwood Park Historic District was designed before eighteen sixty-eight. Its designers used the hilly land to create curving, tree-lined streets. The Central Railroad of New Jersey bought and subdivided most of the lots, and promoted those streets to encourage home ownership. By eighteen eighty-two, only a few buildings stood along Martine Avenue. The homes came in many styles, including Queen Anne, Shingle, Craftsman, Tudor and Dutch Colonial Revival. The district is fifty-two acres, with fifty-seven contributing buildings. It was added to the National Register of Historic Places on May twenty-seventh, two thousand four.

stories.title: The Town That Was Sold by Brochure
stories.blurb: In the late eighteen nineties, a group called the New Orange Industrial Association bought farms in parts of Cranford and Union. It divided them into building lots, and sold them with illustrated brochures. The brochures pictured beautiful parks, lakes, an opera house and yacht clubs. According to the borough, those existed only in the promoters' imaginations. The association did bring in several large industries. It also lured Upsala College from Brooklyn with a gift of free land. The town was confused with the Oranges in Essex County, so it took the name Kenilworth. It became a borough on May thirteenth, nineteen oh seven.

stories.title: The New Year's Day Shooting at Borough Hall
stories.blurb: On New Year's Day, nineteen forty, the people of Kenilworth gathered in the old borough hall for the swearing-in of new officials. The former mayor, then the borough clerk, had just administered the oaths. The borough's seventy-two-year-old tax collector walked in. Ill feeling between him and some officials had built up for years. He had planned to attack five of them. He killed the former mayor. A patrolman ran upstairs and was shot while struggling with him. Residents in the packed council chamber hid or fled. Bystanders took hold of the gunman. The patrolman survived. He left the hospital after eighteen days, returned to duty in February, and later rose to lieutenant.

stories.title: The Hill That Went Away
stories.blurb: Tin Kettle Hill was a hundred eighty-six feet tall, in the northeast corner of Kenilworth. According to the Kenilworth Historical Society, during the Revolutionary War, General George Washington named it a key beacon hill, for alerting soldiers in the heights above Springfield that the British were on the move. The Springfield troops would then fire a cannon to signal the militia. By nineteen oh six, the hill was gone. The Pennsylvania Railroad had removed it, and used the dirt on the approaches to the North River Tunnels, and in its rail yards in Newark and Jersey City.

stories.title: The Last Train Out of Kenilworth
stories.blurb: Kenilworth was the headquarters of the Rahway Valley Railroad. The station, at North Thirty-first Street and the Boulevard, was erected in eighteen ninety-nine. A water tank, a coal bunker and yard tracks followed, and an engine house was added in nineteen nineteen. Across the street stood the railroad's original four industrial customers. The mainline ran seven point one miles, from Aldene through Roselle Park, Kenilworth, Union and Springfield, to Summit. It was completed to Summit on July twenty-sixth, nineteen oh six. On April twenty-first, nineteen ninety-two, the railroad ran its last train, between Kenilworth and Aldene. The Interstate Commerce Commission officially abandoned it on August twenty-seventh of that year.

stories.title: Lyons Farms on the Stagecoach Road
stories.blurb: Before it was Hillside, this land was known as Lyons Farms. It was named for the many families called Lyon who lived there. The name was used for more than two hundred years. Families from Newark and Elizabethtown first settled it in the late sixteen hundreds. The southern part was called Woodruff's Farms. Mills were built along the Elizabeth River. The main road from Elizabethtown to Newark ran through it. During the Revolutionary War, there was constant troop movement. And in the late seventeen hundreds, Lyons Farms was the headquarters of the main stagecoach line between Newark and Philadelphia.

stories.title: Hillside Becomes a Township
stories.blurb: In nineteen thirteen, Hillside was carved out of Union Township and became a township of its own. It was named for the hills around it. Before that, its high school students traveled to Battin High School in Elizabeth. In nineteen seventeen, Hillside started its first high school program at the Central Grammar School.

stories.title: The Lionel Factory
stories.blurb: In nineteen twenty-nine, the Lionel toy train company built a factory in Hillside, at twenty-eight Sager Place, just for making toy trains. It was expanded in nineteen forty, nineteen forty-one, nineteen fifty and nineteen fifty-two. At its peak, the factory employed more than two thousand people. According to Hillside High School's history, Lionel and, later, Bristol-Myers Squibb were the employers of most of the town. In nineteen seventy-four, after financial difficulties, Lionel closed the Hillside plant. Its closing was one of the changes that reshaped the community in the mid-nineteen-seventies.

stories.title: Evergreen Cemetery
stories.blurb: On March twenty-third, eighteen fifty-three, the Evergreen Cemetery Corporation was incorporated, on North Broad Street. It was founded by clergymen and businessmen from Elizabethtown and Newark. A non-profit, non-denominational cemetery was needed, because the small church graveyards in both towns were crowded. The cemetery gave work to local families as grounds keepers, florists, and stonecutters. By nineteen twenty-eight, it covered one hundred fifteen acres across Hillside, Elizabeth, and Newark. The county's tour of the cemetery begins at the grave of author and poet Stephen Crane.

stories.title: The Borough on the Ridge
stories.blurb: Mountainside became a borough on September twenty-fifth, eighteen ninety-five. It was cut out of the northern part of Westfield. The Mountainside Restoration Committee names three founding families, Badgley, Cory and Miller.

stories.title: The Cold War Missile Base
stories.blurb: During the Cold War, the Army had a missile base here in Mountainside and Berkeley Heights. It was called Nike battery NY-seventy-three, and it held Nike Ajax missiles. The missile launchers were in Mountainside, and the radar station was in Berkeley Heights. The base operated from nineteen fifty-eight to nineteen sixty-two. Today, nearly a third of Mountainside is parkland, mostly the Watchung Reservation.

stories.title: The House That Moved Off Route 22
stories.blurb: The Deacon Andrew Hetfield House in Mountainside dates to about seventeen sixty. It was built in stages. The Hetfield family and their descendants owned it until nineteen forty-six. It was used as a tea room in the nineteen thirties, and as an antique store in the nineteen forties and nineteen eighties. It stood on Route twenty-two, and was saved from being torn down. Walter and Richard Kuczynski bought the property in nineteen eighty-four, and gave the house to the people of Mountainside. On Saturday, June twenty-ninth, nineteen eighty-five, the west side of Route twenty-two was closed while the house was lifted from its foundation and moved. Today it is a museum and meeting place, listed on the National Register of Historic Places.

stories.title: The Badgley House on the Watchung Mountain
stories.blurb: In seventeen thirty-six, Peter Willcocks built a sawmill along an old Native American trail near Blue Brook. His in-laws, the Badgleys, built a house along the same trail, on the First Watchung Mountain. A local history describes the Badgley House as the place where Revolutionary residents concealed their valuables from the British. Over the next two hundred fifty years, it was a home, a riding stable and a maintenance garage. About nineteen oh seven, it was moved about two hundred fifty feet north. In nineteen eighty-four, it was destroyed by a fire set by an arsonist. A dip in the lawn near the Scout camping area shows where it stood.

stories.title: The Mountainside Tornado of 1987
stories.blurb: On July twenty-sixth, nineteen eighty-seven, a tornado touched down near Mountainside at eleven-forty in the morning. It was rated F-one, and it stayed on the ground for half a mile. Longtime Mountainside residents recall it in Connie McNamara's book, A History of Mountainside.

stories.title: The Olmsted Plan Behind Echo Lake Park
stories.blurb: By nineteen twenty-one, Union County had more than two hundred thousand people and needed parks. The county set up a park commission that year. The National Park Service says it hired the Olmsted Brothers firm, which sent Percival Gallagher to survey the county. Development of Echo Lake Park in Mountainside began in nineteen twenty-three. The Cultural Landscape Foundation lists the Olmsted Brothers, Percy Jones, and Percival Gallagher as its designers. The borough's website calls it a hundred thirty-nine-acre park with two lakes.

stories.title: Where the Transistor Was Born
stories.blurb: Part of New Providence is a neighborhood called Murray Hill. Bell Labs moved there from New York City in nineteen forty-one. On December twenty-third, nineteen forty-seven, the first transistor was successfully demonstrated at Bell Labs in Murray Hill. Three men are credited with inventing it, William Shockley, John Bardeen and Walter Brattain. Murray Hill is also tied to the invention of the solar cell and the laser.

stories.title: Turkey Town
stories.blurb: New Providence was first settled by a Puritan colony in seventeen twenty. At first, the settlement was called Turkey, or Turkey Town. Wikipedia says it was named for the wild turkeys in the area. In seventeen twenty, Peter Willcox was also granted four hundred twenty-four acres nearby. New Providence Township was incorporated on November eighth, eighteen oh nine. The borough of New Providence was formed on March fourteenth, eighteen ninety-nine.

stories.title: The Balcony That Fell and the Salt Brook
stories.blurb: Settlers first named the community Turkey. Its Presbyterian Church was formed by seventeen thirty-seven. In seventeen fifty-nine, a crowded church balcony collapsed. No one was seriously injured, and people considered it a miracle, a divine act of providence. The town became known as New Providence. According to legend, when British soldiers marched toward Morristown to face George Washington, colonists dumped salt into a local brook so the soldiers would not take it. The brook became known as Salt Brook, and it appears on the borough seal. Wikipedia notes that, ironically, the British Army never crossed the Watchung Mountains into this region.

stories.title: The First Practical Solar Cell
stories.blurb: On April twenty-fifth, nineteen fifty-four, Bell Labs announced a new invention in Murray Hill, New Jersey. It was the first practical silicon solar cell. Three Bell Labs scientists built it: Daryl Chapin, Calvin Fuller, and Gerald Pearson. To show it off, they used it to power a small toy Ferris wheel and a solar-powered radio transmitter. It converted about six percent of light into electricity. The New York Times wrote that it may mark the beginning of a new era. The three were inducted into the National Inventors Hall of Fame in two thousand eight.

stories.title: The Seltzer King's Train Station
stories.blurb: The first railroad station in New Providence was built in eighteen eighty-four. It sat on land donated by Carl Schultz. The New York Times called him the Seltzer King of New York. Wikipedia says he founded a mineral water business on First Avenue in Manhattan. It says he bought a large tract of land here in the eighteen eighties and built a home. He donated the land for the station on one condition. The area had to be known as Murray Hill.

stories.title: The House From the Sixteen Hundreds
stories.blurb: In Clark stands a house built in the sixteen hundreds. The state says it was built in sixteen eighty-six. The museum says about sixteen ninety. It was built on the seven hundred acre farm of Dr. William Robinson. He was one of the first known physicians in the area, and he came from Scotland. Five families lived in the house over the years. It was lived in until nineteen seventy-three, when the township bought it. It was added to the National Register of Historic Places on November nineteenth, nineteen seventy-four. Today it is a museum run by the Clark Historical Society.

stories.title: The Ward That Declared Independence
stories.blurb: In eighteen fifty-eight, Rahway became a city, and the land that is now Clark became its Fifth Ward. In eighteen sixty-four, the three hundred fifty-seven residents of that ward declared their independence from the city and set up their own town. The New Jersey Legislature made it official on March twenty-third, eighteen sixty-four. The new township took its name from a signer of the Declaration of Independence, Abraham Clark.

stories.title: When the Parkway Split Clark in Two
stories.blurb: Clark was once a community of wide open land. Then State Highway Number Four, today's Garden State Parkway, cut the town in half. After World War Two, farmers facing economic changes, and a housing shortage, began selling their land to developers. Over forty years, from nineteen forty-nine to nineteen eighty-nine, those developers changed Clark from wide open land to a town with numerous housing developments and businesses.

stories.title: The Oak Ridge Golf Course Closes
stories.blurb: The Oak Ridge Golf Course in Clark opened in nineteen twenty-seven. It was a public course. One golfer called it a great walking course, a short course with gentle hills and forgiving fairways. In March of two thousand nine, Union County made the decision final to close it for good. The county pointed to declining revenue and a crippled economy. Closing it would save an estimated seven hundred forty thousand dollars a year. Plans for the one hundred sixty-nine acres included a possible multi-use park and restoration of the historic clubhouse.

stories.title: The Judge's Farm in Ash Swamp
stories.blurb: In Clark stands the Homestead Farm at Oak Ridge. It lies in an area known since colonial times as the Ash Swamp. The swamp was used as a hiding place during the Battle of the Short Hills, fought on June twenty-sixth, seventeen seventy-seven. Through most of the nineteenth century, the house was the home of Hugh Hartshorne Bowne. He was a judge, a state legislator, and a founding member of the Republican Party in New Jersey. Bowne was a delegate to the first two national Republican conventions, in eighteen fifty-six and eighteen sixty. They nominated Fremont and Lincoln. The farm was listed on the National Register of Historic Places on October twenty-fifth, nineteen ninety-five.

stories.title: The Hard Winter at Morristown
stories.blurb: Most people have heard of Valley Forge. Fewer know that George Washington's army spent another brutal winter in Morristown. The Continental Army camped there for about six months, from December first, seventeen seventy-nine, to June eighth, seventeen eighty. The soldiers built log cabins in a forest called Jockey Hollow. It was on the farm of Henry Wick, the largest landowner in Morristown, and his trees were what drew the army. Washington called the winter intensely cold and freezing. He used the Ford Mansion as headquarters. The owner, Theodosia Ford, a widow, had to move herself and her four children into two rooms to make space.

https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/

stories.title: The Birthplace of the Telegraph
stories.blurb: In January of eighteen thirty-eight, a crowd packed into a small red factory building at the Speedwell Iron Works in Morristown. Samuel Morse, with Leonard Gale and Alfred Vail, had strung more than two miles of wire inside the building. It was the first public demonstration of the Morse telegraph. The building had been put up by Alfred's father, Stephen Vail, as a hobby when he retired. Today the factory is a National Historic Landmark, and Speedwell is called the Birthplace of the Telegraph.

stories.title: Washington's Crowded Headquarters
stories.blurb: The National Park Service says the Ford Mansion in Morristown was built in the early 1770s for an iron manufacturer who was also a colonel in the county militia. <short pause> It says that in December of 1779, his widow allowed General Washington to use her home as his headquarters. <short pause> She and her four children moved into two rooms. <short pause> Washington, his wife Martha, five aides, and 18 servants took over the rest of the house. <short pause> The American Battlefield Trust says that winter was one of the coldest on record.

stories.title: The Rose City
stories.blurb: Madison, New Jersey, is known as the Rose City. Wealthy New Yorkers spent summer weekends there. Rose growing here began in eighteen fifty-six. The biggest greenhouse range was built in eighteen eighty. Hundreds of workers produced millions of roses a year, which went by train to New York. Immigrants from Italy helped build the mansions and grow the flowers. The rose industry ran for roughly a century, until the early nineteen fifties, when foreign competitors were too strong.
music: Reawakening by Kevin MacLeod (incompetech.com), CC BY 4.0
https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/

stories.title: Florham, a Vanderbilt Estate in Madison
stories.blurb: In Madison stands a Gilded Age estate called Florham. It was the weekend estate of Florence Vanderbilt Twombly and her husband, Hamilton McKay Twombly. The buildings were designed by the firm McKim, Mead and White. The grounds were designed by the Olmsted firm. Today, Florham is the Florham Campus of Fairleigh Dickinson University. A group called the Friends of Florham, formed in nineteen ninety, works to preserve it.
music: There is Romance by Kevin MacLeod (incompetech.com), CC BY 4.0
https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/

stories.title: A Steamboat Tycoon's Seminary
stories.blurb: Drew University says it was established in 1867 as a Methodist seminary with a gift of $250,000 from Daniel Drew, a Wall Street financier and steamboat tycoon. <short pause> The Madison Historical Society says the original mansion was sold to Daniel Drew for the seminary that year. <short pause> The university's history site says the mansion, now Mead Hall, was built by a prominent local family. <short pause> It says the builder wanted to breed and race thoroughbreds. <short pause> It says a fire in 1989 ravaged the hall and it was restored by 1992.
stories.flag: The Gibbons family built it. Drew pages give conflicting build years for Mead Hall (1832 and 1833-36), so no year is given.
music: Tranquility by Kevin MacLeod (incompetech.com), CC BY 4.0
https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/

stories.title: The Iron Forge That Started Dover
stories.blurb: Dover, New Jersey, traces its roots to seventeen twenty-two. That year, a man named John Jackson set up an iron forge on the Rockaway River. Iron became the backbone of the town. Dover grew into a busy industrial center, with mills, machine shops, foundries and railroads. It even had a working basin on the Morris Canal. Dover was formally established as a town in eighteen sixty-nine.
stories.flag: Single source: only one source confirms the details in this story.
music: Dentaneosuchus Hunt by Kevin MacLeod (incompetech.com), CC BY 4.0
https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/

stories.title: The Baker Theater
stories.blurb: The National Register nomination says the Baker Building, or Baker Opera House, was built for local businessman William Baker around 1884. <short pause> It calls it a gathering place for civic and recreational purposes and a landmark in the central business district. <short pause> A local history site says the first theater on the site opened in 1906, seating 1,146 patrons. <short pause> It says that made it one of the largest vaudeville playhouses in the region. <short pause> It says the Baker Theater is listed on the National Register of Historic Places.
stories.flag: The two sources give different dates (about 1884 for the building, 1906 for the first theater), so each is attributed.
music: Destiny Day by Kevin MacLeod (incompetech.com), CC BY 4.0
https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/

stories.title: Boonton's Little Niagara
stories.blurb: In Boonton, the Rockaway River drops thirty-six feet over a waterfall that people call Boonton's Little Niagara. The falls were formed by the Boonton Gorge. Since the early seventeen hundreds, settlers came to use that water power. The Boonton Ironworks grew up beside it. It made iron for plows, tools, kettles, locks and nails, and large iron that was shipped to England. Boonton was incorporated as a town in March of eighteen sixty-seven, from parts of Pequannock and Hanover.
music: Melodie Victoria by Kevin MacLeod (incompetech.com), CC BY 4.0
https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/

stories.title: The Arch Bridge and the Fire Hydrants
stories.blurb: The New Jersey Historic Trust says the stone arch bridge over the river was built around 1866. <short pause> It says it was built as an aqueduct to carry piped water from a pond to the ironworks for fire protection. <short pause> It says the water was piped to fire hydrants throughout the facility. <short pause> It calls the bridge the single remaining intact portion of the industrial complex. <short pause> The trust says the ironworks used the Morris Canal to bring in fuel for its two furnaces and operated until 1911.
music: Rising Tide (faster) by Kevin MacLeod (incompetech.com), CC BY 4.0
https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/

stories.title: Picatinny Arsenal
stories.blurb: In Rockaway Township, the land that is now Picatinny Arsenal once held an iron forge, built in seventeen forty-nine. In eighteen eighty, the federal government bought it, along with eighteen hundred and sixty-six acres, to store gunpowder. On September sixth, eighteen eighty, the War Department named it the Dover Powder Depot. Four days later, it was renamed the Picatinny Powder Depot. In nineteen oh seven, it became Picatinny Arsenal, and its first powder factory opened. In nineteen eleven, a school opened there to teach officers the science of weapons.
music: The Descent by Kevin MacLeod (incompetech.com), CC BY 4.0
https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/

stories.title: The Newspaper Printed in Chatham
stories.blurb: During the Revolutionary War, Chatham had its own newspaper. Shepard Kollock published the New Jersey Journal in Chatham from seventeen seventy-nine to seventeen eighty-three. It was the second newspaper in all of New Jersey, and the first in the northern part of the state. The government sponsored it, and Chatham played a strategic role in the war, including during Washington's winter encampments.
stories.flag: Single source: only one source confirms the details in this story.
music: Ether Vox by Kevin MacLeod (incompetech.com), CC BY 4.0
https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/

stories.title: Greystone, the Giant Hospital on the Hill
stories.blurb: In Parsippany stands a massive landmark, Greystone Park Psychiatric Hospital. It opened in eighteen seventy-six, designed by architect Samuel Sloan with Dr. Thomas Story Kirkbride, a Quaker physician. The building is a huge Second Empire structure on a campus that covers a square mile. Kirkbride believed that patients did better in pleasant surroundings. His approach was called Moral Treatment. In two thousand eight, recreation fields opened in Morris County's Central Park, on the former site of several smaller Greystone buildings.
music: Myst on the Moor by Kevin MacLeod (incompetech.com), CC BY 4.0
https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/

stories.title: The Hotel Breslin and Lake Hopatcong
stories.blurb: In eighteen eighty-six, a hotelier named James Breslin built a hotel in Mount Arlington, near Lake Hopatcong. The Hotel Breslin had four floors and three hundred rooms. Guests passed through stone gates into Breslin Park, an exclusive resort that hosted the rich and famous of its day. It was the most important single factor in Lake Hopatcong becoming a major resort in the Northeast. The Lenape called the region hapakonoesson, which is thought to mean stone water.
music: Starting Out Waltz Vivace by Kevin MacLeod (incompetech.com), CC BY 4.0
https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/

stories.title: Bertrand Island Park
stories.blurb: The Lake Hopatcong Foundation says a trolley company extended its line to the beach at Bertrand Island in Mount Arlington to encourage weekend business. <short pause> It says amusements opened there and Bertrand Island Amusement Park was created under Louis Kraus. <short pause> A local history site says the park was one of New Jersey's most popular summer attractions from the 1920s through 1983. <short pause> It lists a wooden roller coaster called the Wildcat, a dance hall, a diving tower, a haunted house, and bumper cars. <short pause> It says Woody Allen filmed scenes of The Purple Rose of Cairo there in 1983, the year changing lifestyles and big theme parks closed the park.
stories.flag: The two sources differ on the year of the first roller coaster, so no year is given.
music: Local Forecast - Elevator by Kevin MacLeod (incompetech.com), CC BY 4.0
https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/

stories.title: The Coaster That Came in 1925
stories.blurb: A Lake Historical Museum says the amusement park's roller coaster was the lake's first. <short pause> It says it was built over the winter of 1924 to 1925 by the Philadelphia Toboggan Company. <short pause> The Star Ledger says it cost more than $50,000 and used about 280,000 ft of lumber. <short pause> It says the ride had nine dips. <short pause> The museum says a local paper in April of 1925 called it the first roller coaster in Morris County or any of the other northern counties.
music: Hustle by Kevin MacLeod (incompetech.com), CC BY 4.0
https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/

stories.title: Miss Bertrand Island
stories.blurb: A local historical museum says beauty contests were held at the park in the 1930s. <short pause> It says there was a Miss Bertrand Island contest and a contest for the lake. <short pause> It says that in 1934, with no Miss America pageant because of the Depression, a non-sanctioned Miss America contest at the park created excitement. <short pause> It says that in 1937, the woman named Miss Bertrand Island was crowned Miss America in Atlantic City. <short pause> Wikipedia says she won the title representing the amusement park.
music: Chill Wave by Kevin MacLeod (incompetech.com), CC BY 4.0
https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/

stories.title: The Gem of Gems Carousel
stories.blurb: A local historical museum says the park's carousel was carved in the early 1920s by the firm of a famous carousel maker. <short pause> It says it was a Monarch II Supreme, with 48 hand-carved horses riding three abreast and two lion chariots. <short pause> It says the firm carved only three such carousels. <short pause> It says its carver called them the gem of gems, the finest I ever made. <short pause> The museum says the carousel arrived at the park in 1937.
stories.flag: Single source: Lake Hopatcong Historical Museum (both pages). Carousel maker: Marcus C. Illions.
music: Wagon Wheel by Kevin MacLeod (incompetech.com), CC BY 4.0
https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/

stories.title: The Iron Works That Armed Washington
stories.blurb: In the Revolutionary War, iron meant weapons. And one of the most important iron operations was the Long Pond Iron Works, in Kinnelon. The mountains there were wild when English colonists arrived in the seventeen hundreds. But dark streaks in the rock showed iron ore, and the settlers set up forges and burned charcoal to fuel them. George Washington's surveyor, Robert Erskine, stationed militia at Long Pond to protect the furnaces from British raids.
stories.flag: Single source: only one source confirms the details in this story.
music: Egmont Overture Finale by Kevin MacLeod (incompetech.com), CC BY 4.0
https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/

stories.title: The Cigarette Fortune on the Lake
stories.blurb: In 1883, a wealthy cigarette manufacturer bought a large tract of land that included a lake and mines. <short pause> Two sources name him as Francis S. Kinney. <short pause> A history page says he built his estate up to 5,000 acres by buying nearby farms. <short pause> It says his family built a four-story cottage with eight chimneys overlooking the lake. <short pause> It says nearly a hundred local men worked the farms and buildings. <short pause> It says the estate had a chapel on a small island with an interior done by Tiffany and Company. <short pause> Wikipedia says the borough is named for him.
music: Juniper by Kevin MacLeod (incompetech.com), CC BY 4.0
https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/

stories.title: Whippany and the First Church in Morris County
stories.blurb: The name Whippany first shows up in a deed from seventeen twenty-four, which mentions a place called Whippano. The land goes back to sixteen seventy-six, the year generally accepted as when it was discovered. Around seventeen ten, a few families from Newark and Elizabeth moved to the area, drawn by forests, farmland, iron ore, and the power of the Whippany River. They started the Hanover Church, the first church in what is now Morris County. Hanover Township was incorporated on March twenty-fifth, seventeen forty.
music: River Flute by Kevin MacLeod (incompetech.com), CC BY 4.0
https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/

stories.title: The Day Whippenny Became Hanover
stories.blurb: Morris County says the township's name was designated on December 7th, 1720. <short pause> It says the order came from the Hunterdon County Court. <short pause> It says the area was settled in 1676 and officially incorporated in 1740. <short pause> It says seven judges signed the proclamation in the seventh year of the reign of King George I. <short pause> A local history site says the township now claims three historic villages.
music: Two Together by Kevin MacLeod (incompetech.com), CC BY 4.0
https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/

stories.title: Chester's Publick House
stories.blurb: In Chester, at the corner of Main Street and Hillside Road, stands a brick building now called the Publick House. Around eighteen ten, a stagecoach operator named Zephaniah Drake built it as a hotel. He called it the Brick Tavern. It sat at a crossroads on the Washington Turnpike, on a stagecoach route from New York, New Brunswick and Morristown to Phillipsburg. In nineteen sixteen, the Fleming family bought it and renamed it the Chester House. They built a reputation for fine food in an upscale setting.
music: Village Consort by Kevin MacLeod (incompetech.com), CC BY 4.0
https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/

stories.title: Mendham Feeds the Army at Jockey Hollow
stories.blurb: In seventeen eighty, Washington's army suffered through an extreme winter at Jockey Hollow. Mendham villagers rallied with food and supplies for the soldiers. When a smallpox epidemic broke out while the army was quartered in Morristown, hospitals were set up in a barn on the Colonel Drake estate, and at Hilltop Church. Mendham Township had been incorporated in seventeen forty-nine, one of the first townships in Morris County. Mendham Borough followed in nineteen oh six.
stories.flag: Single source: only one source confirms the details in this story.
music: Take a Chance by Kevin MacLeod (incompetech.com), CC BY 4.0
https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/

stories.title: The Names of Mount Olive
stories.blurb: Mount Olive Township is made of two sections, and each one has a story behind its name. Budd Lake is named for John Budd, who acquired thirteen hundred acres of land here in seventeen fourteen. The lake is the largest natural lake in New Jersey. Flanders is named for a group of early settlers who vacationed in Flanders, Long Island. And roads here carry the names of families. Smithtown is named for the many Smiths who lived there, and Drakestown for the Drakes.
music: Carefree by Kevin MacLeod (incompetech.com), CC BY 4.0
https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/

stories.title: Randolph Breaks Away From Mendham
stories.blurb: The first people in what is now Randolph were the Minsi, part of the Lenape. They set up three villages along the Minisink Trail. In the seventeen twenties, a Quaker named John Jackson built the first iron forge. In November of eighteen oh five, the state Legislature let Randolph break away from Mendham, and it became Morris County's sixth municipality. Over the years, Randolph gave up land that became Victory Gardens, Dover and Rockaway Borough.
music: Soaring by Kevin MacLeod (incompetech.com), CC BY 4.0
https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/

stories.title: The Canal That Climbed Mountains
stories.blurb: The Morris Canal ran through Montville. It was built between eighteen twenty-five and eighteen thirty-one, and it ran a hundred and two miles, from Phillipsburg to Jersey City. It was chartered in eighteen twenty-four to carry Pennsylvania coal to markets in the east. Along the way, the canal rose and fell a total of sixteen hundred and seventy-four feet. To handle it, engineers used locks, and also inclined planes. The section in Montville has no locks or inclined planes, but parts of the canal bed and towpath are still there.
music: Realizer by Kevin MacLeod (incompetech.com), CC BY 4.0
https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/

stories.title: The Oldest Iron Mine in New Jersey
stories.blurb: The Dickerson Mine, in Mine Hill, is one of the oldest and most renowned mines in New Jersey. It was the first iron mine registered in the state, in seventeen thirteen. It supplied much of the iron ore used in the Revolutionary War, and it played a major role in the local iron industry for around two hundred years. In nineteen twenty-three, the town broke away from Randolph Township. It took the name Mine Hill, and its old seal showed mining tools.
music: Industrial Revolution by Kevin MacLeod (incompetech.com), CC BY 4.0
https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/

stories.title: Port Oram Votes to Become a Town
stories.blurb: On June twenty-eighth, eighteen ninety-five, voters in five little settlements west of Dover went to the polls. They were Port Oram, Irondale, Luxemburg, Maryville and Mount Pleasant. They voted one hundred forty-three to fifty-one to join together as a town. The new town covered two and a quarter square miles. It took the name of the largest settlement, Port Oram, and today it is called Wharton.
stories.flag: Single source: only one source confirms the details in this story.
music: Promises to Keep by Kevin MacLeod (incompetech.com), CC BY 4.0
https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/

stories.title: Mountain Lakes, A Planned Community
stories.blurb: In nineteen ten, the land that is now Mountain Lakes was rural woodland, owned by a few families named Righter, Grimes, Ball and Van Duyne. Within ten years, the whole place had changed. Mountain Lakes Residential Park was one of the planned communities that sprang up across the country in the early nineteen hundreds. It was designed to bring family and community life together in a natural setting.
music: Relaxing Piano Music by Kevin MacLeod (incompetech.com), CC BY 4.0
https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/

stories.title: Lincoln Park Was Once Beavertown
stories.blurb: Lincoln Park has not always had that name. The area went without a name until eighteen twenty-five, when it became known as Beavertown. The first map of Morris County, published in eighteen fifty-three, labels it that way. In eighteen seventy-two, it was renamed for President Abraham Lincoln. On March eleventh, nineteen twenty-two, Lincoln Park was incorporated as its own borough, separate from Pequannock Township.
music: Shenyang by Kevin MacLeod (incompetech.com), CC BY 4.0
https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/

stories.title: When Rockaway Had Everything
stories.blurb: Early in the nineteen hundreds, Rockaway had two major railroads and a trolley line. It had an iron foundry, a bicycle factory, and a three-story department store. It had an inclined plane and two basins of the Morris Canal. Mines across the mountains supplied local forges. The canal helped turn Rockaway from a quiet settlement into a busy industrial center.
music: Club Diver by Kevin MacLeod (incompetech.com), CC BY 4.0
https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/

stories.title: The Town Built for the War Effort
stories.blurb: Victory Gardens is the smallest town in Morris County, by size and by population. It is also the most densely populated. Its story began in nineteen forty-one, when the federal government bought ninety-one acres in Randolph Township. It built a three-hundred-unit housing project there for workers in the war industry. The government paid for all of the infrastructure, and it named the streets for United States Presidents. The town took its name from the victory gardens that families planted at home during World War Two.
music: Royal Coupling by Kevin MacLeod (incompetech.com), CC BY 4.0
https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/

stories.title: Butler and the Hard Rubber Combs
stories.blurb: Before it was Butler, this was West Bloomingdale. A businessman named Richard Butler bought into a rubber factory there. In eighteen seventy-nine, he became president of the Rubber Comb and Jewelry Company. The factory made hard rubber combs, and later bowling balls. In eighteen eighty-one, the post office was named Butler. On March thirteenth, nineteen oh one, the legislature separated it from Pequannock Township as its own borough. The factory's employment peaked during both World Wars.
stories.flag: Single source: only one source confirms the details in this story.
music: Magic Escape Room by Kevin MacLeod (incompetech.com), CC BY 4.0
https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/

stories.title: The Rubber Man and the Statue of Liberty
stories.blurb: The National Park Service says Richard Butler was a prominent rubber manufacturer. <short pause> It says he was secretary of the American Committee for the Statue of Liberty from 1877 to 1902. <short pause> It says he planned fundraising events for the statue's pedestal. <short pause> It says he used his New Jersey factory to ship statuettes to financial contributors. <short pause> The borough museum's curator says he rode the railroad out to the factory so often that the local stop was informally named Butler.
music: Eternity by Kevin MacLeod (incompetech.com), CC BY 4.0
https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/

stories.title: Florham, The Gilded Age Estate
stories.blurb: In Morris County, along a road once nicknamed Millionaires Row, the Twombly family built a Gilded Age estate. Florence Vanderbilt was a granddaughter of Commodore Cornelius Vanderbilt. Her husband was Hamilton Twombly. They hired the architects McKim, Mead and White, and the landscape designers of Olmsted Associates. They moved in in eighteen ninety-seven. They named the estate Florham, from their first names, Florence and Hamilton. Special trains brought their guests from New York City to a private railroad siding.
stories.flag: Single source: only one source confirms the details in this story.
music: Court of the Queen by Kevin MacLeod (incompetech.com), CC BY 4.0
https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/

stories.title: Greystone Opens Its Doors
stories.blurb: On August seventeenth, eighteen seventy-six, a new state hospital opened its doors in Morris County. It was called the State Asylum for the Insane at Morristown. It had six hundred beds, and it admitted two hundred ninety-two patients. It was New Jersey's second psychiatric hospital. In eighteen ninety-three it was renamed the New Jersey State Hospital at Morris Plains, and in nineteen twenty-five it became Greystone Park. By the late nineteen forties, it held about seven thousand patients. In two thousand eight, the hospital moved to a new treatment center.
music: Ancient Rite by Kevin MacLeod (incompetech.com), CC BY 4.0
https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/

stories.title: Roxbury, Founded in 1740
stories.blurb: On December twenty-fourth, seventeen forty, the New Jersey Legislature created the Township of Roxbury. It covered a vast tract of land that the Lenape had deeded to British mining masters in seventeen oh eight. Iron ore lay close to the surface there, and Roxbury became a center for iron mining and forges. Its forges supplied George Washington and the Continental Army.
music: Journey To Ascend by Kevin MacLeod (incompetech.com), CC BY 4.0
https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/

stories.title: Lake Hopatcong Was Once Two Ponds
stories.blurb: Lake Hopatcong is the largest freshwater lake in New Jersey. But it was not always one lake. It began as two separate bodies of water. The larger was called Great Pond, or Brooklyn Pond. The smaller was called Little Pond, and a stream connected the two. The two were flooded together by damming. Historically, the lake was a resort for vacationing New Yorkers.
music: Airship Serenity by Kevin MacLeod (incompetech.com), CC BY 4.0
https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/

stories.title: Schooley's Mountain Springs
stories.blurb: In Washington Township sits Schooley's Mountain. It was named for the Schooley family, who owned a considerable amount of land there in the seventeen nineties. Natural springs on the mountain helped attract visitors to a resort there. Nearby, German immigrants founded a settlement in the middle of the seventeen hundreds, and it was known as German Valley. Today it is called Long Valley.
stories.flag: Single source: only one source confirms the details in this story.
music: Windswept by Kevin MacLeod (incompetech.com), CC BY 4.0
https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/

stories.title: Denville Is Born
stories.blurb: On April fourteenth, nineteen thirteen, the New Jersey Legislature created the Township of Denville, from portions of Rockaway Township. That year, the Morris County Daily Record cost a penny. Telephone service was just arriving, and crews were putting up poles and running lines out to Craftsman Farms and Mount Tabor. A hundred years later, in twenty thirteen, the Congressional Record honored the township's centennial.
stories.flag: Single source: only one source confirms the details in this story.
music: Hyperfun by Kevin MacLeod (incompetech.com), CC BY 4.0
https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/

stories.title: From Cranberry Pond to Cedar Lake
stories.blurb: The township history says the lake began as a small natural pond called Cranberry Pond. <short pause> It says it was later called Silver Lake. <short pause> It says New York City speculators packaged it for development as Cedar Lake Park in 1907, with home lots advertised at two cents per square foot. <short pause> The town museum says that in 1913, most property owners did not live in town, and many homes were summer homes. <short pause> It says single lots at Cedar Lake and Rock Ridge were assessed at $50.

stories.title: South Stanhope Becomes Netcong
stories.blurb: Netcong began as a place called South Stanhope. In October of eighteen ninety-four, it was incorporated as a borough, using parts of Mount Olive and Roxbury Townships. It covered about one square mile. It took a new name from the Musconetcong River, a name given by the Lenape.
music: Frozen Star by Kevin MacLeod (incompetech.com), CC BY 4.0
https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/

stories.title: Riverdale Was Almost Named West Furnace
stories.blurb: Riverdale became a borough in nineteen twenty-three. When the borough was being organized, the names under consideration were Pompton, West Furnace, Stony Reef and Old Greenwich. In the end, the name chosen was Riverdale.
stories.flag: Single source: only one source confirms the details in this story.
music: Mighty Like Us by Kevin MacLeod (incompetech.com), CC BY 4.0
https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/

stories.title: Saving the Great Swamp from a Jetport
stories.blurb: In nineteen fifty-nine, the Port Authority of New York and New Jersey announced it was considering the Great Swamp, in Morris County, as a site for a big commercial jet airport. The proposed site covered ten thousand acres, and four thousand of them were in the Great Swamp. On December seventeenth, nineteen fifty-nine, they met at the Chatham Fire House. A national campaign raised one million dollars to buy nearly three thousand acres. On November third, nineteen sixty, Congress created the Great Swamp National Wildlife Refuge. It was New Jersey's first national wildlife refuge. Harding Township is home to it.

https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/

stories.title: The Wick House at Jockey Hollow
stories.blurb: Harding Township includes the Jockey Hollow section of Morristown National Historical Park. There stands the Wick House. Henry Wick built it around seventeen fifty, on a fourteen-hundred-acre farm. In the winter of seventeen seventy-nine and seventeen eighty, the soldiers chopped down over six hundred acres of Wick's trees. Major General Arthur St. Clair, who commanded two thousand Pennsylvania soldiers, made his quarters in the house that winter.
stories.flag: Single source: only one source confirms the details in this story.
music: Song of the Volga Boatmen by Kevin MacLeod (incompetech.com), CC BY 4.0
https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/

stories.title: Chatham Township, Named for a Friend of the Colonists
stories.blurb: In eighteen oh six, Chatham Township was incorporated. At first it included what are now Chatham Borough, Madison and Florham Park. It was named in honor of Sir William Pitt, the Earl of Chatham, who had spoken in favor of the colonists in Parliament. Local residents later built Shunpike Road to avoid paying the tolls. In the late eighteen seventies and eighties, greenhouses here grew American Beauty roses.
stories.flag: Single source: only one source confirms the details in this story.
music: Starting Out Waltz Allegretto by Kevin MacLeod (incompetech.com), CC BY 4.0
https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/

stories.title: Passaic Township Becomes Long Hill
stories.blurb: Long Hill Township was incorporated in eighteen sixty-six as Passaic Township. In November of nineteen ninety-two, the voters chose to change the name. They picked Long Hill, for a ridge of the Watchung Mountains. During the Revolution, the Continental Army placed a beacon on that long ridge, to warn of enemy troop movements. The township includes the villages of Gillette, Millington and Stirling.
music: Adeste Fideles (Shorter) by Kevin MacLeod (incompetech.com), CC BY 4.0
https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/

stories.title: East Hanover, Between Two Rivers
stories.blurb: East Hanover Township was incorporated in nineteen twenty-eight. It lies between the Passaic and Whippany rivers. It shares a border with four towns in Essex County. But its roads connect only to Livingston and Roseland. One of its villages, Cedar Knolls, began in nineteen thirteen, when land was subdivided.
stories.flag: Single source: only one source confirms the details in this story.
music: Tiki Bar Mixer by Kevin MacLeod (incompetech.com), CC BY 4.0
https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/

stories.title: The Township That Gave Birth to Towns
stories.blurb: In seventeen forty, Pequannock was created as the largest township in Morris County. Jefferson separated in eighteen oh four. Wharton followed in eighteen ninety-five, and Butler in nineteen oh one. In nineteen twenty-two, Lincoln Park separated from Pequannock too.
stories.flag: Single source: only one source confirms the details in this story.
music: Nowhere Land by Kevin MacLeod (incompetech.com), CC BY 4.0
https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/

stories.title: Morris Township Once Covered Half the County
stories.blurb: In seventeen forty, Morris Township was created. It was named for Lewis Morris, the colonial governor of New Jersey. It originally covered nearly half of Morris County, back when the county had only four municipalities. On December twenty-fourth that same year, a portion of it was taken to form Roxbury. Today Morris County has thirty-nine municipalities.

stories.title: The Powerville Hotel and the Underground Railroad
stories.blurb: In Boonton Township, the Powerville Hotel still stands on North Main Street. It was built near Lock Number Eleven of the Morris Canal, to serve canal and transient trade. Later it became a station on the Underground Railroad. The route ran from Boonton to Powerville, through Rockaway Valley, past where the Split Rock Reservoir is today, and on into West Milford. The hotel's owner was Nathan Hopkins. His son Charles became involved in the railroad as a teenager. In eighteen sixty-one, Charles joined the First New Jersey Volunteer Infantry, and he later became the first mayor of the Town of Boonton.

stories.title: Radio Comes to Boonton Township
stories.blurb: Until the nineteen twenties, Boonton Township kept a bucolic character. Then in nineteen twenty-eight, a highly technical new neighbor arrived. In January of nineteen twenty-nine, an engineering conference marked the opening of the new Radio Frequency Laboratories, with its hangar and flying field. A young Jimmy Doolittle kept his trainer plane at the neighboring Aircraft Radio Corporation. Its staff installed a special radio receiver for an under-the-hood landing at Mitchel Field. By nineteen thirty-three, equipment designed there was installed in the first fighter squadrons of the Army, Air Force and Navy.

stories.title: Chester's Twenty-Eight Iron Mines
stories.blurb: Chester Township started out with the name Black River. Later it was renamed Chester, because Chester, England was the ancestral home of many of its residents. When the Civil War drove up the demand for iron, Chester's mines flourished. By the late eighteen hundreds, the township had twenty-eight active mines. Six of them were on Main Street alone. Then larger deposits were found in Minnesota, in the Mesabi Range. Chester's iron industry quickly waned, and by the eighteen nineties all of its mines had shut down.
stories.flag: Single source: only one source confirms the details in this story.

stories.title: The Log Meeting House Near Ralston
stories.blurb: In seventeen thirteen, an English settler named James Wills bought the land that became Ralston, in Mendham Township. In the seventeen twenties, David Bainard and Eliab Byram set up a settlement along India Brook. They held services in a log meeting house built in the seventeen thirties near the Ralston Curve. That congregation became the First Presbyterian Church, known as Hilltop Church. It moved to its present site on Hilltop Road. Mendham Township itself was officially founded on March twenty-ninth, seventeen forty-nine.

stories.title: The Camp Meeting by the Sea
stories.blurb: In May of eighteen sixty-nine, a group of Methodist ministers searched the New Jersey coast for a place to hold camp meetings. They found a nearly empty grove, free of mosquitoes, between two lakes and the Atlantic. About twenty people gathered in tents and held their first prayer meeting on July thirty-first. In eighteen seventy, the State Legislature chartered the Ocean Grove Camp Meeting Association. The Great Auditorium was built in eighteen ninety-four. At first it held almost ten thousand people. Today it seats sixty-two hundred fifty.

stories.title: The Great Auditorium Organ
stories.blurb: The Garden State Theatre Organ Society says ground was broken for the Great Auditorium in Ocean Grove on December 2nd, 1893, and it was ready for the camp meeting in 1894. <short pause> It says the front was extended in 1907 to make room for a new pipe organ. <short pause> It says the organ was installed in 1908 at a total cost of $26,000, half of it donated by the builder's company. <short pause> The Ocean Grove Camp Meeting Association says the organ got major financial support from Samuel Clemens, better known as Mark Twain. <short pause> It says the organ was dedicated at a concert on July 3rd, 1908, with over 8,000 people in attendance.

stories.title: Molly Pitcher and the Hottest Day at Monmouth
stories.blurb: On June twenty-eighth, seventeen seventy-eight, a battle raged a few miles west of Freehold. It included some of the longest combat of the Revolutionary War, and the largest artillery duel of any battle. Along the American gun line on Perrine Ridge stood twenty-three-year-old Mary Ludwig Hays, with her husband William and the gunners of the Fourth Continental Artillery. Many gunners fell from exhaustion and heat stroke. Mary was seen running pails of water from a spring. She ran ammunition to the gunners. She was recorded helping to load and fire her husband's gun. Soldier Joseph Plumb Martin remembered a woman who attended the gun the whole time. The Americans lost sixty-nine dead, one hundred sixty-one wounded and one hundred forty missing.

stories.title: Springsteen's Freehold
stories.blurb: Freehold is the hometown of Bruce Springsteen. He lived as a toddler in his grandparents' house on Randolph Street, which was later torn down for a church parking lot. At age five, he moved with his family to a two-family house on Institute Street. His last Freehold home was a two-family house on South Street, where, as a teenager, he picked up the guitar and joined his first band. He graduated from Freehold Borough High School in nineteen sixty-seven, and Columbia Records signed him in nineteen seventy-two. In his autobiography, he wrote about leaving Freehold in nineteen sixty-nine: "This town, my town, would never leave me, and I could never completely leave it, but I would never live in Freehold again."

stories.title: America's Oldest Racetrack
stories.blurb: The Associated Press called Freehold Raceway the oldest horse racing track in the United States. <short pause> It says horse racing has been held at the half-mile track since the 1830s. <short pause> It says harness racing became the staple when the Monmouth County Agricultural Society was formed in late 1853. <short pause> U.S. Trotting News says harness racing at Freehold was formally created in 1853. <short pause> Horse Racing Nation says the track ran its last harness race in December 2024, 171 years after it opened.

stories.title: The Iron Village of Howell Works
stories.blurb: In eighteen twenty-two, steam engine builder James Allaire bought land in what is now Wall Township and named it the Howell Works. It grew into a self-sufficient village of four hundred people. It made pig iron, which was shipped to Allaire's foundry in New York for steamship engines and boilers. It also cast pots, kettles and cauldrons. Eighteen thirty-six was its most prosperous year. Then came the economic depression of eighteen thirty-seven. The furnace fires went out in eighteen forty-eight. Thirteen of the original buildings still stand.

stories.title: The Circus Drive-In
stories.blurb: The Circus Drive-In stood on Route Thirty-five in Wall Township. Richard and Barbara Friedel opened it in nineteen fifty-four. The building was round, designed to look like a circus tent. Carhops brought food to customers' cars. Its neon sign was a smiling clown, designed by Barbara Friedel. It was known for its battered onion rings and fried soft-shell crab. The Circus Drive-In closed in two thousand seventeen.

stories.title: Applejack and the Oldest Distillery in America
stories.blurb: In Scobeyville, a section of Colts Neck, stands Laird and Company, called the oldest distillery in the country. Around sixteen ninety-eight, a Scotsman named William Laird settled in Monmouth County. He began distilling apples into apple brandy, called applejack. George Washington asked for Laird's recipe for cider spirits, and received it. According to New Jersey Monthly, in seventeen eighty, Laird's received the new nation's first distillery permit. During Prohibition, it kept going under a federal license to make apple brandy for medicinal purposes. Today the aging and bottling still happen in Scobeyville.

stories.title: Up Goes Huddy
stories.blurb: This is a heavier story. On April twelfth, seventeen eighty-two, a party of Loyalists led by Richard Lippincott hanged Joshua Huddy of Colts Neck on the Navesink Highlands. It was in retaliation for the killing of a Loyalist, Philip White. A note pinned to Huddy ended, "Up goes Huddy for Philip White." His body was brought to Freehold the next day. George Washington threatened to execute a British officer unless Lippincott was turned over. The British refused but tried Lippincott by court-martial, and he was found not guilty. The British officer chosen was nineteen-year-old Captain Charles Asgill, picked by drawing papers from a hat. After months of deliberation, Congress and Washington decided he should be released. On November thirteenth, seventeen eighty-two, Washington notified him.
stories.sensitive: Heavier story: this one covers a wartime hanging in 1782. Listener discretion advised.

stories.title: The Grand Hotel That Burned in Nineteen Hundred
stories.blurb: On April twenty-ninth, eighteen seventy-five, a farm was sold for eighty-two thousand dollars to start a seaside resort called Spring Lake Beach. A minister had first hoped for a Methodist camp like Ocean Grove. The Monmouth House opened in June of eighteen seventy-six, with two hundred fifty rooms, a thousand-seat dining room, and a steam-operated elevator. On September nineteenth, nineteen hundred, the Monmouth House and twelve other buildings burned in the worst fire in Spring Lake's history. Three years later, a rebuilt hotel opened as the New Monmouth Hotel, at a cost of three hundred fifty thousand dollars. It was torn down in nineteen seventy-five.

stories.title: The Jewel of the Jersey Shore
stories.blurb: The Essex and Sussex Hotel stands on Ocean Avenue in Spring Lake. It was built in nineteen fourteen and could hold up to four hundred guests. The Asbury Park Press said it was often considered the Jewel of the Jersey Shore. In its heyday it was open only three months each summer. It was a hotel for seventy-one years, and closed for good in nineteen eighty-five. The building was later restored as a condominium community with a hundred sixty-five units.

stories.title: The Phantom Ball at the Essex and Sussex
stories.blurb: The Essex and Sussex Hotel is said to be haunted. Weird NJ published a reader's story from about nineteen eighty-two. A man working on a carpet crew in the closed hotel in winter said he saw a dark blur moving at the end of a fifth-floor hallway. The caretaker told him he had seen something similar on that floor. The caretaker also said that late at night, in the dead of winter, he sometimes hears a party in the ballroom, with music, talking, laughing, and glasses tinkling. He said it stops when he reaches for the door handle. These are reported accounts, not confirmed facts.
stories.flag: SINGLE-ish: the haunting account rests on one reader story (Weird NJ); nj.com repeats it with a different detail (a ghostly female).

stories.title: The Shark in Matawan Creek
stories.blurb: In July of nineteen sixteen, a heat wave and a polio epidemic sent thousands of people to the Jersey Shore. Between July first and July twelfth, sharks killed four people along the coast. On July twelfth, a retired sea captain on a bridge over Matawan Creek saw a shark about eight feet long, swimming up the creek. Matawan was several miles inland, and looked more like a Midwestern town than a beach resort. He ran through the town shouting warnings. No one believed him. Then, a boy swimming in the creek was attacked. A local shopkeeper and other men dove in to try to recover him. The shopkeeper was attacked as well. Another boy, swimming half a mile away, was bitten, and survived. Two days later, a shark was caught in Raritan Bay, a few miles from the creek. Scientists of the day identified it as a young great white. No more attacks were reported along the Jersey Shore that year.
stories.sensitive: Heavier story: this one covers deadly violence. Listener discretion advised.

stories.title: The Corn King's Mansion
stories.blurb: In Matawan stands the Burrowes Mansion, built in seventeen twenty-three by John Bowne the Third. It is one of Monmouth County's most important early Georgian buildings. In seventeen sixty-nine, Bowne sold it to a wealthy grain merchant, John Burrowes Senior, known as the "Corn King." He was a member of the Sons of Liberty, and he supplied provisions to the Continental Army. His property was opened up as a mustering and training ground for the first New Jersey Company of the Continental Army. His son, John Burrowes Junior, organized the local militia and later served as a Captain, then a Major, in the Continental Army. In seventeen seventy-eight, the mansion was the site of a famous skirmish between local Patriots and Loyalist forces. Today it is a museum.

stories.title: How Squan Village Got Its Name
stories.blurb: Manasquan takes its name from the Manasquan River. But the name was not official until eighteen eighty-seven, when the town broke away from Wall Township to become its own community. During the Revolutionary War, the Manasquan Inlet became a refuge for small boats. A small seaport began to take shape. In eighteen oh eight, an inn called the Osborn House was built. The town was laid out in the shape of a cross, along South Street and Main Street. Timothy Bloomfield ran the inn until eighteen twenty-five. He is credited with naming the settlement Squan Village.

stories.title: From Crabtown to Manasquan
stories.blurb: In eighteen seventy-seven, a newspaper called The Sea Side looked back on Manasquan's past. It said men were still living who remembered when Squan was called "Crabtown." But now, the paper said, "thousands flock hither and are sorry when the time comes for them to leave." In the eighteen eighties, rail service came from both Philadelphia and New York. More than seventy sea captains lived in Manasquan in the nineteenth century. Pound fishing went on until the middle of the twentieth century. Long wooden boats were drawn out of the surf by horse teams.

stories.title: The Life Saving Station on Squan Beach
stories.blurb: On the Manasquan oceanfront stands the Squan Beach Life Saving Station. The Coast Guard's history office says a station here is believed to date to eighteen fifty-six. Its nineteen oh two annual report says the old station was unsuitable and was being replaced by a new structure. The station's own group says the new building was commissioned in nineteen oh four. It became part of the Coast Guard in nineteen fifteen. The group says the Coast Guard left in nineteen ninety-six and the borough bought the station in two thousand for one dollar.

stories.title: The Inlet That Closed
stories.blurb: The Manasquan Inlet connects the Atlantic Ocean to the Manasquan River and divides Monmouth and Ocean counties. A Point Pleasant history timeline says it once disappeared. When the Point Pleasant Canal opened in nineteen twenty-five, the river's water rushed down the canal and the inlet began to close. By nineteen twenty-eight and twenty-nine, the timeline says, the inlet no longer existed and fishermen were out of business. It was reopened in nineteen thirty-one after a year of construction. Jetties were built for the first time to keep it from shifting and closing again.

stories.title: Did Washington Really Sleep at the Village Inn?
stories.blurb: The Village Inn in Englishtown was first built in seventeen thirty-two. Local tradition says George Washington stayed there during the Battle of Monmouth, in late June of seventeen seventy-eight. The tradition says it was here that he wrote the orders for the court-martial of General Charles Lee. The Liberty Trail says the order for Lee to attack the next morning, June twenty-eighth, was given at this tavern. But a federal record of the building says a report in nineteen eighty-two found no documents to support the Washington story, and none to contradict it.

stories.title: The Town Inside the Doughnut
stories.blurb: Englishtown covers just over half a square mile, and it sits entirely inside another town. The borough is completely surrounded by Manalapan Township, which makes it one of the so-called doughnut towns. It was formed from part of Manalapan on January fourth, eighteen eighty-eight, after a referendum the day before. The borough's website says the earliest record is an Englishman, James Johnston, owning property there in sixteen eighty-eight. Sometime before seventeen thirty, the English family bought a large tract, and the area was named Englishtown after the family. In seventeen seventy-seven, one of the county's main roads ran from Monmouth Court House, now Freehold, through Englishtown. Being on a main highway made it a trading center.

stories.title: Musket Shots at the Church Pulpit
stories.blurb: At the Historic Four Corners in Shrewsbury stands Christ Church. The congregation was established in seventeen oh two, and the present building went up between seventeen sixty-nine and seventeen seventy-five. During the Revolution, American soldiers used it as a barracks. The church was Anglican then, a symbol of the British Crown. According to the Shrewsbury Historical Society, in protest, the soldiers fired musket shots at the pulpit, and at the orb and crown on the steeple. At the same intersection, the Allen House became the Blue Ball Tavern in seventeen fifty-four. It ran for almost sixty years, and was called the most noted tavern in Shrewsbury.

stories.title: The Summer Capital at Sea Girt
stories.blurb: In eighteen eighty-seven, the New Jersey Legislature bought one hundred twenty acres at Sea Girt, for fifty-one thousand dollars. The land became a permanent summer camp, rifle range and coastal battery for the National Guard. It also became the summer capital of New Jersey. The governors spent the warm months there until the Second World War. The Sea Girt lighthouse marked the inlet to Wreck Pond. It hosted the first radio beacon on a shore installation in the United States. It was the last shore lighthouse with a keeper's residence built into it on the East Coast. The light was decommissioned in nineteen fifty-five.

stories.title: Robert Louis Stevenson at the Union House
stories.blurb: In May of eighteen eighty-eight, the writer Robert Louis Stevenson arrived at the Union House, a small, quiet inn on the Manasquan River. It stood in what is now Brielle. His health was poor, and he had come to recuperate. He stayed from May second to May twenty-eighth. While there, he finalized plans for a voyage to the South Seas aboard the yacht Casco. According to the borough, he also wrote part of his novel The Master of Ballantrae. In eighteen eighty-one, the Brielle Land Association bought a hundred fifty acres nearby. It named the place Brielle, after a Dutch town one of its members had visited.

stories.title: The Salt Works Scandal
stories.blurb: In the Revolutionary War, a British blockade left the new nation short of salt. Salt kept food from spoiling. A dozen salt works sprang up along the Monmouth shore within a year. The most productive, in April of seventeen seventy-eight, was the Union Salt Works on the Manasquan River, in what is now Brielle. The only force assigned to protect the works was Colonel David Forman's undersized regiment. Historian Michael Adelberg calls it a blatant conflict of interest that Forman used that regiment to build the Union Salt Works. In the resulting scandal, Forman lost command of the regiment. It was sent to Valley Forge in late March. That April, Loyalists and British troops destroyed the works and sacked the settlement around it. After repairs, the works were running again.

stories.title: The Town That Was Built for Garment Workers
stories.blurb: Under the New Deal, a group of activists bought twelve hundred acres in Monmouth County. They planned a community for former garment workers from New York and Philadelphia. They named it Jersey Homesteads in nineteen thirty-six. It became a borough in May of nineteen thirty-seven. The town had a cooperative farm, a cooperative garment factory, and cooperative stores. On November ninth, nineteen forty-five, seven months after the death of President Franklin Roosevelt, the town was renamed Roosevelt in his honor.

stories.title: Ben Shahn's Mural in the Schoolhouse
stories.blurb: In nineteen thirty-seven, the Farm Security Administration commissioned artist Ben Shahn to paint a mural for the new community of Jersey Homesteads. He worked on it with his partner, Bernarda Bryson, who later became his wife. It is a fresco, painted on fresh, moist plaster. It was Shahn's first completed mural. He had learned the technique while working with Diego Rivera on a mural for Rockefeller Center in New York. The two finished it in nineteen thirty-eight. It can still be seen today in the Roosevelt Public School.

stories.title: The Salt Works on the Shark River
stories.blurb: According to the Monmouth County Clerk's archives, salt works were started along the Shark River, in what is now Belmar, about seventeen fifty-five. On April sixth, seventeen seventy-eight, about one hundred thirty-five British soldiers attacked and destroyed them. Local militia drove the raiders off. A report from the time says two Shark River salt works were set on fire. In eighteen seventy-two, twenty-five businessmen who had summered at Ocean Grove decided they wanted a new summer community. They chose the south shore of the Shark River.

stories.title: How Ocean Beach Became Belmar
stories.blurb: Belmar did not start out as Belmar. In eighteen seventy-two, a group of twenty-five businessmen from Philadelphia and New York, who had summered in Ocean Grove, wanted a new summer community. The Ocean Beach Association was incorporated on March thirteenth, eighteen seventy-three. The town was planned with twelve avenues, each eighty feet wide, running from the ocean to the Shark River. The first hotel, the Ocean Beach House, was built that summer. The town was incorporated as Ocean Beach in eighteen eighty-five. But by eighteen eighty-nine, residents wanted a new name, because of confusion with towns like Ocean City and Oceanport. According to Wikipedia, the borough was briefly renamed Elcho for a few weeks. On May fourteenth, eighteen eighty-nine, residents voted sixty-three to none for Belmar, which is French for "beautiful sea."

stories.title: Aeromarine Brings Seaplanes to Keyport
stories.blurb: In March of nineteen fourteen, Inglis Uppercu, president of the Cadillac Motor Car Company of New York, reorganized his business as the Aeromarine Plane and Motor Company, in Nutley. Two years later, he moved it to a sixty-acre waterfront tract in Keyport, on the site of an old brickyard. At the Keyport plant, the company built whole aircraft, including hulls, engines and wings. During World War One, Aeromarine became one of the country's leading builders of seaplanes and flying boats for the Navy. In the nineteen twenties, it also ran an airline. The Smithsonian says an Aeromarine aircraft was the first to fly from New York to Key West to Havana and back.

stories.title: The Astaires Debut in Keyport
stories.blurb: Fred and Adele Astaire made their professional debut in Keyport. Fred was born Frederick Austerlitz in Omaha, Nebraska. At age four, his mother brought him and his sister Adele to New York to study dance. After less than a year of school, the two made their debut in Keyport, billed as "The Astaires." According to Wikipedia, the new name came from their mother, who thought Austerlitz recalled the Battle of Austerlitz. The local paper praised them as "the greatest child act in vaudeville."

stories.title: Two Men Row Across the Atlantic
stories.blurb: On June sixth, eighteen ninety-six, two Norwegian-born men from Atlantic Highlands set out from New York in a rowboat. George Harbo was twenty-seven and a licensed steamboat pilot. Frank Samuelson was thirty-one. They were headed for Le Havre, France. They had spent their savings on an eighteen-foot oak boat, with sealed compartments for flotation. They named it the Fox, after Richard Fox, the owner of the Police Gazette, who had challenged rowers to the crossing. The trip lasted fifty-five days. At a dinner in Paris, Fox gave each man a gold medal. The two never received prize money.

stories.title: Simon Lake Tests a Submarine at Atlantic Highlands
stories.blurb: Simon Lake is considered by some to be the father of the submarine. In the winter of eighteen ninety-four, he built a boat called the Argonaut Junior at Atlantic Highlands, New Jersey. He did most of the work with his own hands. The boat was fourteen feet long, four and one-half feet wide, and about five feet high. Lake tested it at Atlantic Highlands, and the New York Herald reported on the testing in its issue of January eighth, eighteen ninety-five.

stories.title: Steamers and the Pier at Atlantic Highlands
stories.blurb: A substantial pier was built out into the bay at Atlantic Highlands to meet steamboats from New York City. The Central Railroad of New Jersey built a major pier at the end of First Avenue. Several trains at a time could continue to the end of the pier to unload steamboat passengers. From the nineteen-tens through the forties, the steamers Sandy Hook and Monmouth brought businessmen and vacationers. In the nineteen twenties, twenty-six passenger trains passed through the borough every day. In nineteen sixty-two, the railroad pier was destroyed by fire. In nineteen ninety-two, high-speed ferry service began.

stories.title: America's Oldest Racetrack Closes
stories.blurb: In December of eighteen fifty-three, the Monmouth County Agriculture Society was formed to hold an annual fair with harness racing in the Township of Freehold. The next year, it rented a ten-acre plot of land. That plot is now the site of Freehold Raceway. On Saturday, December twenty-eighth, twenty twenty-four, the track ran its last harness race, one hundred seventy-one years after it opened. It was America's oldest active venue for racehorses. About a thousand fans came out in the rain. Eleven races were run. The last was won by a pacer named T's Raider II.

https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/

stories.title: A Touch of Mongolia in Howell
stories.blurb: In nineteen fifty-one, the United States allowed Kalmyk refugees to immigrate. The Kalmyks are an ethnic group of Mongolian origin who moved to southeast Europe in the seventeenth century. About eight hundred of them had been sent to refugee camps near Munich after World War Two. That year, five hundred seventy-one Kalmyks came to the United States. Most settled in Philadelphia or in the Freewood Acres section of Howell Township. By the summer of nineteen fifty-two, about two hundred had settled there for good. Their traditional religion is Tibetan Buddhism, and Howell is home to a Kalmyk Buddhist temple, the Tashi Lhunpo Temple. In nineteen ninety-seven, the Kalmyk-American Cultural Association was founded in Howell.
