stories.title: The Preventorium in Howell
stories.blurb: In eighteen twenty-two, James Allaire bought five thousand acres in Howell and built an iron company town around the Monmouth Furnace. In nineteen oh seven, a journalist named Arthur Brisbane bought five thousand acres in Howell, including the former Allaire Village. He wanted to create a Preventorium. It was a place to keep children who had been in contact with people with tuberculosis so the children would not catch the disease. Up to two hundred thirty children were housed there. Brisbane built it on what is now the site of the Howell Municipal Complex, which houses a library branch.

https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/

stories.title: The First Haskell
stories.blurb: On August third, nineteen sixty-eight, thirty-nine thousand forty-two fans came to Monmouth Park in Oceanport for the closing day of the summer meet. The race was the Monmouth Invitational Handicap, with eleven horses. A thirty-three-to-one longshot named Balustrade, ridden by Eric Walsh, won it in one minute, fifty seconds. The race honored Amory Haskell, the first president of the Monmouth Park Jockey Club, who had died two years earlier. Today, it is known as the Haskell Invitational Stakes.

stories.title: Whitey Ford's Army Years
stories.blurb: In nineteen fifty, New York Yankees pitcher Whitey Ford enlisted in the Army during the Korean War. He was ordered to Fort Monmouth, where his basic training began that November. According to the Fort Monmouth history site, he lived in Monmouth Beach while he was enlisted, and fellow Yankees would often visit. Ford spent two years in the Signal Corps and led the Fort Monmouth Signaleers to an eighty-three and nineteen record. He said, "Army life was rough. Would you believe it, they actually wanted me to pitch three times a week." He was discharged in November of nineteen fifty-two.

stories.title: The Last Drive-In of the Golden Age
stories.blurb: On June thirtieth, nineteen fifty-six, the Loew's Route 35 Drive-In opened in Hazlet. It was built on a former watermelon farm that had been planned for a shopping center. It was the first open-air theater Loew's built in New Jersey, designed as a family-safe destination. Kids got in free. There were hot dogs and other boardwalk food, and restrooms. The first movie on the screen was The Searchers, starring John Wayne. It ran for thirty-five years. It closed on September fourth, nineteen ninety-one, and was demolished. It was the last of the Golden Age drive-ins in New Jersey.

stories.title: The Township That Lost Its Bay
stories.blurb: In eighteen forty-eight, the township of Raritan was created from Middletown Township. It included what are now Holmdel, Aberdeen, Matawan, Keyport, Union Beach, and Keansburg. The name Raritan was chosen because the township had frontage on Raritan Bay. But between eighteen fifty-four and nineteen twenty-five, those towns were split off by acts of the legislature until the township was about five and a half square miles with no bay frontage left. Other places in New Jersey shared the name Raritan, and that became an issue. In nineteen sixty-seven, a vote at the general election changed the name to Hazlet. It came from a landowner by that name in the southern part of the township, part of whose property was used for the new rail line. The name was used for the new train station and the existing post office.

stories.title: The British Army's Unpleasant Stay in Allentown
stories.blurb: On June fifteenth, seventeen seventy-eight, the British Army began crossing the Delaware River into New Jersey. It was slowed by thousands of Loyalists and camp followers and a huge baggage train, and stretched twelve miles along poor roads in unusually hot weather. New Jersey militia made it worse. They felled trees across the roads, fouled the wells, and skirmished along the way. On June twenty-fourth, the front of the army reached Allentown and found the bridge torn up. A German officer wrote that rebuilding it kept them three hours. Sir Henry Clinton's First Division, about eleven thousand soldiers, camped in and around the town. When they left, most expected them to turn northeast, toward Cranbury. They marched east, toward Freehold. Four days later, they met at Monmouth Court House, in the Battle of Monmouth.

stories.title: The Mills and the Brass Door-Knocker
stories.blurb: Around seventeen fourteen, Nathan Allen built a gristmill and a fulling mill in Allentown. He began selling lots. The gristmill processed grain for flour, animal feed, and molasses. At the fulling mill, flax and wool were cleaned for weaving. Colonial Allentown also had a brewery and a molasses factory near the gristmill. In seventeen fifty, Nathan Allen Junior's widow, Elizabeth Salter Allen, sold the Mill House to Stoffel Longstreet. A brass door knocker engraved with the Allen family name was still on the door. About eighteen fifty, Abel Cafferty bought the mill complex. He removed the door knocker and returned it to the Allen family.

stories.title: The Stagecoach Crossroads
stories.blurb: Main Street in Allentown grew out of the Lower York Road. Deputy Governor Gawen Lawrie authorized the road in sixteen eighty-three. It connected Perth Amboy, the capital of East Jersey, with Burlington, the capital of West Jersey. It was also called Lawrie's Road or the Queen's Highway. In seventeen thirty-four, Samuel Rogers Senior of Allentown and Arthur Brown of New York advertised a carriage service between New York and Philadelphia. The trip usually took two or three days. Allentown became a market village and a rest stop for travelers. Taverns, also called ordinaries, were set up to serve them.

stories.title: Who Was Allentown Named For
stories.blurb: Allentown was named for Nathan Allen, according to a local history. Robert Burnett, a Scottish Quaker, patented four thousand acres east of Doctors Creek. His daughter Margaret married Nathan Allen. In seventeen oh six, Allen acquired two pieces of land from his father-in-law. One was a hundred and ten acres east of Doctors Creek. The name Allen's Town appears on a seventeen forty-nine map by Lewis Evans. By seventeen ninety-five, the village was Allentown on a road map. Wikipedia notes that some say it was named for William Allen, a Chief Justice of Pennsylvania, instead.

stories.title: The Flying Jeeps of Red Bank Airport
stories.blurb: During World War Two, residents of Monmouth County saw small military planes overhead. They were called Flying Jeeps, and they were not to be discussed in wartime. They were Stinson L-five Sentinels, light aircraft designed to be reliable, easy to fly, and able to use short, unpaved airstrips. They were based at Red Bank Airport, in what is now Tinton Falls. Air View, Incorporated, built the airport in nineteen twenty-six, with aerial photography, air taxi service, flight training and sightseeing flights. After a series of accidents caused a public outcry, it closed in nineteen seventy.

stories.title: Thirty-Two Soldiers and Two Model T Trucks
stories.blurb: On June third, nineteen seventeen, thirty-two soldiers of the U.S. Army Signal Corps arrived in Little Silver in two Model T Ford trucks. The site would become Fort Monmouth. It was first called Camp Little Silver. The soldiers built a camp, supply facilities and a hospital, all under canvas, to train Signal Corps reserve battalions. On September fifteenth, nineteen seventeen, it was renamed Camp Vail, after Alfred Vail, a colleague of Samuel Morse. The Signal Corps School started classes there in nineteen nineteen. In nineteen twenty-five, the camp became permanent and took the name Fort Monmouth, honoring fallen soldiers of the Battle of Monmouth.

stories.title: Peter Parker and the Name Little Silver
stories.blurb: Peter Parker came from Rhode Island and built a small cabin along the Native American trail now known as Rumson Road. He named his land Little Silver after his father's estate in Portsmouth, Rhode Island. For many years, the area was known as Parkerville. The post office name Parkerville was changed to Little Silver on July thirtieth, eighteen seventy-nine. Parker's descendants lived in the home for eight generations, three hundred thirty years. Their farm grew into a successful apple and peach orchard.

stories.title: Lovett's Nursery and the Prize Grape
stories.blurb: John Thompson Lovett was born in Pennsylvania and moved to Monmouth County at age twenty-five. He worked for a nursery in Rumson for six years, then started his own. His nursery in Little Silver became the largest on the East Coast, according to the borough. In nineteen oh four, Little Silver had about eight hundred twenty-five people, and many worked for Lovett's nursery. On September twenty-fourth, nineteen twelve, Lovett and Dr. Walter Van Fleet won a gold medal in New York for the Caco grape, a Catawba and Concord hybrid. It was the highest award ever given a new variety of grape.

stories.title: The Wreck of the New Era
stories.blurb: On November thirteenth, eighteen fifty-four, the ship New Era, carrying German immigrants from Bremen, was blown onto the shoals off Deal Beach in heavy weather. They were within sight of their destination. Rough seas made the rescue boats of little use, and attempts to get a line to the ship failed. About two hundred forty people died. Investigators found the captain and mate at fault. The disaster provoked revulsion across the nation. In eighteen seventy-eight, Congress established the United States Life-Saving Service as a better-equipped professional organization.

stories.title: The Meteorite That Fell on Deal
stories.blurb: In eighteen twenty-nine, a meteorite fell in Deal, New Jersey. Its fall was observed. According to Wikipedia, it came down at eleven-thirty at night on August fourteenth. The recovered stone weighed twenty-eight grams, less than an ounce. It was officially named "Deal," and it is classified as an ordinary chondrite. The Meteoritical Bulletin lists it as one of just three approved meteorites from New Jersey.

stories.title: The Club That Moved Twice
stories.blurb: Hollywood Golf Club in Deal was established in eighteen ninety-eight. Its first nine-hole course lasted only four years before the club moved to another site. It moved again to its present location in nineteen twelve. The course there was designed by Walter Travis in nineteen seventeen. In two thousand fourteen, Tom Doak's firm, Renaissance Golf Design, restored it. That year, the club hosted the U.S. Senior Women's Amateur.

stories.title: The Chapel That Moved to Survive
stories.blurb: In eighteen eighty-two, a chapel was built in Fair Haven for the African Methodist Episcopal Bethel congregation. It was named Fisk Chapel for Union General Clinton Fisk, who after the Civil War ran the Freedmen's Bureau. Fisk provided the land. The Monmouth Timeline reports he also gave three thousand dollars toward the building. It is a Carpenter Gothic chapel. In nineteen seventy-five, it was moved from Fisk Street to Cedar Avenue to avoid demolition, and was added to the National Register of Historic Places. Today it is the oldest building in Fair Haven, now an events venue called Bicentennial Hall, with a new Fisk Chapel A.M.E. Bethel Church at the original site.

stories.title: The Vaudevillians of the Navesink
stories.blurb: The borough history says steamboats on the New York to Red Bank run made regular stops at Chandler's Dock by 1850. <short pause> It says the boats carried oysters and other river harvests to the city. <short pause> It says two boats depicted on the borough seal brought numerous summer visitors, many of them famous vaudevillians. <short pause> It says the vaudevillians organized the Players Club, whose site is now home to a yacht club. <short pause> The Two River Times says the borough's history includes a colony of actors and tradesmen on the river.

stories.title: The Hospital on the Hill
stories.blurb: Marlboro Psychiatric Hospital began construction in nineteen twenty-nine, and opened in early nineteen thirty-one. It was run by the State of New Jersey. Its campus covered four hundred sixty-eight acres, enclosed by a perimeter fence. The last structures were built in nineteen seventy-four. The hospital closed on July first, nineteen ninety-eight. In October of twenty eleven, the state announced the site would become open space under the Monmouth County Park System. Demolition began in May of twenty fourteen, and by July of twenty sixteen, the buildings, lights, roads and underground structures were completely removed.

stories.title: Marlboro and the Hornet's Nest
stories.blurb: Marlboro takes its name from marl. In seventeen sixty-eight, marl was discovered on a farm just east of Marlboro Village. Marl is made of the remains of prehistoric fish, clams, and other sea life from when New Jersey was part of the ocean bed. Farmers used it to improve their soil before commercial fertilizers existed, and demand from all parts of the country created one of Marlboro's first industries. During the Revolutionary War, there were many skirmishes between British troops and the Monmouth militia. The area around Pleasant Valley Road, where the British foraged, was called the "Hornet's nest" because of the intensity of the militia's attacks. Beacon Hill was one of three Monmouth County sites where beacons warned of the enemy's approach by the bay.

stories.title: Land of Good Bread
stories.blurb: Manalapan Township was formed on March ninth, eighteen forty-eight, out of part of Freehold Township. Leading citizens met in Phebe Perrine's tavern in Englishtown, and held a second meeting on March twenty-fourth, where township officers were elected. The name comes from Lenape words for drinking and bread, and is translated as "good land to settle upon." Records say nothing about how the name was chosen. That same year, a northern part of Freehold Township was set up as Marlboro. And part of the Battle of Monmouth, in seventeen seventy-eight, was fought on land that is now Manalapan and Freehold.

stories.title: A Tavern Meeting Creates Manalapan Township
stories.blurb: In the winter of eighteen forty-eight, the New Jersey Legislature told the people of western Freehold Township that they would become a new independent township. Manalapan Township was officially formed on March ninth, when leading citizens met in Phebe Perrine's tavern in Englishtown. At a second meeting on March twenty-fourth, in the same tavern, they elected township officers. They voted to raise the same amount of school money as the State appropriation, five hundred dollars for highways, and three hundred dollars for the poor. They also resolved that there would be five road districts. The township offices stayed in Englishtown until eighteen eighty-eight. Then Englishtown became its own borough, and the township moved its offices to Tennent.

stories.title: Apple Whiskey and Seven Mills in Manalapan
stories.blurb: Manalapan was a farming community. Its products included wheat, rye, barley, corn, oats, and vegetables. The Beers Atlas of eighteen seventy-three lists twenty-eight businesses. They include farmers, mill owners, blacksmiths, wheelwrights, horse and mule dealers, and distillers of apple whiskey. Seven mills were operating then, including grist and sawmills and two woolen mills. Only the building that housed the gristmill at Millhurst still exists. Goods traveled by horse and wagon over toll roads to the shipping ports of Matawan and Keyport. In the census of eighteen fifty, the township had one thousand nine hundred ten people, and Englishtown was larger than Monmouth Court House, which is now Freehold.

stories.title: A Borough Made by Bill
stories.blurb: Union Beach began as a hundred-acre farm owned by the Poole family since the days of the Revolutionary War. In nineteen oh eight, the farm became the Union Subdivision. The first fire company organized in nineteen twenty, and the post office opened in Charles Parry's grocery store in nineteen twenty-one. A committee brought the question of leaving Raritan Township, now Hazlet, to State Senator William Stevens. His bill passed, and Governor George Silzer signed it on March sixteenth, nineteen twenty-five. Township votes approved within forty days, and Charles Miller chaired the first council meeting as mayor on May eighteenth, nineteen twenty-five.

stories.title: Whitey Ford Joins the Signaleers
stories.blurb: In nineteen fifty, Yankees pitcher Whitey Ford had just helped win the World Series. Then he enlisted in the Army during the Korean War, and was ordered to Fort Monmouth, where he began basic training in November. He joined the Signal Corps baseball team, the Signaleers. They won forty-two games and lost ten in nineteen fifty-one, and won forty-one and lost nine in nineteen fifty-two. Crowds of up to four thousand came to watch. He went on to win the Cy Young Award in nineteen sixty-one, and was elected to the Baseball Hall of Fame in nineteen seventy-four.

stories.title: A Lynching Remembered in Eatontown
stories.blurb: This is a heavier story. In eighteen eighty-six, a mob broke into the borough lockup in Eatontown and lynched a Black man who was being held for a crime against a white woman. He was a former slave and a married father of five. It is New Jersey's only documented lynching of the nineteenth century. Information from a later trial led many people to believe he could have been innocent. In two thousand twelve, a memorial plaque was placed in Wampum Park. Mayor Gerald Tarantolo called it a low point in the history of Eatontown, and he apologized, saying the security at the jail failed. The council president said, a man was lynched here and had no trial.

stories.title: Thomas Eaton's Mill and the Stagecoach Stop
stories.blurb: In sixteen seventy, Thomas Eaton, for whom Eatontown is named, surveyed the area and built a grist mill in what is now Wampum Lake Park. By seventeen ninety-six, a village had grown up across from the mill. A tavern for the New York to Philadelphia stagecoach trade was built where Main and Broad Streets meet. By eighteen fifty, the village had four stores on Main Street and nearly forty homes. The Eatontown Steamboat Company built docks on Oceanport Creek to ship flour and farm produce to New York. James P. Allaire built a four-story stone warehouse there to ship bog iron forged at the Howell Works, fifteen miles away.

stories.title: Rum, a Chief, or Navarumsunk
stories.blurb: Rumson sits on a peninsula, bounded by the Navesink and Shrewsbury Rivers. The borough historian says the area was inhabited for almost four thousand years before English settlers arrived in sixteen sixty-five. The first land purchase was dated January twenty-fifth, sixteen sixty-five. Legend says the name comes from settlers buying the land in exchange for some rum. But as far back as sixteen sixty-three, Native Americans called the area "Navarumsunk," and over the years it was shortened to Rumson. Some sources also point to a Chief Alumson. The area was also known as Black Point, Port Washington, and Oceanic. Rumson became a borough in nineteen oh seven.

stories.title: Golf, Polo and Yachts in One Club
stories.blurb: Rumson Country Club was founded on November twenty-third, nineteen oh eight. It joined three existing clubs into one: the golf club, the polo club, and the yacht club. Its stated aim was the development of outdoor sport and physical exercise and the recreation of its members. The golf course opened in July of nineteen ten, designed by Herbert H. Barker. A fire in nineteen forty-five destroyed the original clubhouse.

stories.title: The First Beach Badges
stories.blurb: Bradley Beach was incorporated on March thirteenth, eighteen ninety-three, and was named for developer James A. Bradley. In the summer of nineteen twenty-nine, the town began issuing metal beach badges, with the year engraved on each one. The borough's history says Bradley Beach was the first town in New Jersey and in the United States to do it. Badges were free to residents and hotel guests. Others who wanted the public beaches were charged a fee for a bath house. Monmouth Timeline calls it the first place in the country to charge sea bathers for beach access.

stories.title: How Ocean Park Became Bradley Beach
stories.blurb: Before it was Bradley Beach, this seaside spot was called Ocean Park. James A. Bradley, a frequent visitor to Ocean Grove, began buying land south of the Grove, then pine forests and sand dunes. William B. Bradner bought a farm across the lake. Observers at the time thought both men were crazy. Bradley patrolled the beaches to make sure bathers were safe. He donated land for churches, public services, and the library, with a ban on selling or making alcohol. Bradner named the land Ocean Park, but the post office confused it with Oceanport. The postmaster reportedly suggested the name Bradley Beach, and the town was named for James A. Bradley.

stories.title: A World Chess Champion Plays at Bradley Beach
stories.blurb: In nineteen twenty-nine, an international world chess tournament was held at a five-hundred-room hotel in Bradley Beach. The thirty-room Bradley Hotel was built next door to take the overflow guests. World champion Alexander Alekhine won the tournament. He scored eight and a half points out of nine, and the American Chess Bulletin reported that he won without losing a single game. The brilliancy prize was funded by S. S. Van Dine, a murder mystery novelist. Alekhine was awarded it for his round eight game against Herman Steiner.

stories.title: The Parade That Made Stephen Crane Famous
stories.blurb: In the summer of eighteen ninety-two, twenty-year-old Stephen Crane was a reporter in Asbury Park. His older brother Townley ran the New-York Tribune's shore office, and Stephen had begun by writing up humdrum doings at Avon-by-the-Sea. On August seventeenth, Crane watched the American Day parade of the Junior Order of United American Mechanics in Asbury Park. His article appeared in the Tribune on August twenty-first. People misread it as an indictment of working men. The Tribune printed an apology and cut ties with Crane, and eventually with Townley too. The Tribune's owner, Whitelaw Reid, was running for vice president with Benjamin Harrison, and it was later said the parade story cost the Republicans the election. Crane went on to write The Red Badge of Courage.

https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/

stories.title: How To Say Avon
stories.blurb: Avon-by-the-Sea sits between Belmar and Bradley Beach. The Asbury Park Press reported in two thousand four that locals pronounce it "Ah-von." It said out-of-towners are more likely to say "Ay-von."

stories.title: The Avon Inn and the Borough
stories.blurb: Batchelor was a tobacco manufacturer from Philadelphia. According to the borough's history, he bought three hundred acres on the Shark River from T. W. Finn for forty-five thousand dollars. The Avon Inn was built in eighteen eighty-three, at the foot of Sylvania Avenue. On March twenty-third, nineteen hundred, the New Jersey Legislature incorporated Avon-by-the-Sea as a borough. It was carved out of part of Neptune City.

stories.title: Where Did "Sea Bright" Come From?
stories.blurb: Sea Bright became a borough on March twenty-first, eighteen eighty-nine, formed from part of Ocean Township. Nobody agrees on the name. Some credit Martha Bayard Stevens. Others say it was named for a Sea Bright in England, though there is no evidence such a place exists. A nineteen sixty Red Bank Register article said Native Americans once called it Nauvoo, meaning bright sea. But historian George Moss wrote that Nauvoo was not a Native American word at all, but Sephardic Hebrew for "beautiful or pleasant place." In eighteen seventy, Swedish fishermen began using Sea Bright, pulling their boats on rollers across the dunes to save eight miles of travel down the river.

https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/

stories.title: A Farm Becomes a Borough
stories.blurb: In the eighteen thirties, Abner Allen cleared trees beside the northeast side of Deal Lake to create a farm. The Allens ran a successful boarding house in the original farmhouse. The Spier family owned a large piece of land next to the Allen farm. By the end of the eighteen hundreds, the area had restaurants, a blacksmith shop, a livery stable, a flower shop, greenhouses, grocery stores, and a real estate agency. The community was named for Abner Allen. It became a borough on April twenty-sixth, eighteen ninety-seven, from part of Ocean Township. Railroad access from New York made it a popular summer destination in the early nineteen hundreds.

stories.title: Gentleman Jim Trains at the Shore
stories.blurb: On June seventeenth, eighteen ninety-two, boxer James "Gentleman Jim" Corbett arrived in Asbury Park to train for the "Fight of the Century" against heavyweight champion John L. Sullivan. His manager, William Brady, chose a cottage in Loch Arbour as his residence and training headquarters. Corbett rose around seven, took a five-mile run, and was fond of handball. He did very little ocean bathing. To offset costs, Brady staged exhibitions in theaters in Red Bank and Long Branch. Sullivan had been champion for ten years. On September seventh, eighteen ninety-two, in New Orleans, Corbett beat him in twenty-one rounds. Sullivan said, "If I had to get licked, I'm glad I got licked by an American."

https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/

stories.title: America's Greatest Aviation Meet
stories.blurb: In August of nineteen ten, the Aero and Motor Club of Asbury Park sponsored "America's Greatest Aviation Meet" on open land in what is now Interlaken. It began on August tenth and offered twenty thousand dollars in prize money. The Wright brothers' planes were flown by other pilots, and the Wrights were there as observers and organizers. On the first day, one plane crashed into the grandstand and injured eleven people, the first crash in aviation history to involve spectators. The meet also saw the first night flight. And on August twentieth, Frank Coffyn flew about a mile, landed, and delivered a letter to a civic leader, who replied. Monmouth Timeline calls it the first air mail delivery in the United States. The show officially closed on August twenty-seventh because of bad weather.

stories.title: A Doctor's Swiss Farm
stories.blurb: The borough's history page says a Boston physician and his wife bought a 364-acre tract in 1888. <short pause> It says they named their farm after a peninsula in Switzerland between two lakes. <short pause> It says that in 1890, he formed a land company to turn the farm into an exclusive residential community. <short pause> It says the cross streets are named for islands off the coast of Scotland. <short pause> A Monmouth County timeline says the borough was formed in 1922.

stories.title: A River, a Millstone and Nine Villages
stories.blurb: Millstone Township was formed on February twenty-eighth, eighteen forty-four, from parts of Freehold Township and Upper Freehold Township. It is named for the Millstone River. The township's history says the Lenape first called the river Mattawong, and early settlers renamed it. Monmouth Timeline says the name comes from an incident in which a millstone was dropped into it. In its early days the township had nine villages: Cars Tavern, Holmeson, Smithburg, Sweetman, Bergen Mills, Bairdsville, Stone Tavern, Clarksburg and Perrineville. Only Clarksburg and Perrineville remain. Clarksburg is said to have been settled before the Revolution by an English tanner named Clark. And John Perrine bought a large tract north of it.

stories.title: South Belmar Becomes Lake Como
stories.blurb: In nineteen twenty-four, a small area was carved out of Wall Township and became the borough of South Belmar. It sits between Belmar to the north and Spring Lake to the south, and covers about one third of a square mile. Eighty years later, on November second, two thousand four, voters approved changing the name to Lake Como. It took effect on January fourth, two thousand five. Fast Company reported that the town hoped the new name would set it apart from Belmar, the larger summer party spot nearby.

stories.title: Rather Be Their Own Town
stories.blurb: The borough master plan says the borough was created on May 6, 1924, by referendum. <short pause> It says 152 voters favored separating from Wall Township and 115 were opposed. <short pause> A local blog says the independence movement began in late 1922, led by a large landowner who did not think he was getting value for his real estate taxes. <short pause> The master plan says the first mayor named three needs: sanitation, street repairs, and parks. <short pause> It says the lakeshore was not made into a park until 1950 and was dedicated as a memorial to those who died in service.

stories.title: Walnford, the Mill on Crosswicks Creek
stories.blurb: In Upper Freehold Township, on Crosswicks Creek, sits Walnford, a rare central New Jersey milling and farming complex. Its manor house is a Georgian style home from seventeen seventy-three. The New Jersey Historic Trust calls its flour mill one of the best examples of a millstone flour mill in the eastern United States. The mill ran continuously from the eighteenth century into the early nineteen hundreds. Today, Historic Walnford is run by the Monmouth County Park System, and shows over two hundred years of history through the Waln family. It is one of the historic sites along the twenty-four mile Upper Freehold Historic Farmland Scenic Byway.

stories.title: The Township That Wanted to Be First
stories.blurb: Aberdeen Township used to be called Matawan Township, and that caused confusion with Matawan Borough next door. On November eighth, nineteen seventy-seven, residents voted to change the township's name, to give their community an identity of its own. They chose Aberdeen. Officials believed the new name would draw attention, because it is listed first alphabetically among New Jersey's five hundred sixty-six municipalities.

stories.title: The Borough That Lost Its Shore
stories.blurb: Neptune City was incorporated as a borough on October fourth, eighteen eighty-one. It was named for Neptune, the Roman water deity, and its location on the Atlantic Ocean. The original borough was bigger. It included all of present-day Neptune City, plus what is now Avon-by-the-Sea and the southern part of Bradley Beach. On March twenty-third, nineteen hundred, a bill created the Borough of Avon-by-the-Sea. Then, on March thirteenth, nineteen oh seven, the eastern part of Neptune City was annexed to Bradley Beach.

stories.title: The Universal Nightshirt
stories.blurb: The first factory in Neptune City was Steiner and Son's Pajama Factory, built in eighteen ninety-one on land donated by James A. Bradley. Immanuel Steiner had been a silk dealer in Austria. After he emigrated to New York City in the late eighteen sixties, he began making pajamas and nightgowns. With his sons Edwin and Clarence, he built a flagship factory at Fourth and Railroad Avenue, now Memorial Drive. It cost seventeen thousand, five hundred ninety dollars to build. Its flagship product, "The Universal Nightshirt," became enormously popular throughout the country.

stories.title: Fifty Cents From Battery Park
stories.blurb: Keansburg Amusement Park is described as the oldest amusement park in New Jersey. In nineteen oh four, founder William Gehlhaus and his associates bought waterfront property to build a summer resort. The first ride was a steam ferry. It brought people over from New York, and the idea was to sell them beachfront property. By nineteen ten, the Keansburg Steamboat Company offered New Yorkers a fifty-cent round trip from Battery Park to the boardwalk and its new attractions. The Gehlhaus family has been there ever since, and the park is now owned by William Gehlhaus's grandsons.

stories.title: The Spook House at Keansburg
stories.blurb: At Keansburg Amusement Park, the Spook House was a dark ride built by the Pretzel Amusement Ride Company. It opened in nineteen thirty-one. The park describes it as one of the oldest operating dark rides in the world up until Hurricane Sandy. In two thousand twelve, Sandy damaged the ride and it was taken apart. The park has since said it is trying to refurbish it. After the storm, the parks reopened following a great deal of teamwork and repairs.

stories.title: Hurricane Donna and the Keansburg Waterfront
stories.blurb: Tourists from New York City ferried over to Keansburg to spend a weekend or a summer vacation. Then, in nineteen sixty, Hurricane Donna wiped out much of the waterfront area. In nineteen sixty-nine, the borough spent seven point nine million dollars on the Bayshore Hurricane Protection Plan. It was developed with state and federal funding and the Army Corps of Engineers. The plan made the beaches bigger to protect against future storms.

stories.title: The Summer White House of 1916
stories.blurb: In the presidential campaign of nineteen sixteen, President Woodrow Wilson used a mansion in West Long Branch as his summer White House. It was called Shadow Lawn, a fifty-two-room wood-frame house first built in nineteen oh three for John A. McCall, president of the New York Life Insurance Company. Its owner in nineteen sixteen, Joseph B. Greenhut, head of a New York department store known as "The Big Store," loaned it to the president. Wilson used it from September first to November eighth, and planned many aspects of his reelection campaign from there.
stories.flag: Single source: only one source confirms the details in this story.

stories.title: The Mansion That Burned and Rose Again
stories.blurb: In nineteen twenty-seven, the original Shadow Lawn mansion was destroyed by fire, shortly after one million dollars had been spent renovating it. Its owners, Woolworth company president Hubert Parson and his wife Maysie, built a replacement. The architects were Horace Trumbauer and his assistant Julian Abele, and the new mansion was built with steel and concrete to be fireproof. It has one hundred thirty rooms and cost more than ten million dollars. In nineteen thirty-nine the mansion passed into municipal ownership. In nineteen fifty-five, Monmouth Junior College bought it for three hundred fifty thousand dollars. And in nineteen eighty-one, scenes for the movie Annie were filmed there.

stories.title: The Township That Once Had the Coastline
stories.blurb: The Township of Ocean was created on February twenty-first, eighteen forty-nine, by an act of the New Jersey Legislature. It was part of Shrewsbury Township, which was divided into two townships. Its original map shows a footprint covering all the land from Sea Bright south to the Shark River, and west to take in Eatontown and Neptune. Its boundaries once embraced sixteen of its neighboring communities and included much of Monmouth County's coastline. Today it covers eleven point one square miles, and is officially called the Township of Ocean, to avoid confusion with Ocean Township in Ocean County.

stories.title: The Night Spring Lake Heights Broke Away
stories.blurb: In the nineteen twenties, residents of the Como and Villa Park sections of Wall Township wanted a new borough of their own. Like their neighbors in Sea Girt, Manasquan, Spring Lake, and Belmar, they were disenchanted with Wall Township's ability to provide adequate services. They held weekly meetings, and card parties and dances to raise money. In March of nineteen twenty-seven, a bill to create a new borough passed the State Senate and was signed by Governor Moore. On May third, nineteen twenty-seven, voters approved it, two hundred eighty to two hundred thirty-eight. After the count, there were fireworks, bells, horns, bonfires and car parades. On May thirty-first, the new Borough of Spring Lake Heights elected its first mayor, Roderick Allgor.

stories.title: The Mud That Made Farms Rich
stories.blurb: Farmingdale's Main Street began as an Indian path toward the Manasquan River. In eighteen thirty, workers building a dam on the Manasquan River discovered marl, a loose, earthy material formed from decomposing prehistoric marine life. Marl had been used as fertilizer since the seventeen hundreds. The deposit was about four miles long and triangular, centered on Farmingdale, which was then called Marsh's Bog. Great amounts were dug out. A writer in eighteen sixty said the marl had made what was once a very poor section of Monmouth County one of the most fertile. Farmingdale itself started with two stores, two taverns, and ten to twelve homes.

stories.title: From a Thousand Square Miles to Almost Nothing
stories.blurb: When Shrewsbury Township was formed in sixteen ninety-three, it was named for Shrewsbury, England, and covered almost one thousand square miles. It stretched from the Navesink River south to include all of present-day Ocean County, and from the Atlantic Ocean west to the present Monmouth County line. In seventeen fifty, Stafford Township was formed, and took most of present-day Ocean County. Over the years, seventy-four new municipalities were created from its former land. What is left today covers just point oh nine seven square miles, and is New Jersey's smallest municipality by area.

stories.title: The Candy Plant on High Street
stories.blurb: In nineteen forty-one, Forrest Mars and Bruce Murrie debuted a candy-coated chocolate that began as a military ration. It was first made in Newark. The company needed more room, so it broke ground in Hackettstown in nineteen fifty-seven. The plant opened in nineteen fifty-eight. nj.com reported that some of the same chocolate-smoothing machines from nineteen forty-one are still in use, brought from Newark. The New Jersey Herald said the plant is the world's largest producer of Peanut M&M's. In Hackettstown, the street signs and benches carry the M&M logo.

stories.title: The State's First Fish Hatchery
stories.blurb: New Jersey's first state fish hatchery was built in Hackettstown in nineteen twelve. It began by raising baby brook trout. A year later, rainbow and brown trout were added. In nineteen fourteen, it began raising trout big enough to be released for anglers. Today, it is the Charles O. Hayford State Fish Hatchery. On the Water magazine reported in twenty sixteen that according to its superintendent, no other hatchery in the country raises as many species of fish.

It was named to mark the hundredth anniversary of Methodism in America. The first building was dedicated on September ninth, eighteen seventy-four. The Hackettstown Historical Society says that on October thirty-first, eighteen ninety-nine, the building burned to the ground. It was rebuilt over two years and reopened in nineteen oh one.

stories.title: The Moravian Village Planned From Scratch
stories.blurb: Hope, in Warren County, is one of the earliest planned communities in the country. German Moravians established it in seventeen sixty-nine. The New York Times reported that the church bought a thousand acres and sent members from Bethlehem, Pennsylvania. The township says the early plans showed streets, homes, wells, businesses, farms, a school, a tavern, and a church. The Library of Congress dates the Moravian grist mill to seventeen seventy. The Times said the village did not prosper, and in eighteen oh eight, the land was sold and most of the settlers left.

stories.title: The Piano Man of Washington
stories.blurb: In the eighteen seventies, Daniel Beatty of Washington, New Jersey, was selling pianos and organs by mail order. He was among the first makers to do it. By the eighteen eighties, his company boasted that its factory was the largest in existence, with seven hundred forty-four hands. Whelan, a historian writing for WFMZ, says Beatty was elected mayor three times. In eighteen ninety-four, a federal court in Vermont heard a motion about an indictment against him for using the mail to defraud. It concerned a circular for a parlor organ offered for thirty-three dollars. The court record we read does not say how the case ended.
stories.flag: Public court record: an indictment is an accusation, not a finding. The opinion read does not state how the case ended.
music: Enter the Maze by Kevin MacLeod (incompetech.com), CC BY 4.0
https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/

stories.title: The Furnace That Fired Up Hot Blast
stories.blurb: The town of Oxford grew up around an iron furnace. It was established in seventeen forty-one and made its first pig iron in seventeen forty-three. It produced firebacks, nails, stoves, and iron pots. Wikipedia says that in eighteen thirty-four, the furnace manager, William Henry, made the first practical use in the United States of hot blast technology. Wikipedia says the change raised production by nearly ten percent, and a hot blast oven added in eighteen thirty-five raised it by nearly forty.
stories.flag: SINGLE: the hot blast "first practical use in the United States" claim and the production gains come only from Wikipedia.
music: River of Io by Kevin MacLeod (incompetech.com), CC BY 4.0
https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/

stories.title: The Courthouse Town
stories.blurb: Newton was chosen as the seat of Sussex County on December twelfth, seventeen sixty-one. The land for the courthouse was deeded by Jonathan Hampton. He also surveyed a town plot with lots for a parsonage, an academy, a meeting house, a public green, and a burial ground. The NJ Skylands site says the first courthouse, built in seventeen sixty-five, burned and was replaced by the Greek Revival courthouse of eighteen forty-eight. The railroad arrived in eighteen fifty-four. In the year eighteen seventy-three, that is, eighteen seventy-three, the Merriam Shoe Factory brought the modern factory system to Sussex County.
stories.flag: SINGLE: the 1765 courthouse burning and the 1848 replacement come only from NJ Skylands.
music: Ebbs and Flows by Kevin MacLeod (incompetech.com), CC BY 4.0
https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/

stories.title: The Newton Theatre
stories.blurb: A local performing arts center says the Newton Theatre was built starting in January 1923 in a stadium style to seat 1,000 patrons. <short pause> It says it used 50 tons of steel provided by the Submarine Boat Corporation of Newark. <short pause> It gives the official opening date as May 15th, 1924. <short pause> It says the theatre reopened on May 16th, 2008, showing first-run movies and classics.
music: Habanera by Kevin MacLeod (incompetech.com), CC BY 4.0
https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/

stories.title: The Lake That Canal Builders Raised
stories.blurb: Lake Hopatcong was not always one lake. There were two glacial lakes about two miles apart called Great Pond and Little Pond. Around seventeen sixty-four, a dam for an iron forge raised the water about six feet. By about eighteen thirty-one, the Morris Canal Company had built its own dam. The lake sits at the highest point of the canal system. The water eventually rose twelve feet above the natural level of Great Pond. Little Pond was swallowed into the larger lake. The Borough of Hopatcong's history page agrees the natural lake was about twelve feet lower than today.
music: Thunderbird by Kevin MacLeod (incompetech.com), CC BY 4.0
https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/

stories.title: The Tudor Mansion in Allamuchy
stories.blurb: Rutherfurd Hall in Allamuchy is an eighteen-thousand-square-foot Tudor mansion. The architect was Whitney Warren. It was built for Winthrop Rutherfurd between nineteen oh three and nineteen oh five and has thirty-eight rooms. The family's farms in Warren and Sussex counties spanned more than six thousand acres by nineteen oh six. In nineteen fifty, the Daughters of Divine Charity bought the house and called it Villa Madonna. The township school board bought it in two thousand eight. It is now a museum on the state and national registers of historic places.
music: Water Droplets on the River by Kevin MacLeod (incompetech.com), CC BY 4.0
https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/

stories.title: The Village the Canal Built
stories.blurb: Waterloo Village, in Byram, grew up around the Morris Canal. <short pause> The National Register says the opening of the canal in the early eighteen thirties essentially created the village. <short pause> Before that, an iron forge had been working there since about seventeen sixty. <short pause> The State Park Service says the Smith Store, from eighteen thirty-one, was built into the canal's embankment so boats and wagons could load and unload. <short pause> It calls Waterloo the only place where you can stroll a small village on the bank of the Morris Canal. <short pause> The canal was dismantled in about nineteen twenty-four.
stories.flag: Single source (NJ Division of Parks and Forestry) for the Smith Store being built into the canal embankment and for the "only village" claim.
music: Wholesome by Kevin MacLeod (incompetech.com), CC BY 4.0
https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/

stories.title: The Lost Hamlet on the Canal
stories.blurb: A Sussex County historical marker describes a lost hamlet along a canal. <short pause> It says the remains lie along the Morris Canal towpath as an example of mid-19th century industrialization. <short pause> It lists the footings of a footbridge over the canal, a foundation for a house where goods were stored from about 1834, and the hamlet's shipping port. <short pause> It says that in 1860, the hamlet included several dwellings, a mansion, and a boarding house for workers. <short pause> It also lists an acid works, a sawmill, a flax factory, a weaver, and several stores.
stories.flag: Single source: Sussex County marker, Lost Hamlet of Byram (marker says "storehouse foundation", Stourport shipping port).
music: Meditation Impromptu 02 by Kevin MacLeod (incompetech.com), CC BY 4.0
https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/

stories.title: Edison's Mine on Sparta Mountain
stories.blurb: In seventeen seventy-two, iron ore was discovered on a mountain above Sparta. <short pause> Mining followed. <short pause> Sparta's historical marker says Thomas Edison operated an innovative iron mine there from eighteen eighty-nine to eighteen ninety-nine, within an electrified worker village. <short pause> Explore North Jersey says he founded the Edison Mines on Sparta Mountain in eighteen ninety-one. <short pause> It says his goal was to automate much of the work with powerful electromagnets. <short pause> The ore traveled by the Ogden Mine Railroad to the Morris Canal at Lake Hopatcong.
stories.flag: Dates differ: the township marker says 1889 to 1899, Explore North Jersey says 1891. Both are attributed.
music: AhDah by Kevin MacLeod (incompetech.com), CC BY 4.0
https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/

stories.title: The Making of Lake Mohawk
stories.blurb: The Lake Mohawk Country Club says the Arthur D. Crane Company, a developer of lake communities, set out to create the largest man-made private lake. <short pause> The Sussex County Historical Society says the company acquired 2,600 acres of farmland at the headwaters of a river, mostly in the township. <short pause> The club says that on August 26, 1926, the chief engineer closed a bronze valve in the dam's core wall. <short pause> It says that on March 17, 1928, he used his boot to swish the lake's water over the spillway's rim to rejoin the river.
stories.flag: The two sources give 1925 and 1924 for the land purchase, so no purchase year is given. The river is the Wallkill River.
music: Swimmey Texture by Kevin MacLeod (incompetech.com), CC BY 4.0
https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/

stories.title: The Monument on the Highest Point in New Jersey
stories.blurb: High Point Monument stands on the highest point in New Jersey, eighteen hundred and three feet above sea level, in Wantage. <short pause> The granite obelisk is two hundred and twenty feet tall. <short pause> Construction began in nineteen twenty-eight, and it was dedicated on June twenty-first, nineteen thirty. <short pause> Colonel and Mrs. Anthony Kuser erected it. <short pause> Its plaque honors New Jersey heroes in all wars. <short pause> New Jersey Skylands calls their gift of the surrounding land the largest land donation in the history of the state parks.
music: Sleep and Then by Kevin MacLeod (incompetech.com), CC BY 4.0
https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/

stories.title: A General Store That Grew Into a Zoo
stories.blurb: In nineteen twenty-seven, Ralph and Elizabeth Space bought a quarter acre in Beemerville, in Sussex County. <short pause> It started as a general store, a repair shop and a shelter for wild animals. <short pause> It grew into Space Farms Zoo and Museum, which calls itself New Jersey's largest combined zoo and museum. <short pause> The Space family says Goliath, listed by Guinness World Records, lived there from nineteen sixty-seven to nineteen ninety-one.
music: Brittle Rille by Kevin MacLeod (incompetech.com), CC BY 4.0
https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/

stories.title: The Iron Town on the Morris Canal
stories.blurb: Stanhope began as a small forge town in the late seventeen hundreds. <short pause> It grew into an iron manufacturing community. <short pause> The borough says iron was made there for about one hundred and forty years. <short pause> The Morris Canal flowed through the heart of town. <short pause> By the early nineteen hundreds the iron works were under the control of the Singer Manufacturing Company of Elizabeth. <short pause> Stanhope had been part of Byram Township until it became its own borough in nineteen oh four. <short pause> The borough says iron making there was over by about nineteen twenty-five.
music: Truth of the Legend by Kevin MacLeod (incompetech.com), CC BY 4.0
https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/

stories.title: The Turntable at the End of the Line
stories.blurb: In eighteen sixty-nine, the Sussex Railroad was completed to Branchville, and the first passenger train arrived on July third. <short pause> The borough's historical marker credits the effort of William H. Bell. <short pause> At the end of the line stood a fifty-seven-foot turntable, used to turn locomotives by hand. <short pause> The last passenger train left Branchville on July tenth, nineteen sixty-six. <short pause> The station was destroyed by a winter storm in nineteen ninety-four.
music: Big Mojo by Kevin MacLeod (incompetech.com), CC BY 4.0
https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/

stories.title: From Brantown to Branchville
stories.blurb: Branchville was once known as Brantown for its mills. <short pause> Sussex County says a settler built the first mill there around sixteen ninety. <short pause> In seventeen ninety-three, James Haggerty bought the land and built more mills. <short pause> In eighteen twenty-one, a schoolmaster named Samuel Bishop gave the place the name Branchville. <short pause> The post office opened in eighteen twenty-four. <short pause> Branchville was incorporated as a borough on March ninth, eighteen ninety-eight.
stories.flag: Single source (Sussex County) for the settler and mill details. The 1821 naming is also in the borough master plan.
music: Industrious Ferret by Kevin MacLeod (incompetech.com), CC BY 4.0
https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/

stories.title: The Horse Show That Became the State Fair
stories.blurb: The Sussex County Farm and Horse Show began in Branchville in nineteen nineteen, as a three-day horse show. <short pause> The fairgrounds' own history says the show was held in Augusta in nineteen twenty-four, and moved to a private track in Branchville in nineteen twenty-six. <short pause> It was incorporated on April twenty-sixth, nineteen forty. <short pause> It was not held from nineteen forty-two to nineteen forty-five, because of World War Two. <short pause> In nineteen fifty-five, Hurricane Connie hit Branchville during the fair. <short pause> In nineteen sixty-three the directors bought a site in Augusta, and new fairgrounds were dedicated in nineteen seventy-six. <short pause> In nineteen ninety-nine the show added the name New Jersey State Fair.
stories.flag: Single source (the fairgrounds' own history page) for the 1924 to 1999 details. The 1919 start is in both sources.
music: Cheery Monday by Kevin MacLeod (incompetech.com), CC BY 4.0
https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/

stories.title: The Dam That Was Never Built
stories.blurb: After hurricanes in August nineteen fifty-five, Congress had the Army Corps of Engineers study dams on the Delaware River. <short pause> One would have stood at Tocks Island. <short pause> The National Park Service says its reservoir would have been about forty miles long. <short pause> Some six hundred families and property owners would have had to be displaced. <short pause> The Walpack Historical Society says most of Walpack was bought by the Army Corps for the project. <short pause> In nineteen seventy-five, the Delaware River Basin Commission voted to shelve the dam. <short pause> The land went to the National Park Service and became the Delaware Water Gap National Recreation Area.
music: Past Sadness by Kevin MacLeod (incompetech.com), CC BY 4.0
https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/

stories.title: The Cement That Built Yankee Stadium
stories.blurb: In eighteen ninety-nine, Thomas Edison founded the Edison Portland Cement Company in New Village, in Franklin Township. <short pause> Warren County Heritage says its production had the first long rotating kilns in the world, as tall as one hundred and fifty feet. <short pause> The company supplied cement for the original Yankee Stadium, built in nineteen twenty-two. <short pause> The Express-Times reported that the stadium used one hundred and eighty thousand bags of it. <short pause> Edison licensed his kilns to other manufacturers.
music: Wepa by Kevin MacLeod (incompetech.com), CC BY 4.0
https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/

stories.title: The Concrete Mile
stories.blurb: About three miles from the Edison cement plant is a stretch of road called the Concrete Mile. <short pause> Warren County Heritage says it was built in nineteen twelve with Edison Portland Cement. <short pause> It calls it the first concrete highway in New Jersey and one of the first in the United States. <short pause> The Express-Times reported that parts of the original cement roadbed are still in today's Route fifty-seven. <short pause> Another slab is on display at the Edison Museum in West Orange.
stories.flag: Both sources are local summaries; the "first" claims are attributed to Warren County Heritage.
music: Sauropod Spotting by Kevin MacLeod (incompetech.com), CC BY 4.0
https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/

stories.title: The Borough Named for a Cement Works
stories.blurb: The borough of Alpha was formerly known as Vulcanite. <short pause> The borough says that at the time of the Blizzard of eighteen eighty-eight, there were only seven houses in what is now Alpha. <short pause> After a referendum on May thirty-first, nineteen eleven, the Legislature incorporated it as a borough on June twenty-sixth. <short pause> Governor Woodrow Wilson signed the act. <short pause> The borough was named for the Alpha Cement Works. <short pause> Less than two years later, it got a streetcar line from Phillipsburg and electric street lights.
music: Townie Loop by Kevin MacLeod (incompetech.com), CC BY 4.0
https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/

stories.title: The Canal Climbs a Hill at Plane Ten West
stories.blurb: The Morris Canal was begun in eighteen twenty-five and ran for one hundred and nine miles. <short pause> The State Historic Trust says it used inclined planes to climb the heights that locks could not reach. <short pause> Inclined Plane Ten West, in Warren County, was finished around eighteen thirty-one. <short pause> It overcame a forty-four-foot change in elevation. <short pause> New Jersey Skylands says the area holds remnants of the canal's locks and planes near its western end. <short pause> The canal operated until nineteen twenty-four, and Warren County later bought the site.
music: Silver Flame by Kevin MacLeod (incompetech.com), CC BY 4.0
https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/

stories.title: The Last Underground Mine in New Jersey
stories.blurb: The Sterling Hill mine, in Ogdensburg, was the last working underground mine in New Jersey. <short pause> The New Jersey Zinc Company consolidated the properties in eighteen ninety-seven. <short pause> The mine reached a depth of twenty-six hundred and seventy-five feet and had thirty-five miles of tunnels. <short pause> It closed in nineteen eighty-six. <short pause> The borough took the property for back taxes, and in nineteen eighty-nine two brothers, Richard and Robert Hauck, bought it at auction. <short pause> It is now a museum, which says it has the largest collection of fluorescent minerals in the world.
music: The Path of the Goblin King v2 by Kevin MacLeod (incompetech.com), CC BY 4.0
https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/

stories.title: Sterling Hill by the Numbers
stories.blurb: The Sterling Hill Mining Museum says the mine closed in 1986 after more than 138 years of almost continuous production. <short pause> It says the mine yielded more than 11 million tons of zinc ore. <short pause> It says the ore averaged more than 20% zinc and was worked to a depth of 2,550 feet. <short pause> It says the workings totaled more than 35 miles in length. <short pause> Wikipedia says it became a museum in 1989 and was added to the National Register of Historic Places on September 3, 1991.
music: Trouble with Tribals by Kevin MacLeod (incompetech.com), CC BY 4.0
https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/

stories.title: New Jersey's First State Park
stories.blurb: Swartswood Lake was purchased in nineteen fourteen for public enjoyment. <short pause> The state established Swartswood State Park the next year, in nineteen fifteen. <short pause> The New Jersey Herald called it New Jersey's first state park when it marked the hundredth birthday in twenty fifteen. <short pause> Wikipedia says it was the first the state established for recreation. <short pause> In the early nineteen hundreds the lake was a resort. <short pause> Stillwater Township's open space plan lists popular hotels such as the Northshore Inn, the Club Casino and the Dove Island Inn.
music: Lotus by Kevin MacLeod (incompetech.com), CC BY 4.0
https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/

stories.title: The Iron Works the Congress Seized
stories.blurb: The Andover Iron Company was formed in seventeen fifty-eight. <short pause> It built an iron furnace in what is now Andover Borough in seventeen sixty. <short pause> The Sussex County historical marker says slaves and indentured servants were employed to extract and process the ore. <short pause> It says the mines, forges and furnaces were confiscated by an Act of the Continental Congress on January fifteenth, seventeen seventy-eight, because the owners were loyal to the British Crown. <short pause> The marker also says George Washington's encampment at Morristown was in part to protect these works.
stories.flag: Single source (the Sussex County marker text) for the Congress seizure and the Washington claim. Marker text is attributed.
music: Shadowlands 2 - Bridge by Kevin MacLeod (incompetech.com), CC BY 4.0
https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/

stories.title: The Railroad That Cut Through the Mountains
stories.blurb: The Lackawanna Cutoff was built by the Delaware, Lackawanna and Western Railroad between nineteen oh eight and nineteen eleven. <short pause> It ran about twenty-eight miles west from near Lake Hopatcong. <short pause> Frelinghuysen Township says the high, raised embankment runs straight through the center of the township. <short pause> The township says it was once ranked a wonder of the world. <short pause> Sussex County calls it an engineering marvel, with deep cuts, tall fills and two large viaducts. <short pause> American Rails says the bridges were arched designs of reinforced concrete.
stories.flag: Sources differ on the finish year (1911 or 1912), so no finish year is given. The 1908 to 1911 construction span is from the Cut-Off history site and the Sussex County fact sheet.
music: Hiding Your Reality by Kevin MacLeod (incompetech.com), CC BY 4.0
https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/

stories.title: The Village Once Called Log Gaol
stories.blurb: The township of Frelinghuysen says its early history centers on the village of Johnsonburg. <short pause> It says that in seventeen fifty-three, Johnsonburg was an important stagecoach stop, and became the county seat, with the county court and jail. <short pause> That is why its first name was Log Gaol. <short pause> In nineteen eleven the Lackawanna railroad opened a station there. <short pause> The township says that was vitally important to dairy farmers, who shipped milk and dairy products east to Newark and New York City.
stories.flag: Single source: the Frelinghuysen Township history page.
music: Ishikari Lore by Kevin MacLeod (incompetech.com), CC BY 4.0
https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/

stories.title: From Ludlum's Mill to Lafayette
stories.blurb: The village of Lafayette was known as Bail's Mill during the American Revolution, when there was only a mill and a dwelling. <short pause> The Union Turnpike was chartered in eighteen oh four and ran through the middle of the hamlet. <short pause> Until eighteen twenty-five it was called Ludlum's Mill, after the mill's owner, James Ludlum. <short pause> It was then renamed for General Lafayette, who had returned to the United States to help celebrate the fiftieth anniversary of the Revolution. <short pause> By eighteen sixty the village had a church, a hotel, a distillery, a foundry and five stores. <short pause> The Sussex Railroad reached Lafayette in eighteen sixty-nine.
music: Celtic Impulse by Kevin MacLeod (incompetech.com), CC BY 4.0
https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/

stories.title: The Lafayette Foundry
stories.blurb: A Sussex County historical marker says the foundry was built in 1836. <short pause> It says the foundry employed many laborers. <short pause> It says its success led to the sale of building lots along the Union Turnpike, now Route 15. <short pause> It says this growth contributed to the establishment of the town by the state legislature on March 20th, 1845. <short pause> It says the foundry business and the population then declined.
stories.flag: Single source: Sussex County marker text (the foundry is the LaFayette Foundry, built by Alexander Boyles).
music: DD Groove by Kevin MacLeod (incompetech.com), CC BY 4.0
https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/

stories.title: From Deckertown to Sussex
stories.blurb: The borough of Sussex was settled by Peter Decker in about seventeen forty-two. <short pause> It was incorporated from Wantage Township as the Borough of Deckertown on October fifteenth, eighteen ninety-one. <short pause> In nineteen oh two the name was changed to Sussex Borough. <short pause> The borough says it was named for the historic county of Sussex in England. <short pause> The borough covers six tenths of a square mile, and is completely surrounded by Wantage Township.
stories.flag: The two sources give different days in March 1902 for the rename, so no day is given.
music: Minstrel Guild by Kevin MacLeod (incompetech.com), CC BY 4.0
https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/

stories.title: The Road Built About Sixteen Fifty
stories.blurb: A historical marker in Montague says Old Mine Road was built about sixteen fifty. <short pause> Warren County Heritage calls it one of the oldest continuously used roads in the United States. <short pause> It says Dutch settlers built it to carry copper from the mines in Pahaquarry. <short pause> The route was one hundred and four miles long. <short pause> The Montague marker also points to Blockhouse Hill, where a blockhouse stood during the French and Indian War. <short pause> It notes the church at Minisink, built in seventeen thirty-seven.
stories.flag: Single source (the marker) for the "about 1650" date and the local landmarks. The Old Mine Road description is in both sources.
music: Eternal Terminal by Kevin MacLeod (incompetech.com), CC BY 4.0
https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/

stories.title: The Church That Went Through Four Names
stories.blurb: Old Greenwich Presbyterian Church, in Stewartsville, says it first gathered in seventeen forty. <short pause> Its earliest record is a call in seventeen thirty-nine for preaching in Mr. Barber's neighborhood. <short pause> The place was also called Mr. Green's Farm, then Green's Ridge, Greenridge and Greenage, until the name became Greenwich. <short pause> The church says the frontier missionary David Brainerd was one of the first ministers to preach in its log church. <short pause> In seventeen seventy-five the congregation built its first stone church at the present site. <short pause> The present, larger church replaced it in eighteen thirty-five.
stories.flag: Single source: the church's own history page.
music: Immersed by Kevin MacLeod (incompetech.com), CC BY 4.0
https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/

stories.title: The Mill Town That Was Moved Back Together
stories.blurb: Millbrook Village sits along Old Mine Road. <short pause> The National Park Service calls it a recreation of a typical nineteenth-century community. <short pause> A National Park Service brochure says that in eighteen thirty-two a farmer named Abram Garis built a grist mill there, along the newly built Columbia-Walpack Turnpike. <short pause> The Park Service says Millbrook was a mill town. <short pause> It says the original grist mill is gone, and another mill was moved in. <short pause> Some of the buildings were moved there from elsewhere in the park.
stories.flag: Single source: National Park Service pages and brochure.
music: Old Road by Kevin MacLeod (incompetech.com), CC BY 4.0
https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/

stories.title: Camp Crystal Lake Is a Scout Camp
stories.blurb: A New Jersey news station says the 1980 film Friday the 13th was shot in and around Hardwick, Blairstown, and Hope in Warren County. <short pause> It says the camp scenes were shot on a working Boy Scout camp in Hardwick. <short pause> It says the camp is still standing and still operates as a summer camp. <short pause> Wikipedia says filming took place in New Jersey in 1979 on an estimated budget of $550,000.
stories.flag: The news station is News 12 New Jersey; the camp is Camp NoBeBoSco. Sources vary on exact 1979 filming dates, so only the year is given.
music: Shamanistic by Kevin MacLeod (incompetech.com), CC BY 4.0
https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/

stories.title: The Changewater Murders of 1843
stories.blurb: In May of 1843, a family was killed in Changewater during a robbery. <short pause> The first body was found on May 2nd. <short pause> In 2017, nj.com named it Warren County's most infamous event. <short pause> Two men were convicted after a lengthy trial. <short pause> Washington Township says they were hanged at the Warren County Courthouse in 1845. <short pause> nj.com gives the date as August 22nd.
stories.sensitive: Heavier story: this one covers deadly violence. No graphic detail, and the victims are not named. Listener discretion advised.
music: Angevin by Kevin MacLeod (incompetech.com), CC BY 4.0
https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/

stories.title: How Brass Castle Got Its Name
stories.blurb: Brass Castle is in the northwest of Washington Township, at the foot of Montana Mountain. <short pause> The township says that, according to local tradition, the village was named for the cabin or castle of Jacob Brass. <short pause> By 1874, it had a school, a sawmill, a gristmill, several blacksmith shops, and about a dozen homes. <short pause> The township says it has grown considerably since 1955 as a suburb of Washington Borough.
stories.flag: SINGLE: township page only. The naming is attributed to local tradition.
music: Healing by Kevin MacLeod (incompetech.com), CC BY 4.0
https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/

stories.title: The Oldest Municipality in Warren County
stories.blurb: The township of Mansfield says it was founded in 1754. <short pause> It calls itself the oldest municipality in Warren County. <short pause> It says Beattystown, first known as Beatty's Mill, was settled at least as early as the 1760s. <short pause> Port Murray was named after a president of the Morris Canal Company. <short pause> The township says Port Murray and Rockport grew as stops on the canal, which was completed in the 1830s. <short pause> Rockport was once home to the state pheasant farm.
stories.flag: SINGLE: township history page only.
music: Beauty Flow by Kevin MacLeod (incompetech.com), CC BY 4.0
https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/

stories.title: The Last Covered Bridge Over the Delaware
stories.blurb: The covered bridge between Columbia, New Jersey and Portland, Pennsylvania opened in 1869. <short pause> The Delaware River Joint Toll Bridge Commission says it was the last wooden covered bridge built across the river between New Jersey and Pennsylvania. <short pause> It says that in 1955, it was the longest wooden covered bridge left in the United States. <short pause> It was destroyed in the Delaware River flood of August 19th, 1955. <short pause> A steel pedestrian bridge was built on its old piers and opened on October 22nd, 1958.
music: Ripples by Kevin MacLeod (incompetech.com), CC BY 4.0
https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/

stories.title: The Township Named for a Royal Governor
stories.blurb: Hardyston Township was formed on February 25th, 1762. <short pause> It was set off from Newton Township by royal charter. <short pause> Wikipedia says it was named for Josiah Hardy, the royal governor of New Jersey from 1761 to 1763. <short pause> The original British spelling was Hardiston. <short pause> It was changed to Hardyston after the Revolutionary War. <short pause> The township says the land was home to the Lenape for thousands of years. <short pause> Franklin and Hamburg were later taken from the township.
music: AngloZulu by Kevin MacLeod (incompetech.com), CC BY 4.0
https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/

stories.title: The Mother Township
stories.blurb: The township says it was formed on February 25th, 1762. <short pause> Wikipedia says it was set off from Newton Township by royal charter and named after Josiah Hardy, the royal governor. <short pause> The township's website says that over time, areas of the township formed their own governments. <short pause> It lists Vernon in 1793, Sparta in 1845, Franklin in 1913, and Hamburg in 1920.
music: Frost Waltz by Kevin MacLeod (incompetech.com), CC BY 4.0
https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/

stories.title: A Name From the Lenape
stories.blurb: A historical marker in Alpha says Pohatcong was first settled in the early 1700s. <short pause> It says farmland and water power drew settlers for gristmills, sawmills, and iron forges. <short pause> The marker says Pohatcong is a Lenape word that may mean "outlet of a stream between two hills." <short pause> The creek is 30.7 miles long. <short pause> Wikipedia says it rises west of Hackettstown and flows southwest to the Delaware River.
stories.flag: SINGLE for the name meaning: marker only, and the marker hedges ("may mean").
music: Dub Eastern by Kevin MacLeod (incompetech.com), CC BY 4.0
https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/

stories.title: The Craft Village in the Water Gap
stories.blurb: Peters Valley School of Craft is in Sandyston Township, inside the Delaware Water Gap National Recreation Area. <short pause> The National Park Service calls it a nonprofit founded in 1970 in partnership with the Park Service. <short pause> The school says the village was a small population center in the 19th century. <short pause> It says a New Jersey map first showed it in 1855. <short pause> The Park Service says the school keeps studios in eight crafts, including blacksmithing and ceramics.
music: Street Party by Kevin MacLeod (incompetech.com), CC BY 4.0
https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/

stories.title: The Township Named for Harmon Shipman
stories.blurb: Harmony Township was incorporated on April 8, 1839. <short pause> Wikipedia and lehighvalleylive.com both say it was named for Harmon Shipman. <short pause> Lehighvalleylive says he was a German settler who bought 200 acres in the township in 1740.
music: Cattails by Kevin MacLeod (incompetech.com), CC BY 4.0
https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/

stories.title: A Township Named for Independence
stories.blurb: Independence Township was formed from Hardwick Township in 1782. <short pause> lehighvalleylive.com says it was named to honor the country's independence from England. <short pause> At that time, the land was still part of Sussex County. <short pause> Warren County later listed it as one of its seven original townships. <short pause> Hackettstown was formed from it in 1853. <short pause> Allamuchy followed in 1873.
music: New Hero in Town by Kevin MacLeod (incompetech.com), CC BY 4.0
https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/

stories.title: Celery, Onions and Black Muck
stories.blurb: Great Meadows in Independence Township was originally called Danville. <short pause> The Ukrainian History and Education Center says it is well known for celery and onion crops. <short pause> It says the soil is a rich black soil known locally as black muck. <short pause> Ukrainian immigrants began arriving in 1906 and later bought farms of their own. <short pause> The center says the farms range from 25 to 600 acres. <short pause> It says St. Nicholas Ukrainian Catholic Church was finished in the spring of 1923.
stories.flag: SINGLE: Ukrainian History and Education Center overview; the earlier name Danville is from the NJ place-name archive.
music: Boogie Party by Kevin MacLeod (incompetech.com), CC BY 4.0
https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/

stories.title: Liberty Splits From Hope
stories.blurb: Liberty Township says it separated from Hope Township in a referendum on March 26, 1926. <short pause> Its newsletter says the name came from that separation. <short pause> Wikipedia lists the township's incorporation as April 30, 1926. <short pause> lehighvalleylive.com also says the township was named after its split from Hope. <short pause> The township was planning a centennial celebration for 2026.
music: Smooth Lovin by Kevin MacLeod (incompetech.com), CC BY 4.0
https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/

stories.title: The Stone Mansion Called The White House
stories.blurb: White Township was incorporated on April 9, 1913, from part of Oxford Township. <short pause> The township says it is the second youngest in Warren County. <short pause> It says it was named for Alexander White. <short pause> The township says he came before 1760 and built a stone mansion called the White House. <short pause> It stood near a place called Roxburg. <short pause> Lehighvalleylive.com says the name is said to come from a family of settlers named White.
music: Ambiment by Kevin MacLeod (incompetech.com), CC BY 4.0
https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/

stories.title: The Church Built Halfway in Tranquility
stories.blurb: Green Township says Tranquility was first known as Kennedy Town. <short pause> It says a disagreement arose over whether to build the Methodist church in Allamuchy or in Kennedy Town. <short pause> The township says a compromise put the church halfway between the two. <short pause> It says the church was named Tranquility to memorialize the agreement. <short pause> The township says Kennedy Town later took the church's name as its own. <short pause> It says nearby Huntsville was once called Pettit's Mills.
stories.flag: SINGLE: township history page only.
music: Impact Andante by Kevin MacLeod (incompetech.com), CC BY 4.0
https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/

stories.title: Green Township Turns Two Hundred
stories.blurb: Green Township was founded on December 27th, 1824. <short pause> It was made from the northern parts of Hardwick and Independence Townships. <short pause> The township says it was named for Ephraim Green, who settled near Greendell in 1770. <short pause> In June of 2024, the Township Journal reported that Green marked its 200th birthday at Green Township Day. <short pause> The township says communities like Tranquility, Huntsville, Greendell, and Yellow Frame keep their own identities.
music: Cruising for Goblins by Kevin MacLeod (incompetech.com), CC BY 4.0
https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/

stories.title: The Two Andovers
stories.blurb: Sussex County has 24 municipalities and only one name is shared. <short pause> The New Jersey Herald says that is Andover Township and Andover Borough. <short pause> The township was founded in 1864. <short pause> The Herald says it took the name of a village that grew around the Andover Iron Works in the 1700s. <short pause> TAPinto says the township first included the borough. <short pause> In 1904, the two split into separate towns.
music: Laserpack by Kevin MacLeod (incompetech.com), CC BY 4.0
https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/

stories.title: The Last Town in Sussex County
stories.blurb: Fredon Township was incorporated on February 24, 1904. <short pause> A historical marker says it became the last town in Sussex County, and the only one with its name in the country. <short pause> The marker says the name was proposed for the nation in the early 1800s and means a place of peace and freedom. <short pause> It says the crossroads called Coursen's Corners became a town center when the Coursen family had a school, a store, and a blacksmith shop there. <short pause> The marker says the Fredon post office ran from 1834 to 1901. <short pause> Historic Stillwater says the railroad tracks became the boundary with Stillwater.
stories.flag: SINGLE for the name meaning and post office dates: the county copy of the township marker only. Incorporation date has two sources.
music: Overheat by Kevin MacLeod (incompetech.com), CC BY 4.0
https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/

stories.title: The Lake That Used to Be Round Pond
stories.blurb: Culver's Lake in Frankford Township was formerly called Round Pond. <short pause> Wikipedia says it is fed by Lake Owassa and Bear Swamp. <short pause> It says the lake is the source of the West Branch of the Paulins Kill. <short pause> Wikipedia says it covers about 555 acres and is up to 50 feet deep. <short pause> It says the lake was used for seasonal recreation in the late 1800s and early 1900s. <short pause> Today it says it is a private year-round community run by the Normanoch Association.
stories.flag: SINGLE: Wikipedia for the lake details; the county plan confirms the two lakes.
music: Beach Party by Kevin MacLeod (incompetech.com), CC BY 4.0
https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/

stories.title: The Sussex County Farm and Horse Show
